The deterministic memory h carries the past; the stochastic latent z is inferred from the observation during training (posterior) and predicted from h alone in imagination (prior). The KL term ties them together; decoders reconstruct the observation and predict the reward.







Scaling to internet video
The Dreamer latents are compact but specific to one domain: Minecraft, or one robot ▶ 45:26. A model of how the visual world moves in general needs internet-scale video ▶ 46:18, and that runs into token counts first ▶ 46:53. Per-frame patches of a 256 by 256 image give 256 tokens; at 20 frames per second, a 10-second clip has 51,200 ▶ 47:41. But video is extremely redundant ▶ 48:38, and tokenizers compress it along three axes ▶ 48:51: spatially (deeper encoders, fewer tokens per frame), temporally (several frames per token, causally if the model must run in a control loop) ▶ 49:30, and adaptively (more tokens for busy scenes, fewer for static ones) ▶ 50:25. Combined 8 times in each spatial direction and 8 times in time, the 51,200 tokens become 100 ▶ 51:41.
Where do actions go in a model trained mostly on video without actions ▶ 52:18? Three answers (Figure 6):

Action-conditioned world models (the Dreamer line) take actions as inputs.
World action models (WAMs) generate future video and actions together as outputs, starting from a pre-trained video model; DreamZero is one ▶ 53:01.
Video action models (VAMs) keep a pre-trained video model frozen and train only a light inverse dynamics model that reads actions off its features, which needs only robot data for the small part; mimic-video is one ▶ 54:10.

Why use expensive video backbones at all ▶ 55:23? A VLA starts from a vision-language model trained on static images and captions: it knows what “cutting a carrot” means but not how a carrot moves when cut, so robot teleoperation data must teach it the dynamics as well as the control ▶ 56:27. A video model has seen how things move; the robot data then only need to teach control. mimic-video reports 10 times better sample efficiency than VLA architectures (from its abstract). Its oracle experiment: an action decoder given the true future frames succeeds almost always, so the bottleneck is the quality of the predicted video, and better video models should directly give better policies ▶ 59:56.
The third toy reproduces both findings. A video model learns from 40 action-free expert videos what the puck does next; an inverse dynamics model learns from \(k\) action-labelled random pushes which push causes a given change. Behavior cloning instead needs \(k\) action-labelled expert transitions. With 25 labels the video model plus decoder succeeds in 100% of runs and behavior cloning in 42%; behavior cloning catches up at 400 labels (Figure 5). Give the decoder the expert’s true next state and it succeeds in about 98% of runs whatever the video model learned; with predicted futures, success goes from 33% with one training video to 98% with 40.

Right: the video model plus decoder with 100 labels, against the number of action-free expert videos, decoding from predicted futures or from the expert’s true next state (oracle).

Do we need pixels at all?
Every approach so far decodes back to pixels somewhere. JEPA models do not: they encode the current frame, predict the embedding of the next frame given the action, encode the real next frame with the same encoder, and minimize the distance between the two embeddings, with no decoder and no pixel loss ▶ 68:50. The catch is collapse: an encoder that maps every frame to the same vector makes the prediction error exactly zero, and gradient descent is happy to find it ▶ 69:53. Remedies include a slowly moving (EMA) copy of the encoder for the targets (V-JEPA 2), a frozen pre-trained encoder (DINO-WM), and a regularizer that forces the embeddings to spread out like a Gaussian (the most recent work the lecture cites) ▶ 70:34.
The second toy shows the trap. Observations are a 16-dimensional view of the puck’s state; a linear encoder maps them to 4-dimensional embeddings, and a linear predictor maps (embedding, push) to the next embedding. Trained on prediction error alone, the embeddings shrink from a spread of 0.68 to 0.067 in 10,000 steps, and are still shrinking; this run has the lowest loss of all variants (0.0019), yet a linear readout recovers only 67% of the puck’s position from them. With a regularizer pulling the embeddings’ covariance to the identity, they use all 4 directions (effective rank 3.97) and the readout recovers 99.9% (Figure 7). The other safeguards also prevent collapse here, but leave the embeddings using about two directions.








Figure 7: The JEPA toy over 10,000 training steps, for five training variants (seed 0). Left: the embeddings’ spread (mean standard deviation per dimension). Right: their effective rank, the number of directions they really use (at most 4).





The lecture closes on its master formula: every family predicts the next state from the current state, an action and a memory, and they differ in how they represent the state, where the actions live, and what data they can use ▶ 71:01.




The puck toy's dream and reality: a run planned entirely inside the learned model, the same pushes on the real table, and a run that looks at the real puck before every replan.

What to watch for. All three runs use the same world model (1,000 transitions, model 0) and the same planner. The blue dream curves over the upper side of the hill and lands exactly on the goal: by its own model’s account the plan is perfect. The orange puck receives the same pushes on the real table. Its path starts close to the dream’s but runs on a slightly wider arc, so every later push, chosen for where the dream puck was, is a little wrong; it passes the goal and ends below it, 0.7 away, with a few wiggles at the end as the remaining pushes, meant to brake at the goal, act on a puck that is elsewhere. The green puck uses the same model but looks before every replan: its path follows almost the orange course, since the real table behaves the same, but each new plan starts from where the puck really is, and it stops on the goal.

title: Week 8 · World Models
text:
Key concepts & formulae
The lecture writes \(s_t\) for the state, \(a_t\) for the action, \(h_t\) for memory and \(z_t\) for a latent; observations are \(o_t\). The ADM book calls the learned transition model \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) and treats model-based reinforcement learning in its chapter on model-based methods.

What a world model is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{policy:}\quad & \pi(a_t \mid s_t, g) \\
\text{world model:}\quad & p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

In words. A policy picks what to do for a goal; a world model predicts what will happen if you do it.
Term by term.

\(g\): the goal, for a VLA a language instruction.
\(p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)\): a distribution, because the same action can have several outcomes. It is the transition model \(P\) of Week 2’s MDP, now learned instead of given.


\[
p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t, h_t)
\tag{2}\]

In words. The next state, predicted from the current state, the action and a memory of the past.
Term by term.

\(h_t\): memory, needed because the robot’s observation is not the full state (Week 7) and because motion is only visible across frames.
The action input is what separates a world model from a video model \(p(\text{video} \mid \text{text})\).



Planning with a model

\[
\begin{aligned}
a^*_{t:t+H-1} &= \arg\min_{a_{t:t+H-1}} \sum_{k=1}^{H} c(\hat s_{t+k}),
\quad \hat s_{t+k} \sim p(\cdot \mid \hat s_{t+k-1}, a_{t+k-1})
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]

In words. Search for the action sequence whose imagined rollout has the lowest cost, execute its first action, observe, and search again.
Term by term.

\(\hat s_t = s_t\): each search starts from the latest real state; that reset is what keeps errors from compounding.
\(c\): the task cost; in the puck toy, the distance to the goal at every step plus the final speed.
The search here is the cross-entropy method: sample sequences from a Gaussian, keep the best, refit the Gaussian to them, repeat (Week 4 used it over single actions).


\[
e_{k+1} \le L\, e_k + \varepsilon
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
e_H \le \varepsilon\, \frac{L^H - 1}{L - 1}
\tag{4}\]

In words. If each predicted step adds a small error \(\varepsilon\), and the dynamics can stretch an existing error by a factor \(L\), the error after \(H\) imagined steps can grow exponentially in \(H\).
Term by term.

\(e_k\): distance between the imagined and the real state after \(k\) steps.
\(L\): how much the (model’s) dynamics can amplify a difference in one step; \(L > 1\) for dynamics that spread nearby states apart.
Why it holds: the next error is the model’s own one-step error plus the old error carried through the dynamics; unroll the recursion and sum the geometric series. With \(L = 1\) the bound is \(\varepsilon H\), linear.
Numeric check: in the puck toy (1,000 transitions) the error grows 38 times from step 4 to step 40, while the horizon grows 10 times (Figure 2).



Latent world models

\[
\begin{aligned}
z_t &= \mathrm{enc}(o_t) \\
p(z_{t+1} \mid a_t, z_t, h_t) &= \textstyle\sum_i \pi_i\, \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma_i^2) \\
a_t &= W [z_t; h_t] + b
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]

In words. A VAE compresses each frame; a recurrent network predicts a mixture of Gaussians over the next latent; a linear controller acts on latent and memory.
Term by term.

\(\pi_i, \mu_i, \sigma_i\): weights, means and spreads of the mixture, output by the recurrent network (here \(\pi_i\) is a mixture weight, not a policy).
\(W, b\): the controller’s only parameters, found by an evolution strategy (CMA-ES) on imagined rollouts.


\[
\begin{aligned}
h_t &= f(h_{t-1}, z_{t-1}, a_{t-1}) \\
z_t &\sim q(z_t \mid h_t, o_t) \;\;\text{(training)}, \qquad z_t \sim p(z_t \mid h_t) \;\;\text{(imagination)} \\
\mathcal{L} &= \textstyle\sum_t \big[ -\log p(o_t \mid h_t, z_t) - \log p(r_t \mid h_t, z_t) \\
&\qquad + \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z_t \mid h_t, o_t) \,\|\, p(z_t \mid h_t)\big) \big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]

In words. A deterministic memory is updated each step; a stochastic latent is inferred from the observation in training and predicted from memory in imagination; the loss reconstructs observations and rewards and keeps the prior close to the posterior.
Term by term.

\(f\): a recurrent cell; \(h_t\) is never sampled, so sampling noise cannot corrupt the memory.
\(q\): the posterior (encoder), which sees the observation; \(p(z_t \mid h_t)\): the prior, which must do without.
KL term: trains the prior to predict what the posterior would have inferred, so imagined latents stay in the region the decoders understand.


\[
\max_\phi\; \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{H-1} \gamma^k \hat r_{t+k} + \gamma^H v_\psi(\hat h_{t+H}, \hat z_{t+H})\Big],
\quad \hat a_{t+k} \sim \pi_\phi(\cdot \mid \hat h_{t+k}, \hat z_{t+k})
\tag{7}\]

In words. Roll the actor out inside the frozen world model for \(H\) steps, add up the imagined rewards and the critic’s estimate of what follows, and improve the actor by backpropagating through the model.
Term by term.

\(\hat r\), \(\hat h\), \(\hat z\): imagined rewards and states; nothing here touches the real environment.
\(v_\psi\): the critic, trained on the same imagined rollouts; it lets a short horizon \(H\) account for the long-term future.
Dreamer uses a \(\lambda\)-weighted mix of such returns; the form above shows the idea.



Video and actions

\[
N_{\text{tokens}} = \underbrace{\frac{H W}{p^2}}_{\text{per frame}} \times \underbrace{f\, T}_{\text{frames}} \;\div\; (c_s^2\, c_t)
\tag{8}\]

In words. Tokens per frame times the number of frames, divided by the tokenizer’s compression in each spatial direction (\(c_s\), applied twice) and in time (\(c_t\)).
Term by term.

\(H, W, p\): image height, width and patch size; \(f\): frames per second; \(T\): seconds.
Numeric check: \(256 \cdot 256 / 16^2 = 256\) tokens per frame, \(\times\, 20 \cdot 10 = 200\) frames, gives 51,200; with \(c_s = c_t = 8\) it becomes 51,200 / 512 = 100.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{WAM:}\quad & p_\theta(o_{t+1:t+k},\, a_{t:t+k-1} \mid o_{\le t}, \ell) \\
\text{VAM:}\quad & \hat o_{t+1:t+k} \sim p_\theta(\cdot \mid o_{\le t}, \ell), \quad a_{t:t+k-1} = g_\psi(o_t, \hat o_{t+1:t+k})
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\]

In words. A world action model generates the next stretch of video and the actions jointly. A video action model generates (or partially generates) the video plan and lets an inverse dynamics model \(g_\psi\) read off the actions.
Term by term.

\(\ell\): the language instruction.
\(g_\psi\): small, trained on robot data only; in the toy, \(k = 1\) and \(g_\psi\) is an MLP of the state and the predicted change.
Both start from a video model pre-trained on internet video, which supplies the dynamics; mimic-video does not even generate the full video, it uses the model’s features part-way through denoising ▶ 62:10.



Predicting embeddings

\[
\begin{aligned}
z_t &= \mathrm{enc}_\theta(o_t), \quad \hat z_{t+1} = \mathrm{pred}(z_t, a_t) \\
\mathcal{L} &= \big\| \hat z_{t+1} - \mathrm{sg}\big[\mathrm{enc}_{\bar\theta}(o_{t+1})\big] \big\|^2
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}\]

In words. Predict the embedding of the next observation; compare it with the actual next observation’s embedding, computed by a target encoder that receives no gradient.
Term by term.

\(\mathrm{sg}\): stop-gradient. \(\bar\theta\): the target encoder’s weights, an EMA of \(\theta\) (V-JEPA 2), or fixed (a frozen encoder).
Without \(\mathrm{sg}\) and a separate target, \(\mathrm{enc}_\theta \equiv 0\) is a perfect solution: collapse.
The regularized alternative keeps \(\bar\theta = \theta\) and adds a penalty such as \(\lambda \|\mathrm{Cov}(z) - I\|^2\), which makes the constant solution costly.
Numeric check: in the toy, stop-gradient alone already prevents collapse (spread 1.28 after 10,000 steps), as does the EMA target (1.26), but only the covariance regularizer uses all 4 directions.

The first samples are random pushes. Refitting the Gaussian to the 20 best moves the whole population towards better plans: the mean cost of the samples falls in every iteration, from 46.3 to 39.1. Six iterations do not make the samples agree, though: their spread shrinks only from 0.50 to 0.39. That is enough for MPC, which executes only the first push and then plans again from a warm start. The mean of the last Gaussian is the plan. CEM needs no gradient of the model, which is why it works equally with the true table and with a learned model.


Example 2: compounding, by hand
A model makes a one-step error of \(\varepsilon = 0.01\), and the dynamics stretch any existing error by \(L = 1.1\) per step. After 20 imagined steps the bound of Equation 4 is \(0.01 \times (1.1^{20} - 1)/0.1 = 0.01 \times 57.3 = 0.57\), against \(0.01 \times 20 = 0.2\) if errors simply added up (\(L = 1\)). After 40 steps the two are \(4.4\) and \(0.4\). With replanning from real observations every step, the horizon that matters is 1, and the bound is \(\varepsilon\).

title: Week 8 · World Models
Week 8 · World Models
text:
Algorithm & code

Planning in a learned model

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def rollout(step, s0, actions) -> Array:
    """States s_0..s_H under an action sequence (n, H, 2) from s0 (n, 4)."""
    states = [s0]
    for t in range(actions.shape[1]):
        states.append(step(states[-1], actions[:, t]))
    return np.stack(states, axis=1)                       # (n, H + 1, 4)

def cost(states) -> Array:
    """Distance to the goal at every step, plus the final speed: (n,)."""
    dist = np.linalg.norm(states[:, 1:, :2] - GOAL, axis=-1)
    return dist.sum(axis=1) + 2 * np.linalg.norm(states[:, -1, 2:], axis=-1)

def cem_plan(step, s0, rng, H=15, n=200, elite=20, iters=6, a_max=A_MAX,
             init=None) -> tuple[Array, float]:
    """Cross-entropy method over action sequences in a (true or learned) model.

    Sample n sequences of H pushes from a Gaussian, roll each out in `step`,
    keep the `elite` cheapest, refit the Gaussian, repeat. Returns the final
    mean sequence (H, 2) and its cost according to `step`.
    """
    mu = np.zeros((H, 2)) if init is None else init.copy()
    std = np.full((H, 2), a_max / 2)
    for _ in range(iters):
        A = np.clip(mu + std * rng.standard_normal((n, H, 2)), -a_max, a_max)
        c = cost(rollout(step, np.repeat(s0[None], n, 0), A))
        best = A[np.argsort(c)[:elite]]
        mu, std = best.mean(axis=0), best.std(axis=0) + 0.05
    return mu, float(cost(rollout(step, s0[None], mu[None]))[0])

def run_mpc(plan_step, rng, T=60, H=15, a_max=A_MAX, look=True, start=None):
    """Model predictive control: plan H steps, execute the first push, repeat.

    look=True: every plan starts from the real puck's state. look=False:
    the agent never looks; it replans from the state its own model
    predicted, so the whole run happens in imagination, and the pushes are
    then replayed on the real table. Returns (real path, imagined path),
    each (T + 1, 4); with look=True the two coincide.
    """
    s0 = START_STATE if start is None else start
    real, imag = [s0.copy()], [s0.copy()]
    prev = None
    for _ in range(T):
        here = real[-1] if look else imag[-1]
        # Warm start from the last plan, shifted by one step.
        init = None if prev is None else np.r_[prev[1:], prev[-1:]]
        prev, _ = cem_plan(plan_step, here, rng, H=H, a_max=a_max, init=init)
        a = prev[0]
        real.append(true_step(real[-1], a))
        guess = plan_step(imag[-1][None], a[None])[0]
        imag.append(real[-1] if look else guess)
    return np.array(real), np.array(imag)


import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from rlc.toys import w08_world as w8

torch.manual_seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Data: random transitions of the page's puck table.
s, a, s2 = (torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32)
            for x in w8.random_transitions(2000, rng))
scale_in = torch.tensor(w8.IN_SCALE, dtype=torch.float32)
delta = s2 - s
scale_out = delta.std(0)

# World model: (state, push) -> change of state, both scaled to unit size.
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(6, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 64),
                      nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 4))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
X = torch.cat([s, a], dim=1) / scale_in
for epoch in range(300):
    for idx in torch.randperm(len(X)).split(256):
        loss = ((model(X[idx]) - delta[idx] / scale_out) ** 2).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()


@torch.no_grad()                     # planning needs no gradients of the model
def step(state, push):
    x = torch.cat([state, push], dim=-1) / scale_in
    return state + model(x) * scale_out


@torch.no_grad()
def cem(state, H=15, n=200, elite=20, iters=6):
    """CEM over push sequences, all n candidates rolled out as one batch."""
    goal = torch.tensor(w8.GOAL, dtype=torch.float32)
    mu, std = torch.zeros(H, 2), torch.full((H, 2), 0.5)
    for _ in range(iters):
        A = (mu + std * torch.randn(n, H, 2)).clamp(-1, 1)   # (n, H, 2)
        x, c = state.expand(n, 4), torch.zeros(n)
        for t in range(H):
            x = step(x, A[:, t])
            c += (x[:, :2] - goal).norm(dim=1)
        best = A[c.argsort()[:elite]]                         # (elite, H, 2)
        mu, std = best.mean(0), best.std(0) + 0.05
    return mu


# Model predictive control on the real (NumPy) table.
state = torch.tensor(w8.START_STATE, dtype=torch.float32)
for t in range(60):
    push = cem(state)[0]
    state = torch.tensor(w8.true_step(state.numpy(), push.numpy()),
                         dtype=torch.float32)
final = (state[:2] - torch.tensor(w8.GOAL, dtype=torch.float32)).norm()
assert final < 0.1, final



The planner never differentiates the model: CEM only needs to evaluate rollouts, so batching all candidates is the main speed-up. Dreamer replaces this search with an actor trained by backpropagating through the model (Equation 7).


Predicting embeddings, and collapse

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def jepa_train(variant, seed, steps=3000, n=512, lr=0.01, tau=0.99,
               lam=1.0) -> dict:
    """Train a linear encoder W and predictor (P_z, P_a) on next-embedding
    error.

    z = o W, prediction = z P_z + a P_a, target z' = o' W_target.
    plain: the target uses W itself and gradients flow into both sides.
    stop-gradient: same W, but the target is treated as a constant.
    EMA target: W_target is a slow moving average of W (no gradient).
    frozen encoder: W stays at its random start; only the predictor learns.
    covariance regularizer: plain, plus lam * ||Cov(z) - I||^2.
    Returns W and the history of the loss, the embeddings' spread and
    their effective rank.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W = rng.standard_normal((OBS_DIM, EMB_DIM)) / np.sqrt(OBS_DIM)
    P_z, P_a = np.eye(EMB_DIM), np.zeros((2, EMB_DIM))
    W_tgt = W.copy()
    hist = {"loss": [], "spread": [], "rank": []}
    for _ in range(steps):
        o, a, o2, _ = jepa_data(n, rng)
        z = o @ W                                      # (n, k)
        target = o2 @ (W if variant in ("plain", "stop-gradient",
                                        "covariance regularizer",
                                        "frozen encoder") else W_tgt)
        r = z @ P_z + a @ P_a - target                 # (n, k) residual
        loss = float((r**2).sum(1).mean())
        dr = 2 * r / n
        dP_z, dP_a = z.T @ dr, a.T @ dr
        dz = dr @ P_z.T                                # through the prediction
        dW = o.T @ dz
        if variant in ("plain", "covariance regularizer"):
            dW -= o2.T @ dr                            # through the target too
        if variant == "covariance regularizer":
            zc = z - z.mean(0)
            C = zc.T @ zc / (n - 1)                    # (k, k)
            loss += lam * float(((C - np.eye(EMB_DIM)) ** 2).sum())
            dW += o.T @ (4 * lam * zc @ (C - np.eye(EMB_DIM)) / (n - 1))
        if variant == "frozen encoder":
            dW = 0 * dW
        W, P_z, P_a = W - lr * dW, P_z - lr * dP_z, P_a - lr * dP_a
        W_tgt = tau * W_tgt + (1 - tau) * W            # used by "EMA target"
        hist["loss"].append(loss)
        hist["spread"].append(float(z.std(0).mean()))
        hist["rank"].append(effective_rank(z))
    return {"W": W, **{k: np.array(v) for k, v in hist.items()}}

def effective_rank(z) -> float:
    """How many directions the embeddings really use: (sum l)^2 / sum l^2
    over the eigenvalues l of their covariance; EMB_DIM if all are equal,
    1 if everything lies on one line."""
    lam = np.clip(np.linalg.eigvalsh(np.cov(z.T)), 0, None)
    return float(lam.sum() ** 2 / (lam**2).sum())


import copy

OBS, EMB = w8.OBS_DIM, w8.EMB_DIM


def train_jepa(target="ema", steps=3000, reg=0.0, tau=0.99):
    """Encoder + predictor on next-embedding error. target: 'same' (gradient
    flows into the target too), 'ema' (slow copy, no gradient)."""
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    enc = nn.Linear(OBS, EMB, bias=False)
    pred = nn.Linear(EMB + 2, EMB, bias=False)
    enc_tgt = copy.deepcopy(enc).requires_grad_(False)
    opt = torch.optim.SGD([*enc.parameters(), *pred.parameters()], lr=0.01)
    data_rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for _ in range(steps):
        o, a, o2, _ = (torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32)
                       for x in w8.jepa_data(512, data_rng))
        z = enc(o)                                         # (B, EMB)
        z_next = enc(o2) if target == "same" else enc_tgt(o2).detach()
        # Squared error summed over the EMB dimensions, averaged over the
        # batch (F.mse_loss would also average over dimensions).
        err = pred(torch.cat([z, a], dim=1)) - z_next
        loss = (err ** 2).sum(dim=1).mean()
        if reg:
            zc = z - z.mean(0)
            cov = zc.T @ zc / (len(z) - 1)
            loss = loss + reg * ((cov - torch.eye(EMB)) ** 2).sum()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        with torch.no_grad():                              # EMA update
            for p_t, p in zip(enc_tgt.parameters(), enc.parameters()):
                p_t.mul_(tau).add_((1 - tau) * p)          # in-place ops
    return z.std(0).mean().item()


spread_same = train_jepa("same")
spread_reg = train_jepa("same", reg=1.0)
assert spread_same < 0.5 * spread_reg     # no safeguard: embeddings shrink
assert abs(spread_reg - 1) < 0.1          # regularized: unit spread



detach() is the stop-gradient of Equation 10: the target is treated as a constant, so the loss cannot be lowered by moving it. Without it, and without a regularizer, the cheapest way to predict the target is to shrink both towards zero.

title: Week 8 · World Models
text:
Papers

Papers discussed in class






Learning Universal Policies via Text-Guided Video Generation Du et al. · NeurIPS 2023
UniPi turns decision making into text-conditioned video generation. A video diffusion model, given the current frame and a task in words, generates a short video of the task being done; a separately trained inverse dynamics model then reads off the actions that move between consecutive generated frames.

Policy as video: images are a shared state space across environments, and text specifies the goal, which supports combining instructions in new ways (Abstract).
First-frame conditioning (‘tiling’) and temporal super-resolution keep the generated plan consistent with the scene (Sec. 3.1).
The inverse dynamics model is trained independently of the video planner, on a separate, smaller data set (Sec. 3.1).
Pre-training on internet videos lets it produce realistic plans for real-robot tasks not in the robot data (Abstract, Sec. 4.3).

On this page: The video-action toy on this page, which also pairs a model of what happens next with an inverse dynamics model that decodes actions from it.









Training Agents Inside of Scalable World Models Hafner, Yan & Lillicrap · arXiv 2025
Dreamer 4 learns a transformer world model of Minecraft from video and trains an agent by reinforcement learning inside it. It is the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from offline data, without ever interacting with the game during learning.

A shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer give real-time interactive inference on a single GPU (Abstract).
Learns action conditioning from 2,500 hours of video with only 100 hours of paired actions, reaching over 80% of the accuracy of training with all actions (Fig. 7).
Obtaining diamonds needs sequences of over 20,000 mouse and keyboard actions from raw pixels; it learns from the 2.5K-hour VPT contractor data set alone (Abstract, Sec. 4.1).
Outperforms OpenAI’s VPT offline agent while using 100 times less data (Sec. 1).

On this page: The latent world models of this page’s Intuition: imagination training without real interaction, here scaled up and pre-trained on action-free video.









World Action Models are Zero-shot Policies Ye et al. · arXiv 2026
DreamZero is a 14-billion-parameter world action model: a video diffusion model, pre-trained on web video, that jointly generates the robot’s future camera frames and its actions. Predicting how the world will evolve gives it physical priors that VLAs, built on static image-text models, lack.

Over 2 times better generalization to new tasks and environments than state-of-the-art VLAs in real-robot experiments (Abstract).
Model and system optimizations give a 38 times inference speed-up, so the 14B autoregressive model runs closed-loop control at about 7 Hz (Sec. 1).
Video-only demonstrations from other robots or humans improve unseen-task performance by over 42% (relative) with 10–20 minutes of data (Abstract).
Adapts to a new robot with 30 minutes of play data while keeping zero-shot generalization (Abstract).

On this page: The page’s world action models; its closed-loop inference, which swaps real observations into the model’s context, is the ‘look’ option of this page’s puck toy. The guest speaker is a co-author.





Key papers from the lecture






Deep Visual Foresight for Planning Robot Motion Finn & Levine · ICRA 2017
Combines an action-conditioned video prediction model with model-predictive control. The model, trained on unlabeled data the robot collected itself, predicts how pixels will move under candidate actions; the planner picks the actions whose predicted motion moves a chosen pixel to its goal.

Entirely unlabeled training data: no calibrated camera, instrumented set-up or precise sensing (Abstract).
A real robot pushes objects, including objects not seen in training (Abstract).

On this page: The pixel world models at the start of the lecture, and the plan-with-a-model-then-replan loop of this page’s puck toy.









World Models Ha & Schmidhuber · NeurIPS 2018
A world model in three parts: a VAE that compresses each frame to a latent vector, a recurrent network that predicts the next latent, and a tiny controller acting on both. The controller can be trained entirely inside the model’s own ‘dream’ and transferred back to the real environment.

Unsupervised learning of a compressed spatial and temporal representation of the environment (Abstract).
Features from the world model make a very small policy sufficient (Abstract).
A policy trained purely in the hallucinated environment transfers to the actual one (Abstract).

On this page: The first latent world model in the lecture’s lineage, and the drift problem that RSSM later fixes.









Learning Latent Dynamics for Planning from Pixels Hafner et al. · ICML 2019
PlaNet learns a latent dynamics model from images and chooses actions by fast online planning in that latent space. Its recurrent state-space model has both a deterministic and a stochastic part.

The recurrent state-space model (RSSM): deterministic and stochastic transition components (Abstract).
Latent overshooting, a multi-step variational objective for predicting rewards several steps ahead (Abstract).
Solves continuous control from pixels with substantially fewer episodes than strong model-free methods (Abstract).

On this page: The RSSM equations on this page: a learned prior over the next latent, kept close to the posterior by a KL term.









Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination Hafner, Lillicrap, Ba & Norouzi · ICLR 2020
Dreamer replaces PlaNet’s planning at every step with an actor and a critic trained inside the learned world model, by back-propagating value gradients through imagined trajectories.

Learns behaviors purely by latent imagination (Abstract).
Propagates analytic gradients of learned state values back through imagined trajectories (Abstract).
Beats existing approaches on 20 visual control tasks in data efficiency, computation time and final performance (Abstract).

On this page: Amortizing the planner of this page’s puck toy into a policy; the start of the Dreamer line that ends in Dreamer 4.









DayDreamer: World Models for Physical Robot Learning Wu, Escontrela, Hafner, Abbeel & Goldberg · CoRL 2022
Applies Dreamer, unchanged, to four real robots learning online without simulators.

A quadruped learns to roll off its back, stand up and walk from scratch in 1 hour, and adapts to pushes within 10 minutes (Abstract).
Two robot arms learn pick and place from camera images and sparse rewards, approaching human performance (Abstract).
The same hyperparameters in every experiment (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s case that imagination training saves real-world trial and error.









mimic-video: Video-Action Models for Generalizable Robot Control Beyond VLAs Pai, Achenbach et al. · arXiv 2025
A video-action model: a pre-trained internet-scale video model plans in video space, and a flow-matching action decoder, acting as an inverse dynamics model, turns its latent representation into robot actions.

Argues that vision-language pre-training captures semantics but is blind to physical causality, while video captures both (Abstract).
10 times better sample efficiency and 2 times faster convergence than traditional VLA architectures (Abstract).

On this page: The video-action toy on this page and its oracle test. The lecturer is a co-author.

title: Week 8 · World Models
text:
Guest spotlight
Scott Reed (NVIDIA’s GEAR lab, earlier Google DeepMind, where he led the Gato generalist agent) asked what the right backbone for a robot policy is: the network that encodes cameras, robot state and instructions into a shared representation for predicting actions ▶ 01:09. It decides not only how the policy runs but how much knowledge it can soak up in pre-training and carry to new tasks. The options are training from scratch, starting from a vision-language model (a VLA), and the newer choice of starting from a video model.
On VLAs, he walked from OpenVLA’s binned action tokens ▶ 05:28 to the π models, which pair discrete FAST tokens with a separate flow-matching action expert ▶ 06:15. His reasons: back-propagating flow-matching gradients straight through the language model can destroy its language abilities ▶ 07:13, and a continuous expert never produces the malformed decodes that discrete tokens occasionally do, which on a robot arm is a safety issue ▶ 07:55. He singled out TRI’s large-behavior-model study for its double-blind, statistically careful real-robot evaluation, which found that multi-task pre-training does help ▶ 09:42. The weaknesses he sees: reasoning happens in action space, action outputs are bolted on after pre-training with a risk of forgetting, and data from different robots may stay as separate “data islands” with little transfer between them ▶ 11:35.
World action models predict the world in pixels before or while acting, so pre-training can extract more from each video than action prediction alone ▶ 13:09. DreamZero, of which he is a co-author, encodes frames with a VAE and jointly denoises a chunk of future frames and actions with a block-causal transformer; a “Flash” variant barely denoises the frames and performs as well ▶ 14:01. Its failures mostly came from bad video generation rather than bad action prediction, and performance rose with model size (14B better than 2B), which suggests better video models will directly mean better policies ▶ 20:05. The costs: sampling is expensive, modelling every pixel is probably overkill for control, and context length is limited ▶ 21:20.
From scratch is coming back through human data: wearable sensors and head-mounted cameras can record far more demonstrations than robots can, and recent work shows scaling-law behavior as human data grows ▶ 24:52. He ended “bullish” on world action models combined with large-scale human data ▶ 26:11. In the Q&A he called JEPA-style latent world models promising but unproven, since nobody yet knows which features control needs ▶ 27:02, expected hand-built simulators to keep their place for whole-body control while learned simulators help with contact and deformables, and expected tactile data to be needed in much smaller amounts than video ▶ 30:57.
How it connects to this week. The talk is the lecture’s second half from the inside: the choice between VLMs and video models as the backbone is the choice between “semantics first” and “dynamics first”, and DreamZero’s failure analysis is the same finding as mimic-video’s oracle test and this page’s third toy.

title: Week 8 · World Models
text:
Solved problems
1. Bounding a rollout. A world model has a one-step error of 0.01, and the dynamics stretch errors by at most \(L = 1.1\) per step. Bound the error after 20 imagined steps. How does the bound change if the robot replans from a real observation every 5 steps?






TipSolution





Equation 4 gives \(0.01 \times (1.1^{20} - 1)/0.1 = 0.01 \times 57.3 \approx 0.57\). Replanning from a real observation resets the error to 0 every 5 steps, so the worst error is that of a 5-step rollout: \(0.01 \times (1.1^5 - 1)/0.1 = 0.01 \times 6.1 \approx 0.061\), nine times smaller. That is what looking at the real puck buys in Figure 3.



2. Counting video tokens. A 30-second clip at 30 frames per second, 256 by 256 pixels, 16 by 16 patches. How many tokens per frame and in total without compression? With a tokenizer that compresses 8 times in each spatial direction and 8 times in time?






TipSolution





\(256 \cdot 256 / 16^2 = 256\) tokens per frame and \(30 \cdot 30 = 900\) frames, so 230,400 tokens: far beyond a typical context. With \(c_s = c_t = 8\): \(256/64 = 4\) tokens per frame-group and \(900/8 = 112.5\), about 113 time steps, so about 450 tokens. (Equation 8; temporal compression rounds up at the end of the clip.)



3. Why collapse is a minimum. For the plain JEPA loss \(\|\mathrm{pred}(\mathrm{enc}(o_t), a_t) - \mathrm{enc}(o_{t+1})\|^2\) with linear encoder \(z = oW\) and linear predictor, show that \(W = 0\), \(P_a = 0\) gives zero loss. Why does a stop-gradient target change the picture?






TipSolution





With \(W = 0\) every embedding is 0, the predictor’s output \(0 \cdot P_z + a P_a\) is 0 when \(P_a = 0\), and the target is 0: the loss is exactly 0, its global minimum, while carrying no information about the observation. Gradient descent on both sides moves the target towards the prediction as well as the prediction towards the target, and shrinking everything reduces the loss. With a stop-gradient, the target is a constant at each step; the encoder is then only pushed to make predictions match fixed targets, and shrinking the online embeddings no longer shrinks the target. Whether collapse is then avoided depends on the training dynamics: in this page’s linear toy it is, but the lecture’s methods add an EMA target or a regularizer to make it robust.



4. Which family can use which data? You have (a) internet videos of people cooking, (b) 50 hours of robot play data with actions but no instructions, (c) 5 hours of instruction-labelled teleoperation. Which data can an action-conditioned world model (Dreamer-style), a world action model and a video action model each use, and for what?






TipSolution





An action-conditioned model learns dynamics from (b), including failures, and from (c); (a) has no actions, but Dreamer 4 shows dynamics can be pre-trained on action-free video and then conditioned on actions with a little labelled data. A world action model starts from a video model pre-trained on data like (a), then learns joint video and action prediction from (c); (b) is harder to use because the model is conditioned on instructions, unless the play is relabelled with instructions after the fact. A video action model also starts from (a); its inverse dynamics model can learn from (b) and (c), since it needs (observation, next observation, action) triples, not instructions. This matches the lecture’s comparison of the families ▶ 65:55.



5. Dream or look? Your planner reports that its plan reaches the goal, but the robot misses. Name two different causes, and say which one replanning from real observations fixes.






TipSolution






Compounding: small one-step errors grow along the imagined rollout, so the plan’s later steps are made for a state the robot is not in. Replanning from real observations fixes this, because every plan starts from the truth and only its first step is executed. (ii) Exploitation: the planner chose actions outside the data, where the model is wrong in its favour, such as pushes beyond the motor’s limit. Replanning limits the damage but does not remove it, since every new plan still trusts the model’s wrong prediction; the fixes are constraining the planner to the data’s range, penalizing model uncertainty, or collecting data where the planner wants to go.

title: Week 8 · World Models
text:
Recap

A world model predicts consequences of actions. \(p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t, h_t)\); without the action it is a video model, not a world model. Why it matters: only an action-conditioned model lets a robot ask “what if?”.
Planning in a model needs feedback. Imagined rollouts compound their errors, and replanning from real observations resets them each step. Why it matters: it is why MPC and closed-loop world action models work while open-loop dreams drift.
Planners exploit model errors. Optimization finds the actions where the model is wrong in its favour, especially outside the data. Why it matters: every imagination-trained policy inherits the risk.
Latent world models make imagination cheap. World Models, then RSSM’s deterministic memory and learned prior, then Dreamer’s actor-critic in imagination, up to Dreamer 4’s offline Minecraft diamonds. Why it matters: real-robot learning in hours (DayDreamer) instead of days.
Video backbones supply dynamics; robot data then teach control. World action models generate video and actions together; video action models decode actions from video features; failures trace back to video quality. Why it matters: it is the main challenger to VLAs as the backbone of generalist policies.
Predicting embeddings needs a guard against collapse. Stop-gradient targets, EMA or frozen encoders, or covariance regularizers. Why it matters: the lowest prediction loss can be the worst representation.

Common pitfalls.

Calling a text-to-video model a world model: without action conditioning it cannot evaluate your plan.
Executing a long imagined plan open loop; the dream always looks perfect.
Letting the planner use actions or states outside the training data, and believing its predicted cost.
Judging a JEPA by its prediction loss alone; a collapsed encoder has the lowest loss.
Judging collapse with a scale-invariant probe only: shrinking embeddings still decode well until noise dominates; track their spread and effective rank.
Comparing world-model families without saying which data each can use.

Connections. Week 2’s transition model \(P(s' \mid s, a)\) is what a world model learns. Week 4 used CEM over actions and Q-learning without a model; Dreamer’s actor-critic is Week 5’s, trained in imagination. Week 3’s compounding errors return here as compounding prediction errors, and the fix is again feedback from the real world. Week 6’s VAEs and flow matching are the encoders and video generators of this week; Week 7’s tokenizers and transformers become video tokenizers and causal video transformers. Week 9 returns to VLAs as generalist policies. In the ADM Companion: learning a model from data, model predictive control and open versus closed loop, which is this page’s “dream or look”.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
Week 3 ended on a problem: when demonstrators do the same task in different ways, a policy trained with squared error averages them, and the average can drive straight into the obstacle the demonstrators went around. The fix was a policy that outputs a distribution over actions. This week is about the machinery for that: generative models, which the lecture presents in three families, latent-variable models, diffusion models and flow models, and then shows in robot policies ▶ 00:30. Week 7 turns to sequence models, and Week 9’s generalist policies use the flow-matching idea from this week to produce actions.
The question this week answers: how can a policy represent, and sample from, a complicated distribution over actions?


The key ideas at a glance

A generative model turns simple noise into data. Start from samples of a standard Gaussian; learn a transformation whose outputs look like the training data. For a robot, the “data” are actions or action sequences, and the transformation is conditioned on what the robot sees.
Latent-variable models squeeze each example into a small code and decode it back. A variational autoencoder (VAE) makes that code a random variable with a known distribution, so new codes can be sampled. A vector-quantized VAE (VQ-VAE) uses a codebook of discrete codes instead, which turns data into tokens.
Diffusion models learn to undo noise. Training adds Gaussian noise to clean examples in many small steps; a network learns to predict the noise that was added. Sampling starts from pure noise and removes it step by step.
Fewer steps and steering. DDIM samples deterministically with far fewer steps; classifier-free guidance strengthens the effect of a condition such as an instruction.
Flow matching learns a velocity field that carries noise to data along straight lines, and samples by following it with a few integration steps. It is now the most common way vision-language-action models produce actions.
In robots: Diffusion Policy denoises sequences of future actions conditioned on camera images; later work scales the idea with transformers, and π0 uses flow matching.



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Generative model
A model you can draw new samples from that look like the training data


Latent variable \(z\)
A hidden code that, once chosen, determines (most of) the output


Encoder, decoder
Networks that map data to a code and a code back to data


VAE
Autoencoder whose codes follow a known distribution, so new codes can be sampled


VQ-VAE
Autoencoder whose code is one of a finite set of learned vectors (a codebook)


Diffusion model
Generates data by starting from noise and removing it step by step


Noise schedule \(\beta_i\)
How much noise each forward step adds


DDPM, DDIM
Two ways to sample a diffusion model: with fresh noise at each step, or deterministically with fewer steps


Classifier-free guidance
Mixing conditional and unconditional predictions to follow a condition more strongly


Flow matching
Learning a velocity field that moves noise to data along straight paths





After this week you can

Explain why a policy needs a distribution, and what each generative family does to represent one.
Write the DDPM training loss and sampling step, and say why the network predicts noise.
Explain the speed–quality trade-off of DDIM and flow-matching sampling, and why one sampling step falls back to averaging.
Describe how Diffusion Policy and π0 turn these models into robot policies.

title: Week 6 · Generative Models
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Imagine a sand sculpture slowly eroded by wind until it is a smooth, featureless heap. Undoing the whole erosion in one go is hopeless; there are endless sculptures that could have become that heap. But undoing one gust is easy: a slightly blurred sculpture tells you a lot about the slightly sharper one before it. A diffusion model learns to undo one gust at a time, and running it many times turns a heap of noise into a sculpture. Because each run starts from a different heap, it produces different sculptures: one passing left of the tree, another passing right.



Actions are a distribution, not a function
The opening point of the lecture: for a robot, the mapping from what it sees to what it should do is not a function but a distribution ▶ 00:30. The toy on this page makes that concrete. Two thousand demonstrated actions form two curved groups, like a gripper that passes an obstacle on the left or the right at different heights; no demonstration goes through the middle (|x| < 0.5).








Figure 2: The same demonstrations, modelled six ways. Grey: 1,000 of the 2,000 demonstrated actions (every second one). Each other panel shows 1,000 samples from a model. MSE regression gives a single action, the mean, in the empty middle. One Gaussian spreads into the middle; a mixture of two Gaussians finds the two groups but cannot bend into crescents. Diffusion and flow matching follow the curved shapes.





The averaging failure from Week 3 is in the second panel: the mean of the demonstrations sits in the empty middle. A single Gaussian is no better; 35% of its samples land in the middle. A mixture of two Gaussians puts every sample on a side but cannot follow the curve: 6.9% of its samples land away from any demonstration (more than 0.2 from the nearest one). The diffusion model and the flow-matching model, given no hint about how many groups there are, put 0.2% and 0.2% of their samples in the middle, averaged over 5 training runs.


A generative model turns noise into data
Every model in this lecture does the same job in a different way: learn a transformation from a simple distribution you can sample, usually a standard Gaussian, to the complex distribution of the data ▶ 03:08. The three families differ in how: encode the data into a code, transport noise to data step by step, or move noise along a velocity field.


Latent-variable models: autoencoders, VAEs and VQ-VAEs
Week 3 already met the idea of a latent variable \(z\) that selects a mode: “go left” or “go right”. An autoencoder learns such codes without labels: an encoder squeezes the input into a small code, a decoder reconstructs the input, and the bottleneck forces the code to keep what matters ▶ 04:12. But its code space has no structure and nothing to sample from. A variational autoencoder makes the encoder output a Gaussian over codes and pulls those Gaussians towards a standard normal prior, so that at test time you can draw \(z\) from the prior and decode it ▶ 06:42. Training needs a trick, because drawing a random sample has no gradient: write the sample as the mean plus the standard deviation times independent noise, and gradients flow through the mean and standard deviation (Equation 2) ▶ 08:53.
VAEs have two known failures ▶ 14:05. A powerful decoder can learn to ignore \(z\) (posterior collapse). And a code sampled from the prior can fall between the regions the training codes occupy, where the decoder has never been trained, and produce an action halfway between two modes: a hallucination, and in robotics possibly an unsafe one. A VQ-VAE replaces the continuous code by the nearest entry of a learned codebook, which forces a commitment to one discrete code ▶ 15:37; since a nearest-neighbour lookup has no useful gradient, training copies the gradient straight past it (Equation 3) ▶ 17:40. The codes form a vocabulary, so a transformer can then be trained to produce sequences of them, the same tokens-for-everything idea as RT-2’s action tokens in Week 1 ▶ 20:45.


Diffusion: learn to remove noise
Diffusion models skip the bottleneck and model the data directly ▶ 24:32. The forward process adds a little Gaussian noise many times, shrinking the signal a bit each time, until nothing but noise is left (Equation 4) ▶ 25:45.








Figure 3: The forward process on the demonstrated actions: each row shows the same points after 0, 5, 10, 25 and 50 noising steps, with a linear schedule (top) and a cosine schedule (bottom). Both end as a featureless Gaussian blob; the cosine schedule keeps the two groups recognisable for longer.





The backward process is what we want: from a noisy point, the slightly less noisy one before it. Predicting that directly is ill-posed, since many clean points could have produced the same noisy one. The key move is to ask the network for something simpler: the noise that was added ▶ 27:09. That is an easy regression target with a plain squared-error loss (Equation 6). Training can jump straight to any noise level in one step, which makes it fast (Equation 5) ▶ 30:34.




Diffusion versus averaging, on this page's toy. The demonstrations (grey) leave the middle empty; MSE regression answers with one point there (blue). Noise samples (orange) follow the trained diffusion model's 50 denoising steps and settle on the two sides.

What to watch for. The clip opens on the demonstrations, with the empty middle shaded. First the MSE answer appears: a single blue dot, the average, in the one place no demonstrator went. Then a cloud of noise samples appears, centred on that same dot. As the step counter runs, the cloud changes slowly for most of the 50 steps (the early steps remove only a little noise each) and then, in the last few steps, splits: every orange point moves away from the blue dot to one of the crescents. The clip ends on both crescents filled and the middle empty, then fades back to the start.
To sample, start from pure noise and repeatedly subtract the predicted noise. DDPM also adds a little fresh noise at each step, which sounds backwards but keeps samples spread over the whole distribution instead of collapsing towards its mean ▶ 32:22. It needs many steps; image models use around a thousand, too slow for robot control. DDIM visits only a few steps, estimating the clean point and re-noising it deterministically to the next visited step (Equation 8) ▶ 34:20. In the toy, 10 DDIM steps leave 2.8% of samples off the demonstrations; 2 steps leave 87% (Figure 5).


Conditioning and guidance
So far the samples are unconditional: draws from the data distribution with no say over which. A robot needs actions for this observation and this instruction. The simple fix is to give the condition to the noise predictor as an extra input ▶ 35:56. Networks may still learn to half-ignore it, so classifier-free guidance trains one network both with and without the condition (dropping it at random) and, at sampling time, pushes the prediction further in the direction the condition points (Equation 9) ▶ 37:00.


Diffusion as a robot policy
Diffusion Policy applies all of this to actions: instead of denoising pixels, denoise a short sequence of future robot actions, with the camera images and robot state as the condition ▶ 38:59. It trains with the DDPM loss, samples with DDIM, computes the observation features once per decision, and conditions the denoising network with FiLM, a learned per-feature scale and shift ▶ 40:46. It handles multimodal demonstrations well but has been harder to scale to many tasks. Follow-ups attach a diffusion head to a large transformer trained on many robots (Octo) ▶ 42:05, or condition through adaptive layer normalization, borrowed from diffusion transformers for images, which trains more stably and scales to long two-armed tasks ▶ 42:52.

The robot executes only the first few actions of the result, then observes again (receding-horizon control, Chi et al. 2023, Sec. 3).







Flow matching: straight lines from noise to data
Flow matching drops the noise schedule: pair each noise sample with a data point, draw the straight line between them, and train a network to predict the velocity along that line (Equation 10) ▶ 43:43. Sampling integrates the learned velocity from noise to data in a few Euler steps. With a linear schedule it is equivalent to diffusion up to a change of variables ▶ 45:35; in practice its paths are straighter and need fewer steps. Rectified flow retrains on noise–data pairs produced by the flow itself, which untangles crossing paths and straightens them further ▶ 46:54. Physical Intelligence’s π0 was, to the lecturer’s knowledge, the first vision-language-action model to produce actions with flow matching; it samples the training time from a shifted Beta distribution to concentrate on the noisier, harder part of the path ▶ 48:03.
One step of flow matching is worth a look. With a single Euler step, the toy’s samples collapse onto the data mean: 98% land in the empty middle. That is not a bug; it is exactly MSE regression again (see Worked example 3).

title: Week 6 · Generative Models
text:
Key concepts & formulae
The lecture’s notation: \(x_0\) is a clean data point (an action, or an image), \(x_i\) the same point after \(i\) noising steps, \(i = 1, \dots, T\); \(\varepsilon\) is standard Gaussian noise; \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) are network parameters. For flow matching, a continuous time \(t \in [0, 1]\) runs from noise (\(t = 0\)) to data (\(t = 1\)).

Variational autoencoder

\[
\begin{aligned}
\log p_\theta(x) \;\ge\;\; & \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] \\
-\; & \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\big\|\, p(z)\big)
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

In words. Maximize how well codes inferred from \(x\) let the decoder reconstruct \(x\), while keeping those codes close to a fixed prior that can be sampled at test time.
Term by term.

\(q_\phi(z \mid x)\): the encoder, a Gaussian over codes with mean and variance computed from \(x\).
\(p_\theta(x \mid z)\): the decoder; the first term is the reconstruction quality, averaged over codes drawn from the encoder.
\(p(z)\): the prior, usually \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\); the KL term is the regularizer that gives the code space its structure.
\(\log p_\theta(x)\): the likelihood we would like to maximize but cannot compute, because it averages over all codes. Week 3’s goal-conditioned version adds a context \(c\) to every term.


\[
z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
\tag{2}\]

In words. Draw the randomness from a fixed distribution first, then shift and scale it with the encoder’s outputs.
Term by term.

\(\mu_\phi(x)\), \(\sigma_\phi(x)\): the encoder’s mean and standard deviation; \(\odot\) multiplies element by element.
\(\varepsilon\): noise with no learnable parameters, so the sampling step is just arithmetic on \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), and gradients reach the encoder.

Why it helps. The alternative, the score-function estimator that reinforcement learning calls REINFORCE (Weeks 4–5), only sees whether a sample scored well, not which way to move it, so its gradient estimates are noisy. With the reparameterization the gradient of the loss with respect to \(\phi\) goes through \(\partial f / \partial z\), the decoder’s own signal about which direction to move the code.

\[
\begin{aligned}
k &= \arg\min_j \big\lVert z_e(x) - e_j \big\rVert_2 \\
z_q &= z_e + \mathrm{sg}\big[e_k - z_e\big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]

In words. Replace the encoder’s output by the nearest codebook vector; for the backward pass, pretend the replacement didn’t happen.
Term by term.

\(z_e(x)\): the encoder’s continuous output; \(e_1, \dots, e_K\): the learned codebook.
\(k\): the chosen code, a discrete token.
\(\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]\): stop-gradient, the identity going forward and zero going backward. So \(z_q\) equals \(e_k\) in the forward pass, while \(\partial z_q / \partial z_e = 1\) copies the decoder’s gradient to the encoder.
Training adds two terms to the reconstruction loss: one moving codebook vectors towards the encoder outputs, and a commitment term keeping the encoder outputs near their codes.



Diffusion

\[
x_{i} = \sqrt{1 - \beta_{i}}\; x_{i-1} + \sqrt{\beta_{i}}\; \varepsilon_{i}, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
\tag{4}\]

In words. Each step shrinks the point a little towards zero and adds a little Gaussian noise.
Term by term.

\(\beta_i\): the noise schedule, small numbers set in advance. This page uses \(T =\) 50 steps with \(\beta\) rising linearly from 0.001 to 0.2.
\(\sqrt{1-\beta_i}\): the shrink factor, chosen so that a point with unit variance keeps unit variance.


\[
\begin{aligned}
x_i &= \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\; \varepsilon \\
\bar\alpha_i &= \prod_{j=1}^{i} (1 - \beta_j)
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]

In words. After \(i\) steps, the point is a shrunken copy of the clean point plus one combined dose of noise, so training can produce any noise level in one step instead of \(i\).
Term by term.

\(\bar\alpha_i\): how much of the signal survives after \(i\) steps, falling from near 1 to near 0.
\(\varepsilon\): a single standard Gaussian draw that stands for all \(i\) steps’ noise.

Why it holds. Apply Equation 4 twice: \(x_2 = \sqrt{\alpha_2\alpha_1}\,x_0 + \sqrt{\alpha_2(1-\alpha_1)}\,\varepsilon_1 + \sqrt{1-\alpha_2}\,\varepsilon_2\) with \(\alpha_j = 1 - \beta_j\). The two noise terms are independent Gaussians, so their sum is Gaussian with variance \(\alpha_2(1 - \alpha_1) + (1 - \alpha_2) = 1 - \alpha_1\alpha_2\). Repeating the argument gives the formula.
Numeric check. With the linear schedule, \(\bar\alpha\) falls below one half after 19 of the 50 steps; with the cosine schedule of Nichol & Dhariwal (2021) it takes 25 steps, which is why the cosine rows of Figure 3 stay recognisable for longer. At the last step \(\bar\alpha_T\) is 0.0045 (linear): almost nothing of the data is left.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} &= \mathbb{E}_{i,\, x_0,\, \varepsilon}\Big[\big\lVert \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(x_i,\, i)\big\rVert^2\Big] \\
x_i &= \sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\,\varepsilon
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]

In words. Pick a training example, a noise level and a noise sample; make the noisy point; ask the network what noise was added; penalize the squared error.
Term by term.

\(i \sim \text{Uniform}\{1, \dots, T\}\): every noise level is trained.
\(\varepsilon_\theta(x_i, i)\): the noise predictor, one network for all steps, told which step it is at.
The whole expression comes from the same evidence lower bound as the VAE, spread over \(T\) steps with a fixed encoder (the forward process); Ho et al. (2020) found that dropping its weighting terms trains better ▶ 28:35.

Numeric check. In the toy the loss starts near 1 (the variance of the noise, what predicting zero would give) and falls to 0.45 over training: the network explains about half the noise on average, much more at low noise levels than at high ones.

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{i-1} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_i}}\Big(x_i - \frac{1 - \alpha_i}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}}\; \varepsilon_\theta(x_i, i)\Big) \\
&\quad + \sigma_i\, z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]

In words. Remove the predicted share of noise, undo the shrink, then add a little fresh noise.
Term by term.

\(\alpha_i = 1 - \beta_i\); the bracket is the estimated mean of the previous, less noisy point.
\(\sigma_i z\): fresh noise (\(\sigma_i^2 = \beta_i\) here), skipped on the very last step. It keeps different starting points from collapsing onto the same output.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{x}_0 &= \frac{x_i - \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\; \varepsilon_\theta(x_i, i)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}} \\
x_{i'} &= \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i'}}\; \hat{x}_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{i'}}\; \varepsilon_\theta(x_i, i)
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]

In words. Use the predicted noise to estimate the clean point, then put back exactly the amount of that same noise that the next visited step \(i' < i\) should have.
Term by term.

\(\hat{x}_0\): invert Equation 5 with the predicted noise in place of the true one.
\(i'\): the next step in a short subset of steps, for example 10 out of 50, so far fewer network calls.
No fresh noise: the same start always gives the same result.



Guidance

\[
\hat\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\theta(x_i, i, \varnothing) + w\,\big(\varepsilon_\theta(x_i, i, c) - \varepsilon_\theta(x_i, i, \varnothing)\big)
\tag{9}\]

In words. Predict the noise with and without the condition; the difference is the direction the condition pulls in; move \(w\) times as far in that direction.
Term by term.

\(c\): the condition (an instruction, an observation); \(\varnothing\): a “no condition” token, used for a random share of training examples so one network learns both.
\(w\): the guidance scale. \(w = 1\) is plain conditional sampling; larger \(w\) follows the condition more closely at the cost of variety.



Flow matching

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_t &= (1 - t)\,\varepsilon + t\,x_0, \qquad t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1] \\
\mathcal{L} &= \mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_0,\,\varepsilon}\Big[\big\lVert v_\theta(x_t, t) - (x_0 - \varepsilon) \big\rVert^2\Big] \\
x_{t + \Delta t} &= x_t + v_\theta(x_t, t)\,\Delta t
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}\]

In words. Move along the straight line from a noise sample to a data point; the network learns that line’s constant velocity; to sample, start at noise and take Euler steps along the learned velocity.
Term by term.

\(x_t\): a point on the straight path, pure noise at \(t = 0\), data at \(t = 1\).
\(x_0 - \varepsilon\): the true velocity along that path, the same at every \(t\).
\(v_\theta\): the learned velocity field; at a given \((x_t, t)\) many lines pass through, so it learns their average direction.
\(\Delta t\): the step size; \(1/\Delta t\) steps take noise to data.

Why one step gives the mean. At \(t = 0\) the point is the noise, \(x_0\) is independent of it, and the best squared-error prediction is \(v_\theta(\varepsilon, 0) = \mathbb{E}[x_0] - \varepsilon\). One Euler step of length 1 then lands at \(\varepsilon + \mathbb{E}[x_0] - \varepsilon = \mathbb{E}[x_0]\), the mean, for every starting noise. In the toy, the one-step samples sit 0.039 from the data mean with a spread of only 0.17. Multimodality needs several steps, because later velocities depend on where the earlier steps went.
