title: Week 6 · Generative Models
text:
Algorithm & code

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def train_ddpm(data, betas, rng, **kw):
    """Train the noise predictor eps_theta(x_t, t) with the simple DDPM loss:
    pick a step t and noise eps, jump to x_t, regress eps."""
    T, abar = len(betas), alpha_bar(betas)

    def batch(n, rng):
        x0 = data[rng.integers(len(data), size=n)]
        t = rng.integers(1, T + 1, size=n)                # 1..T
        eps = rng.normal(size=x0.shape)
        return features(noise_to(x0, t, abar, eps), t / T), eps

    return train_net(batch, rng, **kw)

def ddpm_sample(params, betas, n, rng, keep_path=False):
    """Start from pure noise and take T denoising steps; each step removes
    the predicted noise and adds back a little fresh noise (sigma_t^2 =
    beta_t). Returns samples (n, 2), or the whole path (T+1, n, 2)."""
    T, abar = len(betas), alpha_bar(betas)
    x = rng.normal(size=(n, 2))
    path = [x]
    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        a, ab = 1 - betas[t - 1], abar[t - 1]
        eps = nn.predict(params, features(x, t / T))      # (n, 2)
        mean = (x - (1 - a) / np.sqrt(1 - ab) * eps) / np.sqrt(a)
        # Fresh noise keeps samples spread out; none on the last step.
        z = rng.normal(size=x.shape) if t > 1 else 0.0
        x = mean + np.sqrt(betas[t - 1]) * z
        path.append(x)
    return np.array(path) if keep_path else x

def train_flow(data, rng, **kw):
    """Train the velocity field v_theta(x_t, t) on straight paths
    x_t = (1 - t) eps + t x0, t in [0, 1], whose velocity is x0 - eps."""
    def batch(n, rng):
        x0 = data[rng.integers(len(data), size=n)]
        eps = rng.normal(size=x0.shape)
        t = rng.uniform(0, 1, size=n)
        xt = (1 - t)[:, None] * eps + t[:, None] * x0
        return features(xt, t), x0 - eps

    return train_net(batch, rng, **kw)

def flow_sample(params, n, rng, steps=10, keep_path=False):
    """Euler integration of the learned velocity from noise (t = 0) to
    data (t = 1): x <- x + v(x, t) dt."""
    x = rng.normal(size=(n, 2))
    path, dt = [x], 1.0 / steps
    for k in range(steps):
        x = x + nn.predict(params, features(x, k * dt)) * dt
        path.append(x)
    return np.array(path) if keep_path else x


import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

from rlc.toys import w06_generative as toy

torch.manual_seed(0)
data = torch.tensor(toy.crescents(2000, np.random.default_rng(0)),
                    dtype=torch.float32)                   # (2000, 2)
T = 50
betas = torch.tensor(toy.linear_schedule(T), dtype=torch.float32)
abar = torch.cumprod(1 - betas, dim=0)                     # (T,)


class NoiseNet(nn.Module):
    """eps_theta(x_i, i): a small MLP; the step enters as t = i / T."""

    def __init__(self, hidden=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, 2))

    def forward(self, x, t):                   # x: (B, 2), t: (B,) in (0, 1]
        return self.net(torch.cat([x, t[:, None]], dim=1))


eps_net = NoiseNet()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(eps_net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
losses = []
for _ in range(1500):
    x0 = data[torch.randint(len(data), (512,))]            # (B, 2)
    i = torch.randint(1, T + 1, (512,))                    # step 1..T
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    a = abar[i - 1][:, None]                               # (B, 1) broadcasts
    xi = a.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - a).sqrt() * eps              # jump to step i
    loss = F.mse_loss(eps_net(xi, i / T), eps)             # predict the noise
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    losses.append(loss.item())


@torch.no_grad()                               # sampling needs no gradients
def ddpm_sample(n):
    x = torch.randn(n, 2)
    for i in range(T, 0, -1):
        t = torch.full((n,), i / T)
        alpha, ab = 1 - betas[i - 1], abar[i - 1]
        mean = (x - (1 - alpha) / (1 - ab).sqrt() * eps_net(x, t)) / alpha.sqrt()
        x = mean + (betas[i - 1].sqrt() * torch.randn_like(x) if i > 1 else 0)
    return x


samples = ddpm_sample(500)
assert np.mean(losses[-100:]) < np.mean(losses[:20])
assert (samples[:, 0].abs() < toy.GAP).float().mean() < 0.1   # middle empty
class VelocityNet(NoiseNet):
    """v_theta(x_t, t): same architecture, now predicting a velocity."""


v_net = VelocityNet()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(v_net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
for _ in range(1500):
    x0 = data[torch.randint(len(data), (512,))]
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    t = torch.rand(512)                                    # (B,) in [0, 1)
    xt = (1 - t)[:, None] * eps + t[:, None] * x0          # straight path
    loss = F.mse_loss(v_net(xt, t), x0 - eps)              # its velocity
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()


@torch.no_grad()
def flow_sample(n, steps):
    x, dt = torch.randn(n, 2), 1.0 / steps
    for k in range(steps):                                 # Euler steps
        x = x + v_net(x, torch.full((n,), k * dt)) * dt
    return x


in_gap = lambda s: (s[:, 0].abs() < toy.GAP).float().mean().item()
assert in_gap(flow_sample(500, steps=1)) > 0.5    # one step: the mean
assert in_gap(flow_sample(500, steps=20)) < 0.1   # many steps: two modes



The two training loops differ in one line each: what point is made from the clean example and the noise, and what the network is asked to predict. The two samplers differ in whether they remove noise with fresh noise added back (DDPM) or follow a velocity (flow matching).

title: Week 6 · Generative Models
text:
Papers

Papers discussed in class






Planning with Diffusion for Flexible Behavior Synthesis Janner, Du, Tenenbaum & Levine · ICML 2022
Instead of learning a dynamics model and handing it to a separate trajectory optimizer, Diffuser trains a diffusion model on whole trajectories, so that planning becomes sampling: start from noise and denoise a full plan at once, nudging the samples towards high reward or towards a required start or goal.

A diffusion model over complete state-action trajectories that refines a whole plan in parallel rather than step by step (Abstract, Fig. 1).
Recasts classifier-guided sampling as planning for reward and image-style inpainting as planning to fixed start and goal states (Abstract).
Useful properties for long-horizon tasks: handles sparse rewards, plans for new rewards without retraining, and stitches together pieces of trajectories it has seen into new ones (Sec. 7).

On this page: Diffusion applied to trajectories instead of single actions, the same move Diffusion Policy makes for action sequences; guidance is a cousin of classifier-free guidance on this page.









Implicit Behavioral Cloning Florence et al. · CoRL 2021
Rather than a network that outputs the action, Implicit BC learns an energy function over (observation, action) pairs and picks the action with the lowest energy. Because the policy is an argmin, it can represent several equally good actions and sharp jumps, which a regression network smooths over.

Reformulates behavioral cloning with energy-based models and inference-time optimization over actions (Sec. 1, Sec. 7).
Often outperforms explicit policies trained with mean-squared error or mixture densities, including with image inputs and action spaces of up to 30 dimensions (Abstract, Sec. 7).
Real-robot tasks from human demonstrations that need about 1 mm precision (Abstract).
An analysis of why implicit models handle discontinuous and multi-valued functions, and a universal-approximation result for them (Abstract, Sec. 7).

On this page: Another answer to the averaging problem from Week 3; Diffusion Policy sets itself against both explicit and implicit policies like this one (its Fig. 1).









Steering Your Diffusion Policy with Latent Space Reinforcement Learning Wagenmaker et al. · arXiv 2025
A diffusion policy turns random noise into an action. DSRL keeps the trained policy fixed and instead learns, with reinforcement learning, which input noise to feed it, steering the policy towards actions that earn reward without touching its weights.

Diffusion steering via RL: run RL over the policy’s latent-noise space rather than its parameters (Abstract).
Needs only black-box access to the policy and is sample-efficient enough for real-world improvement (Abstract).
Shown on simulated benchmarks, real robot tasks, and for adapting pretrained generalist policies (Abstract).

On this page: The noise a diffusion or flow policy starts from is an input you can choose; Weeks 4–5 supply the RL that does the choosing.





Key papers from the lecture






Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models Ho, Jain & Abbeel · NeurIPS 2020
Shows that a diffusion model, which learns to undo a gradual noising process step by step, can generate high-quality images. The key practical step is to train the network to predict the noise that was added, with a plain squared error.

High-quality image synthesis from diffusion models, with an FID of 3.17 on unconditional CIFAR-10 (Abstract).
A link between diffusion models and denoising score matching with Langevin dynamics (Abstract).
The simplified training objective: predict the added noise with a squared error, L_simple (Sec. 3.4, Eq. 14).

On this page: The DDPM loss and sampler on this page.









Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion Chi et al. · RSS 2023
Represents a robot’s visuomotor policy as a conditional diffusion process: starting from noise, it denoises a whole sequence of future actions, conditioned on the current observations. This handles demonstrations with several valid ways of doing a task, and trains stably.

Across 15 tasks from 4 manipulation benchmarks, an average improvement of 46.9% over prior state-of-the-art methods (Abstract of the extended arXiv version).
Practical ingredients for real robots: receding-horizon control over predicted action sequences, visual conditioning, and a time-series diffusion transformer (Abstract).
An analysis of why it works: multimodal action distributions, high-dimensional action sequences, and training stability (Sec. 4).

On this page: The lecture’s main case study and this week’s guest speaker’s work; the conditional version of the toy on this page.









Flow Matching for Generative Modeling Lipman, Chen, Ben-Hamu, Nickel & Le · ICLR 2023
Trains a continuous normalizing flow by regressing a velocity field along simple, fixed paths from noise to data, with no simulation during training. Diffusion paths are one special case; straight-line (optimal-transport) paths train and sample faster.

Flow Matching: a simulation-free objective that regresses the vector field of chosen conditional probability paths (Abstract).
Covers Gaussian paths including diffusion’s, and finds training diffusion paths with it more robust (Abstract).
Optimal-transport (straight-line) paths that give faster training and sampling and better results on ImageNet (Abstract).

On this page: The flow-matching toy on this page, and π0, which generates robot actions this way (Week 9).

title: Week 6 · Generative Models
text:
Guest spotlight
Cheng Chi, lead author of Diffusion Policy and author of the Universal Manipulation Interface (a hand-held data-collection gripper), is now co-founder and CTO of Sunday Robotics. His talk, “Robotics Beyond Algorithms”, is about what he learned after his PhD that algorithms courses don’t teach ▶ 02:07.
Hardware is a supply chain. A hardware project’s bill of materials plays the role of a software project’s dependency list, but “installing” it means procurement, and every part has suppliers with their own suppliers ▶ 06:44. Retail creates the illusion of instant availability; ordering in quantity, or changing a part, means coordinating that whole tree, which shapes what to build and what to buy ▶ 10:31. Building a thousand data-collection gloves then needs written assembly procedures, a serial number on every unit, calibration and quality checks, and software that traces every glove’s history all the way into the training data loader, so a researcher can drop data from a faulty batch with a config change ▶ 14:42.
Data collection is about people. Collecting data as a few researchers is easy; scaling from tens of collectors to thousands made data collection an operation, where clear communication and trust mattered more than clever tooling ▶ 16:44. His conclusion is that robotics sits at the intersection of every engineering discipline, so the people who make robots work are those who understand the stack from hardware to learning ▶ 23:17.
How it connects to this week. Diffusion Policy is the method this lecture builds up to, and its author’s message is that the method was the smaller part: the demonstrations a generative policy learns from come from hardware and people, and their quality decides what the model can learn.

title: Week 6 · Generative Models
text:
Solved problems
1. The average again. Half the demonstrations at a state choose action \(+1\) and half \(-1\). What does an MSE-trained policy output, what fraction of a single Gaussian fit’s samples fall in \((-0.5, 0.5)\), and what does a two-component mixture do?






TipSolution





MSE outputs the mean, 0, which no demonstrator chose. A single Gaussian fit has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (the data’s), so \(\Pr(|a| < 0.5) = 2\Phi(0.5) - 1 \approx 0.38\): over a third of its samples are between the modes. A two-component mixture can put one narrow Gaussian at each of \(\pm 1\) with weight one half, matching the data. The catch, shown in Worked example 1, is that you must choose the number of components, and Gaussians can’t follow curved modes.



2. Signal left after noising. With \(\beta_i = 0.1\) at every step, what fraction of the signal amplitude survives 10 steps, and what is the noise standard deviation then?






TipSolution





\(\bar\alpha_{10} = 0.9^{10} \approx 0.349\). The signal is scaled by \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{10}} \approx 0.59\), and the noise has standard deviation \(\sqrt{1 - 0.349} \approx 0.81\) (Equation 5). After 50 such steps \(\bar\alpha \approx 0.0052\) and the signal is scaled by about 0.07: almost pure noise.



3. Why predict the noise? Give two reasons a diffusion network is trained to predict \(\varepsilon\) rather than \(x_{i-1}\).






TipSolution





First, the target is well-posed and simple: \(\varepsilon\) is a standard Gaussian draw that we know exactly, while many different \(x_{i-1}\) are consistent with a given \(x_i\). Second, the loss becomes a plain squared error at every noise level, the simplified objective of Ho et al. (Equation 6); with Equation 5, one training example can be made at any noise level in a single step. Predicting the noise is equivalent to predicting the clean point \(\hat x_0\) (Equation 8), so nothing is lost.



4. Guidance by numbers. At some step the unconditional prediction is \(\varepsilon_\theta(x, i, \varnothing) = (0.2, 0.1)\) and the conditional one is \(\varepsilon_\theta(x, i, c) = (0.5, -0.1)\). What is the guided prediction for \(w = 1\) and \(w = 3\)?






TipSolution





The difference is \((0.3, -0.2)\). With \(w = 1\): \((0.2, 0.1) + (0.3, -0.2) = (0.5, -0.1)\), the plain conditional prediction. With \(w = 3\): \((0.2, 0.1) + (0.9, -0.6) = (1.1, -0.5)\), pushing three times as far in the condition’s direction (Equation 9).



5. Real-time budget. A robot runs its policy at 10 Hz and a denoising network call takes 8 ms. How many sampling steps fit in the budget, and which sampler would you use?






TipSolution





At 10 Hz there are 100 ms per decision, so at most 12 network calls, less in practice once observation encoding and communication are counted. A 50-step DDPM is out; DDIM with about 10 steps, or flow matching with about 10 Euler steps, fits, and in the toy 10 steps lose little quality (Worked example 3). Predicting a whole action sequence per decision, as Diffusion Policy does, buys more time.

title: Week 6 · Generative Models
text:
Recap

A policy should represent a distribution of actions. Why it matters: it is the fix for Week 3’s averaging failure, and the basis of every modern robot policy that learns from human demonstrations.
Latent-variable models encode, VAEs make codes samplable, VQ-VAEs make them tokens. Why it matters: discrete codes let the transformers of Weeks 7 and 9 treat images, actions and plans as sequences.
Diffusion learns to predict noise, then removes it step by step. In the toy it leaves the empty middle 0.2% full without being told how many modes there are. Why it matters: Diffusion Policy brought this to robot manipulation.
Steps cost time. DDIM and flow matching need about 10 steps here; one step falls back to the mean. Why it matters: robots run in real time, which drives the choice of sampler.
Flow matching follows straight paths from noise to data. Why it matters: it is how π0 and later vision-language-action models produce actions (Week 9).

Common pitfalls.

Judging a generative policy by its training loss alone. Sample from it and look at the samples.
Too few sampling steps: below about 10 in the toy, quality falls fast, and one step returns the mean.
Choosing the number of mixture components by counting obvious modes; curved or uneven modes need more.
Forgetting that DDPM’s fresh noise is deliberate: removing it without switching to DDIM’s update collapses the samples.

Connections. Week 3 showed why averaging fails and previewed mixtures, discretization and diffusion; Week 1 showed actions as tokens, which VQ-VAEs generalize. Week 7 covers the transformers used as noise and velocity networks in later policies, and Week 9 the generalist policies, including π0, that generate actions with flow matching. Weeks 4–5 supply the reinforcement learning that DSRL uses to steer a diffusion policy’s noise.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
Imitation learning (Week 3) copies an expert, so it can never do better than the expert. Reinforcement learning (RL) removes that ceiling: the robot tries things, receives rewards, and improves by trial and error ▶ 01:02. Week 2 defined the goal, the policy with the highest expected discounted return, but not how to find it. This week gives the first family of answers, built on value functions: numbers that say how good it is to be in a state, or to take an action there. Week 5 gives the second family, which improves the policy directly by gradient ascent (policy gradients and actor-critic methods).
The question this week answers: how can a robot work out what to do from rewards alone, first with a model of the world, then without one, and finally with images and continuous actions?


The key ideas at a glance

Expectations smooth things out. A reward can be a step function (on the road or off the cliff) with no useful gradient, yet its expected value under a stochastic policy changes smoothly with the policy’s parameters. That is why RL can optimize what looks non-differentiable.
Values and the Bellman equation. The value of a state is the reward now plus the discounted value of where you land next. This one-step recursion replaces waiting until the end of the episode.
Dynamic programming. With a known model, value iteration applies the Bellman optimality update until the values stop changing; policy iteration alternates exact evaluation and greedy improvement. Both converge to the optimal policy.
Q-functions and Q-learning. Storing a value per state and action lets a robot act without a model: pick the action with the highest Q. Q-learning learns Q from sampled transitions, and because its target uses the best next action it can learn from any data (off-policy); SARSA learns the value of the exploring policy itself (on-policy).
Deep Q-learning. DQN replaces the table with a convolutional network and stabilizes it with a replay buffer and a target network. Taking a maximum over noisy estimates overestimates values; Double DQN fixes it.
Continuous actions. The maximum over actions is no longer a lookup. Options: discretize cleverly (pixels as actions), search with sampling or the cross-entropy method (QT-Opt), or learn the argmax with an actor network (DDPG).



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Value function \(V^\pi(s)\)
Expected discounted return from state \(s\) when following \(\pi\)


Q-function \(Q^\pi(s, a)\)
Expected discounted return after taking action \(a\) in \(s\), then following \(\pi\)


Bellman equation
Value now = reward now + discounted value next


Bootstrapping
Updating an estimate using another estimate (the next state’s value)


Dynamic programming
Solving the Bellman equations with a known model, by repeated sweeps


Model-free
Learning from sampled experience, with no transition model


TD target
The one-sample estimate \(r + \gamma \cdot(\text{value of next state})\) that an update moves towards


On-policy, off-policy
Learning the value of the policy that collects the data, or of another one


Replay buffer
A store of past transitions, sampled at random for training


Target network
A slowly updated copy of the Q-network that computes the TD targets


Actor, critic
A network that outputs actions, and one that scores them with Q





After this week you can

Explain why the expected reward of a stochastic policy is smooth even when the reward is a step.
Write the Bellman equations for \(V^\pi\), \(V^*\) and \(Q^*\), and say what value iteration and policy iteration do with them.
Explain the difference between Q-learning and SARSA, and predict which route each learns along a cliff.
Name DQN’s two stabilizers and the bias Double DQN removes.
Compare discretization, sampling (CEM) and an actor network (DDPG) as ways to choose a continuous action.

title: Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Think of learning the way home in a new city without a map. At first you wander. Over time you learn how promising each street corner is: “from here it’s about ten minutes”. Once every corner has such a number, choosing a turn is easy: take the street to the corner with the best number. You never need to plan the whole route; the numbers carry the long-range information. Value functions are those numbers, and the Bellman equation says how a corner’s number relates to its neighbours’: this corner is worth one minute plus the next corner.



A step reward, a smooth objective
The lecture opens with a car on a narrow mountain road: +1 for each step on the road, -1 for falling off the cliff ▶ 03:41. As a function of the car’s position this reward is a step: flat on either side, with a jump at the edge. Its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the edge, so gradient descent on the reward itself learns nothing ▶ 04:12. RL never optimizes the reward of one action, though; it optimizes the expected reward under a stochastic policy ▶ 05:15. If the car’s position is spread out by the policy’s randomness, the expected reward is the step averaged over that spread: a smooth curve whose slope is never zero ▶ 06:16. In this page’s version, with a spread of 0.6, the slope two units from the edge is still -0.005: small, but it points the right way (Figure 2).








Figure 2: A step reward and its expectation. Grey: the reward as a function of the car’s sideways position, +1 on the road and -1 past the edge at 1. Coloured: the expected reward when the position is Gaussian around μ with standard deviation σ. The wider the policy’s randomness, the smoother the curve and the further from the edge its slope reaches.







Value: how good is it to be here?
The expected return tells you how good a policy is overall, but to learn from it you would have to run every episode to the end: let the car fall off the cliff before learning that falling is bad ▶ 07:19. The Markov property offers a shortcut. Because the future depends only on the current state, a single number per state can summarize everything ahead: the value \(V^\pi(s)\), the expected return from \(s\) onwards ▶ 08:57. Any return splits into the reward now plus the discounted return from the next state, so values satisfy a one-step recursion, the Bellman equation (Equation 3) ▶ 11:01. Updating a value from the next state’s estimated value, rather than waiting for the real outcome, is called bootstrapping ▶ 11:31.
The optimal value \(V^*(s)\) is the best any policy can achieve from \(s\) ▶ 12:02. Once you have it, acting optimally needs no long-range planning: from each state, take the action whose one-step lookahead is best ▶ 13:05.


Value iteration: the ripple
Value iteration starts with every value at zero and applies the Bellman optimality update to every state, again and again ▶ 14:09. In a grid world with one reward at the goal, the first sweep gives value only to the cells next to the goal; the second to their neighbours; information flows backwards from the goal one step per sweep ▶ 16:13. The update is a contraction, so the values converge ▶ 14:39.
This page’s warehouse grid has a start on the left, a goal on the right, a short route that runs along a row of hazards (-1), and a longer route round the top past some walls. Each move goes the intended way with probability \(1 - p\) and slips sideways otherwise, half to each side; \(p = 0.2\) is the lecture’s 80/10/10. With no slips, the optimal route is the short one: 6 steps. With \(p = 0.2\), a sideways slip on the short route could drop the robot into a hazard, and the optimal policy takes the long way round: 13.5 steps on average, reaching the goal in 99.4% of episodes. The goal’s value reaches the start after 6 sweeps either way. With slips, though, it takes 110 sweeps for the values to settle, against 9 without.




Value iteration on the warehouse grid with slip probability 0.2: values spread back from the goal sweep by sweep, settle, and the greedy policy they imply carries a robot to the goal.

What to watch for. At sweep 1 only the goal’s neighbours turn blue; each sweep adds one more ring of cells, so the colour reaches the start at sweep 6. The cells beside the hazards stay paler than the top row: from there, one slip in ten ends in a hazard. After the jump to the converged values the arrows appear, and the route from the start goes up and round the top. Two arrows in the bottom row point straight into the wall: pushing against the wall means a slip can only go sideways, never up into a hazard. The robot then slips 5 times on its way, 3 of them into a wall or the edge of the grid, where it stays put; each time, the arrow in its new cell points it back onto the route.


Policy iteration: measure, then improve
Policy evaluation answers a simpler question than value iteration: how good is this policy? It uses the same update with the maximum replaced by the policy’s own action ▶ 17:47. Policy iteration alternates: evaluate the current policy exactly, then switch every state to its greedy action under those values ▶ 19:21. Each round can only improve the policy, and there are finitely many policies, so it stops at the optimum, usually after few rounds ▶ 20:56. On the warehouse grid it needs at most 9 rounds for every slip probability tried (Figure 4).


Q-functions: bake the model into the values
Both methods need the transition model, and acting with \(V^*\) needs it too: the greedy step averages over where each action might lead. A robot rarely has such a model, and evaluating it for every candidate action at every control step would be slow ▶ 21:58. The Q-function stores a value per state and action: the expected return after taking \(a\) in \(s\). The averaging over the dynamics is done once, during training, and baked into Q; at test time acting is just “pick the action with the largest Q” ▶ 22:59.


Q-learning: learn from samples
Q-learning removes the model from training as well: instead of averaging over all possible next states, it takes one action, observes one transition, and nudges Q towards the TD target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) ▶ 25:34. The world becomes its own simulator. The price is data: Q-learning needs many more transitions than dynamic programming needs sweeps ▶ 27:10.
Because the target always uses the best next action, regardless of what the robot actually did next, Q-learning learns the optimal policy’s values from data collected by any policy: random exploration, an old policy, a human. It is off-policy ▶ 28:45. SARSA changes one thing: its target uses the action the robot will actually take next, exploration included. It learns the value of the exploring policy itself (on-policy), and so it is wary of states where its own random moves are dangerous ▶ 29:47.
On a cliff walk, where the shortest route runs along the edge, the difference is visible ▶ 30:51. With 10% random moves, Q-learning’s greedy route runs along the edge in all 20 training runs (11 steps), but while it is still exploring it keeps falling off and averages -40.9 per episode over the last 100 episodes. SARSA’s greedy route runs along the top row, as far from the edge as the grid allows (median 15 steps), and SARSA earns -23.9 per episode while exploring (Figure 5).


Deep Q-learning
Tables do not scale to camera images: an 84 × 84 frame stack has astronomically many possible states ▶ 32:26. DQN replaces the table by a convolutional network that maps frames to one Q-value per action, trained with Q-learning targets ▶ 33:28. With one architecture and one set of hyperparameters it learned 49 Atari games from pixels ▶ 34:02. Two stabilizers made it work. A replay buffer stores transitions and trains on random minibatches, which breaks the correlation between consecutive samples ▶ 35:05. A target network, a slowly updated copy, computes the targets, so an update does not immediately move its own target ▶ 36:08.
One flaw remains: the maximum of noisy estimates is, on average, larger than the maximum of the true values ▶ 37:42. In this page’s toy, with 8 actions whose true values are all 0 and whose estimates carry unit noise, the maximum estimate averages 1.43. Double DQN lets the online network choose the action and the target network score it; with independent errors, the toy’s bias drops to +0.001 ▶ 38:14.


Continuous actions: the max is a search
DQN takes a maximum over a list of actions. A robot arm’s action is a continuous vector, and there is no list to scan ▶ 39:15. The lecture gives three ways out ▶ 39:47:

Discretize. Ten bins per joint for a 7-joint arm is \(10^7\) actions. Discretizing where it matches the task can work well: the pushing-and-grasping system scores every pixel of a top-down image as a place to push or grasp, and learns by itself to push objects apart before grasping ▶ 41:19.
Search. Sample candidate actions and keep the best, or refine the samples with the cross-entropy method (CEM): sample, keep the best few, fit a Gaussian to them, repeat ▶ 44:21. CEM can lock onto a lower peak, and its cost is paid at every control step. QT-Opt used it to learn grasping from over 580,000 real grasp attempts ▶ 45:54.
Learn the argmax. DDPG trains a second network, the actor, to output the action the critic (the Q-network) rates highest; choosing an action becomes one forward pass ▶ 46:56. The actor follows the critic’s gradient with respect to the action, and explores by adding Gaussian noise to its output ▶ 49:00. It is notoriously sensitive to hyperparameters ▶ 50:04.

In this page’s 7-dimensional toy, CEM with 640 evaluations of Q reaches the true peak in 72% of runs and settles on a lower peak in 17%; even 64,000 uniform samples average only 0.91 of the peak’s value 1. Gradient ascent climbs whichever hill it starts on: 58% of random starts reach the top, 40% the lower peak (Figure 8).

title: Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
text:
Key concepts & formulae
The lecture’s notation: \(V^\pi\) and \(Q^\pi\) for values, \(P(s' \mid s, a)\) for the dynamics, \(r(s, a)\) for the reward, \(\gamma\) for the discount. The ADM book writes \(U^\pi\) for \(V^\pi\) and \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) for the dynamics.

Smoothing by expectation

\[
J(\mu) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)}\big[r(y)\big] = 2\,\Phi\Big(\frac{c - \mu}{\sigma}\Big) - 1
\tag{1}\]

In words. For the step reward (+1 on the road, -1 past the edge at \(c\)), the expected reward is the chance of staying on the road minus the chance of falling off, a smooth function of the policy’s mean.
Term by term.

\(y\): the car’s sideways position, drawn from the policy.
\(\mu\), \(\sigma\): the policy’s mean (its parameter) and spread.
\(\Phi\): the standard normal cumulative distribution, \(P(y < c) = \Phi((c - \mu)/\sigma)\).
Its derivative, \(-\frac{2}{\sigma}\varphi\big(\frac{c - \mu}{\sigma}\big)\), is negative everywhere: moving away from the edge always helps, a little.

Why it holds. In general \(J(\theta) = \int r(y)\, p_\theta(y)\, dy\): the parameters enter only through the density, which is smooth, so \(J\) is smooth however rough \(r\) is. Week 5’s policy gradient turns this observation into an algorithm.


Value functions and the Bellman equation

\[
\begin{aligned}
V^\pi(s) &= \mathbb{E}_\pi\Big[\sum_{t \ge 0} \gamma^t r_t \;\Big|\; s_0 = s\Big] \\
J(\pi) &= \mathbb{E}_{s_0 \sim p(s_0)}\big[V^\pi(s_0)\big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]

In words. The value of a state is the expected discounted return when starting there and following \(\pi\). Averaging it over start states gives back Week 2’s objective.
Term by term.

\(\mathbb{E}_\pi\): over the policy’s choices and the world’s random transitions.
\(V^\pi\) is a local version of \(J(\pi)\): one number per state instead of one for the whole policy.


\[
\begin{aligned}
V^\pi(s) &= \textstyle\sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \big[ r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s'} V^\pi(s') \big] \\
\mathbb{E}_{s'} f(s') &= \textstyle\sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, f(s')
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]

In words. A state’s value is the expected reward of this step plus the discounted expected value of the next state.
Term by term.

\(r(s, a)\): the expected immediate reward.
\(\mathbb{E}_{s'} V^\pi(s')\): the value of where the action leads, averaged over the dynamics (second line); the rest of this page uses this shorthand.
For a fixed \(\pi\) this is a linear system: one equation per state.

Why it holds. Split the return: \(G_0 = r_0 + \gamma (r_1 + \gamma r_2 + \dots) = r_0 + \gamma G_1\). Take expectations given \(s_0 = s\); by the Markov property, \(\mathbb{E}[G_1 \mid s_1 = s'] = V^\pi(s')\) whatever happened before.

\[
\begin{aligned}
V^*(s) &= \max_a \big[ r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s'} V^*(s') \big] \\
\pi^*(s) &= \text{the maximizing } a
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]

In words. The best achievable value of a state is the best one-step lookahead using the best achievable values of the next states. The optimal policy picks the action that attains that maximum.
Term by term.

The maximum replaces the policy’s average over actions in Equation 3.
\(\pi^*\) is greedy with respect to \(V^*\): all long-range reasoning is already inside \(V^*\).



Dynamic programming

\[
\begin{aligned}
V_{k+1}(s) &= \max_a \big[ r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s'} V_k(s') \big] \\
\lVert V_{k+1} - V^* \rVert_\infty &\le \gamma\, \lVert V_k - V^* \rVert_\infty
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]

In words. Apply the right-hand side of Equation 4 to the current guess, for every state at once. Each sweep shrinks the largest error by at least a factor \(\gamma\).
Term by term.

\(V_0 = 0\): start knowing nothing.
\(\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty\): the largest error over all states.
The second line is the contraction property: two value functions get at least \(\gamma\) times closer under one sweep, so the sweeps converge to the unique fixed point \(V^*\).

Numeric check. On the warehouse grid (\(\gamma =\) 0.95), value iteration stops changing by more than \(10^{-8}\) after 9 sweeps without slips and 110 with \(p = 0.2\). Without slips every path to the goal is at most a few steps long, and the values are exact from sweep 8, once the ripple has passed; with slips, a robot can wander, and the error shrinks geometrically instead (Figure 4, left).

\[
\begin{aligned}
V^{\pi}_{k+1}(s) &= \textstyle\sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \big[ r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s'} V^{\pi}_k(s') \big] \\
\pi_{i+1}(s) &= \arg\max_a \big[ r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s'} V^{\pi_i}(s') \big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]

In words. Policy evaluation repeats the Bellman equation of a fixed policy until it converges to \(V^\pi\). Policy iteration alternates that evaluation with greedy improvement.
Term by term.

First line: no maximum, so no improvement; it only measures. (It can also be solved directly as a linear system.)
Second line: the greedy step. If it changes nothing, the policy is optimal.
Policy improvement theorem: the new policy is at least as good in every state, \(V^{\pi_{i+1}} \ge V^{\pi_i}\).

Numeric check. With \(p = 0.2\), the start state’s value under successive policies is 0.001, 0.028, 0.136, 0.164, 0.227, 0.526, 0.527, 0.527: never decreasing, optimal after 8 rounds.








Figure 4: Dynamic programming on the warehouse grid. Left: the largest error of value iteration’s estimate after each sweep (log scale), for four slip probabilities. Without slips the error drops to zero once the ripple has crossed the grid; with slips it shrinks geometrically, more slowly the more slippery the floor. Right: the start state’s value under each successive policy of policy iteration; it never decreases and reaches the optimum within a few rounds.







Q-functions and model-free learning

\[
\begin{aligned}
Q^*(s, a) &= r(s, a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{s'} \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \\
V^*(s) &= \max_a Q^*(s, a) \\
\pi^*(s) &= \arg\max_a Q^*(s, a)
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]

In words. The value of taking \(a\) in \(s\) and acting optimally afterwards. Once known, the optimal action is a lookup, with no model needed.
Term by term.

The sum over \(s'\) (the dynamics) now sits inside \(Q^*\): it is computed during training, not at decision time.
One extra input dimension (the action) is the price.


\[
\begin{aligned}
y &= r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') \qquad \text{(TD target)} \\
Q(s, a) &\leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \big[ y - Q(s, a) \big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]

In words. After one real transition \((s, a, r, s')\), move the stored value a fraction \(\alpha\) of the way towards the reward plus the discounted best value of the state actually reached.
Term by term.

\((s, a, r, s')\): one sampled transition, from any policy.
The TD target replaces the sum over \(s'\) in Equation 7 by the single \(s'\) that happened. Averaged over many updates, the samples stand in for the expectation.
\(\max_{a'}\): the target assumes the best next action, whatever the robot did next: off-policy.
\(\alpha\): the learning rate.


\[
\begin{aligned}
y &= r + \gamma\, Q(s', a'), \qquad a' \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s') \\
Q(s, a) &\leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \big[ y - Q(s, a) \big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\]

In words. The same update, but the target uses the action \(a'\) the robot actually takes next, chosen by its own (exploring) policy.
Term by term.

The name lists the update’s ingredients: \(s, a, r, s', a'\).
On-policy: it learns \(Q^\pi\) of the \(\varepsilon\)-greedy policy, mistakes included, not \(Q^*\).









Figure 5: Q-learning (orange) versus SARSA (blue) on a cliff walk, both acting ε-greedily with ε = 0.1, 20 runs each. Top: the greedy route each has learned after 500 episodes (the most common route across runs). Q-learning’s runs along the cliff edge; SARSA’s runs along the top row, as far from the edge as possible. Bottom: return per episode while learning (mean over runs, smoothed over 20 episodes). Q-learning’s random moves keep tipping it over the edge, so it earns less while exploring.







Deep Q-learning

\[
\begin{aligned}
y &= r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q_{\theta^-}(s', a') \\
\mathcal{L}(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{(s, a, r, s') \sim \mathcal{D}} \big[ (y - Q_\theta(s, a))^2 \big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}\]

In words. Regress the network’s Q-value towards the TD target, on transitions sampled at random from a replay buffer, with the target computed by a frozen copy of the network.
Term by term.

\(\mathcal{D}\): the replay buffer of past transitions; random minibatches break the correlation of consecutive steps.
\(\theta^-\): the target network’s weights, copied from \(\theta\) only every so often (or moved towards it slowly), so the target does not shift with every update.
The square: an ordinary regression loss; the target is treated as a fixed label (no gradient flows into it).

Figure 6: DQN’s training loop. The agent acts ε-greedily with the online network and stores every transition in the replay buffer. Training samples random minibatches from the buffer, computes targets with the target network, and updates the online network; every so often the target network copies the online one.






\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\big[\max_a \hat Q_a\big] &\ge \max_a \mathbb{E}\big[\hat Q_a\big] \\
a^\star &= \arg\max_{a'} Q_\theta(s', a') \\
y^{\text{double}} &= r + \gamma\, Q_{\theta^-}(s', a^\star)
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}\]

In words. The maximum of noisy estimates is on average at least as large as the largest true value, so Q-learning targets are biased upwards. Double DQN picks the next action with one network and scores it with the other.
Term by term.

\(\hat Q_a\): the estimate for action \(a\) in the next state, with zero-mean noise. The action with the luckiest noise wins the max, so the noise does not average out.
First line: Jensen’s inequality, since the maximum is a convex function.
\(y^{\text{double}}\): the Double DQN target. If the two networks’ errors are independent, the scoring network’s error at the chosen action has mean zero.

Numeric check. With \(K\) actions of true value 0 and unit noise, the bias of the plain maximum is the expected maximum of \(K\) standard normals: 0.564 for 2 actions (\(1/\sqrt{\pi}\)), 1.424 for 8, 2.344 for 64. The toy’s measured biases are 0.568, 1.427 and 2.342; the double estimator’s are -0.003, +0.001 and -0.015 (Figure 7).








Figure 7: Bias of the maximum over K noisy action-value estimates whose true values are all 0 (unit noise, 20,000 trials per point). Orange: the plain maximum, as in the Q-learning target; the line is the exact expected maximum of K standard normals. Blue: the double estimator, which picks the action with one set of estimates and scores it with an independent set.







Continuous actions

\[
\nabla_\phi J \approx \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}} \Big[ \nabla_a Q_\theta(s, a)\big|_{a = \mu_\phi(s)}\; \nabla_\phi\, \mu_\phi(s) \Big]
\tag{12}\]

In words. Ask the critic which way to change the action to raise Q, and change the actor’s weights so that its output moves that way.
Term by term.

\(\mu_\phi(s)\): the actor, a network that outputs a continuous action.
\(\nabla_a Q_\theta(s, a)\): the critic’s slope with respect to the action, at the actor’s current choice.
\(\nabla_\phi \mu_\phi(s)\): how the actor’s output depends on its weights. The product is the chain rule; automatic differentiation computes it by backpropagating \(Q_\theta(s, \mu_\phi(s))\) through both networks.
The critic itself is trained as in Equation 10, with the actor’s action in place of the max.









Figure 8: Finding the best action in a 7-dimensional action space, with a Q-function that has a global peak (Q = 1) and a lower one (Q = 0.7). Left: the best Q found by uniform random sampling against the number of samples (mean of 40 runs, ±1 standard deviation), with the cross-entropy method at its cost of 640 evaluations. Right: where 200 runs of CEM and of gradient ascent from a random start end up.

title: Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
text:
Algorithm & code
The course’s homework asks students to implement value iteration, policy iteration, DQN, PPO and SAC, so this page shows results for those, not code. The code below covers the two other ideas of the lecture: tabular TD control, and choosing a continuous action.

Q-learning and SARSA

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def cliff_step(pos, a) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], float, bool]:
    """One move on the cliff grid: -1 per step; stepping into the cliff (the
    bottom row between start and goal) costs -100 and sends the agent back
    to the start; reaching the goal ends the episode."""
    r = min(max(pos[0] + ACTIONS[a][0], 0), CLIFF_ROWS - 1)
    c = min(max(pos[1] + ACTIONS[a][1], 0), CLIFF_COLS - 1)
    if r == CLIFF_ROWS - 1 and 0 < c < CLIFF_COLS - 1:
        return CLIFF_START, -100.0, False
    return (r, c), -1.0, (r, c) == CLIFF_GOAL

def eps_greedy(q_row, eps, rng) -> int:
    """Random action with probability eps, else the best (random tie-break)."""
    if rng.random() < eps:
        return int(rng.integers(4))
    best = np.flatnonzero(q_row == q_row.max())
    return int(rng.choice(best))

def td_control(method, rng, episodes=500, eps=0.1, alpha=0.5, gamma=1.0):
    """Tabular Q-learning ("q") or SARSA ("sarsa") on the cliff grid.

    Both act epsilon-greedily. Q-learning's target uses the best next
    action (off-policy); SARSA's uses the next action it will actually take
    (on-policy). Returns the Q-table (rows, cols, 4) and each episode's
    return, shape (episodes,)."""
    Q = np.zeros((CLIFF_ROWS, CLIFF_COLS, 4))
    returns = np.empty(episodes)
    for ep in range(episodes):
        pos, total = CLIFF_START, 0.0
        a = eps_greedy(Q[pos], eps, rng)
        for _ in range(1000):                 # cap for very early episodes
            nxt, r, done = cliff_step(pos, a)
            total += r
            a2 = eps_greedy(Q[nxt], eps, rng)
            if done:
                target = r                    # no value beyond the goal
            elif method == "q":
                target = r + gamma * Q[nxt].max()    # best next action
            else:
                target = r + gamma * Q[nxt][a2]      # SARSA's next action
            Q[pos][a] += alpha * (target - Q[pos][a])
            pos, a = nxt, a2
            if done:
                break
        returns[ep] = total
    return Q, returns


import numpy as np
import torch

from rlc.toys import w04_rl as cliff     # the cliff walk on this page

torch.manual_seed(0)
gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)


def td_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, a2, done, method, alpha=0.5, gamma=1.0):
    """One tabular update in place. Q: (rows, cols, 4) tensor.

    Indexing with a tuple of ints gives a 0-d tensor; += on it writes
    through to Q (it is a view), so no reassignment is needed."""
    if done:
        target = torch.tensor(r)
    elif method == "q":
        target = r + gamma * Q[s2].max()          # off-policy: best a'
    else:
        target = r + gamma * Q[s2][a2]            # on-policy: actual a'
    Q[s][a] += alpha * (target - Q[s][a])


def act(Q, s, eps):
    if torch.rand(1, generator=gen).item() < eps:
        return int(torch.randint(4, (1,), generator=gen))
    return int(Q[s].argmax())                     # ties -> first index


for method in ("q", "sarsa"):
    Q = torch.zeros(cliff.CLIFF_ROWS, cliff.CLIFF_COLS, 4)
    for _ in range(300):
        s = cliff.CLIFF_START
        a = act(Q, s, 0.1)
        for _ in range(500):
            s2, r, done = cliff.cliff_step(s, a)
            a2 = act(Q, s2, 0.1)
            td_update(Q, s, a, r, s2, a2, done, method)
            s, a = s2, a2
            if done:
                break
    path = cliff.greedy_path(Q.numpy())
    assert path[-1] == cliff.CLIFF_GOAL           # greedy route reaches it
    if method == "q":
        assert len(path) - 1 == cliff.CLIFF_COLS + 1   # along the edge



The two methods differ in one line: the target. Everything else, including how they act, is shared.


Choosing a continuous action: CEM and an actor

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def cem_argmax(rng, n=64, elite=8, iters=10, init_std=0.6):
    """Cross-entropy method: sample n actions from a Gaussian, keep the
    `elite` best by Q, refit the mean and std to them, repeat.
    Returns the final mean action and its Q; costs n * iters evaluations."""
    mu, std = np.zeros(DIM), np.full(DIM, init_std)
    for _ in range(iters):
        noise = rng.standard_normal((n, DIM))
        a = np.clip(mu + std * noise, -1, 1)               # (n, DIM)
        best = a[np.argsort(q_landscape(a))[-elite:]]      # (elite, DIM)
        mu, std = best.mean(axis=0), best.std(axis=0) + 1e-3
    return mu, float(q_landscape(mu))


import torch.nn as nn

DIM = cliff.DIM                    # 7-dimensional action, as in the toy


def critic(s, a):
    """Stand-in for a trained Q-network: the toy's landscape, in torch,
    shifted by the state. s: (B, 1), a: (B, 7) -> (B,)."""
    peak = torch.full((DIM,), 0.5) + 0.1 * s           # (B, 7)
    decoy = torch.full((DIM,), -0.5)
    w2 = 2 * cliff.WIDTH ** 2
    return (torch.exp(-((a - peak) ** 2).sum(-1) / w2)
            + 0.7 * torch.exp(-((a - decoy) ** 2).sum(-1) / w2))


@torch.no_grad()                   # action selection needs no gradients
def cem_action(s, n=64, elite=8, iters=10):
    """QT-Opt-style CEM for one state s: (1,) -> action (7,)."""
    mu, std = torch.zeros(DIM), torch.full((DIM,), 0.6)
    for _ in range(iters):
        a = (mu + std * torch.randn(n, DIM)).clamp(-1, 1)   # (n, 7)
        q = critic(s.expand(n, 1), a)                        # (n,)
        best = a[q.topk(elite).indices]                      # (elite, 7)
        mu, std = best.mean(0), best.std(0) + 1e-3
    return mu


s0 = torch.tensor([0.0])
assert critic(s0[None], cem_action(s0)[None]).item() > 0.6   # a peak

# DDPG's actor: learn the argmax instead of searching for it.
actor = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, DIM),
                      nn.Tanh())                    # actions in [-1, 1]
nn.init.zeros_(actor[2].weight)
with torch.no_grad():
    actor[2].bias.fill_(0.3)                        # start near the peak
opt = torch.optim.Adam(actor.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
states = torch.rand(256, 1)                         # a batch from "replay"
q_before = critic(states, actor(states)).mean().item()
for _ in range(200):
    # Maximize Q(s, mu(s)): backprop goes through the critic into the
    # actor (eq. dpg). Only the actor's weights are in the optimizer.
    loss = -critic(states, actor(states)).mean()
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
q_after = critic(states, actor(states)).mean().item()
assert q_after > q_before and q_after > 0.99



CEM spends its effort at decision time: 640 evaluations of Q per action in this toy. The actor spends it during training, and then answers with one forward pass, but only where the critic’s gradient leads: started near the lower peak, it would stay there.

title: Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
text:
Papers

Papers discussed in class






Evolution Strategies as a Scalable Alternative to Reinforcement Learning Salimans, Ho, Chen, Sidor & Sutskever · arXiv 2017
Trains neural-network policies without value functions or backpropagation through time: perturb the weights with Gaussian noise, run each perturbed policy, and move the weights towards the perturbations that scored well. Its appeal is that it parallelizes almost perfectly across many machines.

Workers share random seeds, so each needs to send only one number, the return of its perturbed policy; this scaled to over a thousand workers with near-linear speed-ups (Abstract, Sec. 1).
With 1,440 CPU workers, ES solved the MuJoCo 3D humanoid task in under 10 minutes (Sec. 1).
On Atari it matched A3C’s final scores on most games using 3 to 10 times as much data, while skipping backpropagation and value functions (Sec. 1).
As a black-box method it is unaffected by action frequency, delayed rewards and long horizons, and needs no discounting (Abstract).

On this page: The scaled-up relative of Week 2’s random search; this week’s value-based methods take the opposite route, exploiting the MDP’s step-by-step structure.









Learning Synergies between Pushing and Grasping with Self-supervised Deep Reinforcement Learning Zeng, Song, Welker, Lee, Rodriguez & Funkhouser · IROS 2018
Learns when to push and when to grasp in cluttered piles by Q-learning, rewarded only for successful grasps. Two fully convolutional networks score every pixel of a top-down image as a place to push or to grasp, at several gripper orientations, and the robot takes the best-scoring action.

Actions as pixels: each network outputs a dense map of Q-values over end-effector positions and orientations, so the argmax over actions is an argmax over an image (Abstract, Sec. 1).
Pushing emerges without being rewarded directly: the Q-function values pushes that make later grasps succeed (Abstract).
Fully self-supervised by trial and error, it learns in a few hours of training and beats baseline grasping systems in simulation and on a real robot, including on new objects (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s example of handling a large action space by discretizing it in a way that matches the geometry of the task.









Precise and Dexterous Robotic Manipulation via Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning Luo, Xu, Wu & Levine · Science Robotics 2025
A system that trains vision-based manipulation policies with reinforcement learning directly on real robots, in hours. It combines a sample-efficient off-policy RL algorithm with human demonstrations and with corrections a person makes during training, plus a pretrained visual backbone.

Near-perfect success rates and fast cycle times on dynamic, precise and dual-arm tasks within 1 to 2.5 hours of real-world training (Abstract).
On average twice the success rate and 1.8 times faster execution than imitation-learning baselines and earlier RL approaches (Abstract).
Off-policy learning lets demonstrations, human corrections and the robot’s own experience share one replay buffer (Sec. 1).

On this page: Off-policy Q-learning with a replay buffer, this week’s core machinery, made practical on real hardware; human corrections echo DAgger from Week 3.





Key papers from the lecture






Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning Mnih et al. · Nature 2015
The deep Q-network (DQN): Q-learning with a convolutional network that reads raw game frames and outputs one Q-value per action. One algorithm, network and set of hyperparameters learned 49 Atari games from pixels and the score alone.

Experience replay: store transitions and train on random minibatches of them, which breaks the correlation between consecutive samples (Abstract).
A separate target network, updated only periodically, computes the learning targets and stabilizes training (Abstract).
Performance comparable to a professional human games tester across the set of games (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s bridge from tabular Q-learning to deep RL, and the source of the replay buffer and target network.









Deep Reinforcement Learning with Double Q-learning van Hasselt, Guez & Silver · AAAI 2016
Shows that DQN systematically overestimates action values on Atari, and fixes it by letting the online network choose the next action while the target network scores it.

Evidence that DQN’s overestimations are common and harm performance in several Atari games (Abstract).
Double DQN: a one-line change to the target that decouples choosing the best action from evaluating it (Abstract).
Lower value estimates and much better scores on several games (Abstract).

On this page: The overestimation toy on this page: the maximum of noisy estimates is biased upward, and a second, independent estimate removes the bias.









QT-Opt: Scalable Deep Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Based Robotic Manipulation Kalashnikov et al. · CoRL 2018
Closed-loop grasping from an over-the-shoulder RGB camera, learned by Q-learning from over 580,000 real grasp attempts. Continuous actions are handled by picking the action with the cross-entropy method on the Q-function.

A Q-function with over 1.2 million parameters reaches 96% grasp success on unseen objects (Abstract).
Learned behaviors include regrasping, probing objects, pushing them into better positions before grasping, and reacting to disturbances (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s example of the sampling route to the argmax over continuous actions: the cross-entropy method at every control step.









Continuous control with deep reinforcement learning Lillicrap et al. · ICLR 2016
Deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG): an actor network outputs the action directly and is trained to maximize a Q-network critic, so continuous actions need no search at test time.

An actor-critic, model-free algorithm based on the deterministic policy gradient that carries DQN’s ideas to continuous action spaces (Abstract).
One algorithm, architecture and set of hyperparameters solved more than 20 simulated physics tasks, some directly from pixels (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s third route to the argmax over actions: learn it with a second network instead of searching for it.

title: Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
text:
Guest spotlight
Aviral Kumar (Carnegie Mellon University and Google DeepMind) asks what it would take to copy the recipe behind large language models in robot learning ▶ 02:08. For language models that recipe has three stages: pre-training on internet text, a mid-training stage that teaches behaviors useful for problem solving, such as long chains of thought that search, backtrack and retry, and post-training with reinforcement learning on the model’s own attempts ▶ 03:40. Robot learning today has pre-training on expert demonstrations and fine-tuning on more of them, with no analogue of mid-training and no RL post-training ▶ 04:43.
His proposal for mid-training is to collect recovery and correction data: let a policy run, and when it heads somewhere bad, have a person first back it up to a familiar state and then show the correct continuation ▶ 10:55. His argument is that recovering is easier to learn than solving the task from wherever the mistake left the robot, because there are many good states to go back to ▶ 12:27. The policies then retry the way reasoning models do, and success grows with the number of recoveries in an episode; on a shirt-hanging task he reports results comparable to a prior system trained on 89 hours of expert data, from 5 hours of this kind of data ▶ 17:05.
For post-training he describes policy-agnostic RL. Expressive policies (diffusion, flow matching, transformers that sample tokens) are hard to update with the usual actor-critic gradient through the policy’s output ▶ 23:44. Instead, improve the actions: sample several from the policy, keep the ones the Q-function rates highest, take gradient steps on those actions with respect to Q, and then train the policy to imitate the improved actions with its ordinary likelihood loss ▶ 24:45. He reports fine-tuning the OpenVLA model on a real robot in about 40 minutes, with no demonstrations ▶ 26:16.
How it connects to this week. Policy-agnostic RL is this lecture’s continuous-action problem in a new setting: its “keep the best samples” step is the sampling route of QT-Opt, its “gradient step on the action” is DDPG’s \(\nabla_a Q\), and it sidesteps DDPG’s need to differentiate through the policy. Recovery data relates to Week 3’s DAgger, with one difference: the human first goes back, then continues.

title: Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
text:
Solved problems
1. Bellman by hand. A robot in state A can wait (reward 0, stay in A) or move to B (reward 0). In B, any action gives reward 1 and ends the episode. With \(\gamma = 0.9\), what are \(V^*(A)\), \(V^*(B)\), and the optimal action in A?






TipSolution





\(V^*(B) = 1\) (one reward, then nothing). For A, Equation 4: \(V^*(A) = \max(0 + 0.9\,V^*(A),\; 0 + 0.9\,V^*(B))\). Waiting forever gives \(V = 0.9 V\), so \(V = 0\) along that branch; moving gives \(0.9 \times 1 = 0.9\). So \(V^*(A) = 0.9\) and the optimal action is to move. Value iteration finds this in two sweeps: \(V_1 = (0, 1)\), \(V_2 = (0.9, 1)\).



2. How many sweeps? Value iteration starts at \(V_0 = 0\), rewards are at most 1 in absolute value, and \(\gamma = 0.95\). How many sweeps guarantee an error below \(10^{-6}\)? Why did the slip-free warehouse grid need far fewer?






TipSolution





The initial error is at most \(\max|V^*| \le 1/(1 - \gamma) = 20\). By Equation 5 the error after \(k\) sweeps is at most \(20 \cdot 0.95^k\); this is below \(10^{-6}\) once \(k > \ln(5 \times 10^{-8}) / \ln 0.95 \approx 328\). The bound is a worst case. On the slip-free grid every episode reaches a terminal state within a few steps, and after that many sweeps the values are exact: value iteration is then computing a finite-horizon answer. With slips the robot can bounce around for a long time, and the error really does shrink geometrically, as Figure 4 shows.



3. Grids, samples and actors. A 7-joint arm’s action is discretized into 10 levels per joint. How many Q-values must DQN’s output layer have? How many evaluations of Q does CEM with 64 samples and 10 iterations need per action, and how many does a DDPG actor need?






TipSolution





Discretized: \(10^7\) outputs, one per joint combination, which is impractical to train and to maximize. CEM: \(64 \times 10 = 640\) evaluations of the Q-network per control step, affordable in a batch on a GPU but paid every step. DDPG: zero evaluations of Q at decision time; one forward pass of the actor. The cost moved into training, where the actor learns to follow \(\nabla_a Q\) (Equation 12).



4. Which data can each learner use? A lab has thousands of hours of logged robot data from an old controller and some human teleoperation. Can Q-learning learn from it? Can SARSA?






TipSolution





Q-learning: yes in principle. Its target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) needs only \((s, a, r, s')\), not who chose \(a\) or what came next, so any transitions can be replayed (Equation 8). In practice, purely offline Q-learning struggles when the data cover few actions per state, because the max then queries actions it has never seen. Week 5 returns to this. SARSA: not directly, since its target needs the next action \(a'\) of the policy being evaluated; with logged data it would learn the value of the old controller, not of a better one.



5. Two actions, one coin flip. Two actions have true value 0 and estimates with independent unit Gaussian noise. What is the expected value of the larger estimate? What if the noise has standard deviation 0.5?






TipSolution





For two independent standard normals, \(\max(X, Y) = \frac{X + Y}{2} + \frac{|X - Y|}{2}\), and \(X - Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2)\), so \(\mathbb{E}|X - Y| = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{2/\pi} = 2/\sqrt{\pi}\). Hence \(\mathbb{E}[\max] = 1/\sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.564\), matching the toy’s 0.568 (Equation 11). The bias scales with the noise: with standard deviation 0.5 it is \(0.5/\sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.282\). It never averages away, because every Q-learning target takes such a maximum.

title: Week 4 · Reinforcement Learning I
text:
Recap

RL optimizes expectations, and expectations are smooth. A stochastic policy turns a step reward into a smooth objective. Why it matters: it is the reason any RL algorithm can learn from success/failure signals, and the starting point of Week 5’s policy gradients.
Values summarize the future, and the Bellman equation computes them one step at a time. Why it matters: bootstrapping from the next state’s value is what makes learning from single transitions possible.
With a model, dynamic programming finds the optimal policy. Value iteration ripples values back from the rewards; policy iteration alternates evaluation and improvement and converges in few rounds. Why it matters: every later value-based method is an approximation of these updates.
Q-functions remove the model from acting, and Q-learning removes it from learning. Q-learning is off-policy; SARSA is on-policy and more cautious while exploring. Why it matters: off-policy learning lets robots reuse every past transition, which is how real-robot RL (QT-Opt, HIL-SERL) becomes affordable.
Deep Q-learning needs stabilizers and fails in characteristic ways. Replay buffers and target networks stabilize it; the maximum over noisy estimates overestimates, and double estimators fix it. Why it matters: these tricks recur in nearly every deep RL system for robots.
Continuous actions turn the max into a search. Discretize with structure, search with CEM, or learn an actor. Why it matters: the same choice appears in Week 5’s actor-critic methods and in fine-tuning large robot policies, as the guest talk shows.

Common pitfalls.

Treating the TD target as a label that should receive gradients. It is a fixed target; in PyTorch, compute it under torch.no_grad() or with .detach().
Forgetting terminal states: the target at a terminal transition is just \(r\).
Expecting Q-learning’s greedy route to be safe while exploring; it optimizes for a robot that has stopped exploring.
Reading high Q-values as high performance: the max over noisy estimates is biased upward.
Assuming CEM or gradient ascent finds the global best action; both settle on the nearest good peak.
Exploring a real robot with random joint commands; add small noise to a sensible action instead.

Connections. Week 2 gave the MDP and the objective; this week computed it with values. Week 3’s DAgger reappears in HIL-SERL’s human corrections and in the guest’s recovery data. Week 5 optimizes the policy directly with gradients and combines both ideas in actor-critic methods. In the ADM Companion: value iteration and policy iteration with worked examples, and Q-learning and SARSA on a towpath next to a canal.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
Week 1 argued that robots need feedback: a policy that looks again at every step beats a plan executed blind. This week builds the vocabulary for both halves of that statement. The first half is robot control: how to describe a robot’s body, where its hand is for given joint angles, which joint angles put the hand where you want it, and how motors follow a motion smoothly and accurately. The second half is the Markov decision process (MDP): the mathematical frame in which a policy picks actions, the world responds, and rewards say how well it went. Every later week works inside this frame. Week 3 learns policies by copying an expert, Weeks 4 and 5 learn them from reward, and from Week 6 on the policies grow into large generative models.
The question this week answers: how does a robot turn a goal into motor commands, and how do we describe the decision-making above that, for any robot, in one language?


The key ideas at a glance

Rigid bodies and frames. A robot is a chain of rigid parts. A part’s pose is a position plus an orientation, stored as a \(4 \times 4\) (or, in the plane, \(3 \times 3\)) matrix; multiplying these matrices converts coordinates between frames, such as from a camera on the roof to the car’s base.
Three spaces. The configuration space holds every combination of joint angles; the workspace holds every point the hand can reach; the task space is where the job itself is defined. An arm with more joints than the task needs is redundant: it can move its elbow while keeping its hand still.
Kinematics. Forward kinematics (joint angles to hand pose) is a formula. Inverse kinematics (hand pose to joint angles) can have several answers or none; in practice it is solved by gradient steps using the Jacobian.
Trajectories and PID. A robot cannot jump to new joint angles. Quintic time scaling starts and ends a move with zero velocity and acceleration, unlike straight-line interpolation. A PID controller then makes the motors follow: the P term pulls towards the target, the D term damps, the I term cancels a steady load such as gravity.
Policies, states and observations. A policy \(\pi_\theta(a_t \mid o_t)\) is a distribution over actions given what the robot observes. Unlike a classifier’s mistake, a policy’s action changes what it sees next.
The MDP. States, actions, transition probabilities and a reward: \((\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R)\). The goal is the policy with the highest expected (discounted) return. Whether rewards are sparse or dense can decide whether learning gets started at all.



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Pose
Where a rigid body is and which way it faces


Frame
A coordinate system attached to a body: the base, a camera, the gripper


Link, joint, end effector
A rigid part, a connection that lets two parts move, and the tool at the end of the arm


Degrees of freedom (DoF)
How many numbers it takes to pin down the robot’s configuration


Configuration space (C-space)
The set of all joint configurations


Workspace, task space
Points the hand can reach, and the space the task is defined in


Forward / inverse kinematics
Joint angles to hand pose, and hand pose back to joint angles


Jacobian
How much the hand moves when each joint turns a little


Waypoint
An intermediate target on the way from one configuration to the next


PID controller
A feedback rule that turns tracking error into motor commands


Policy
The rule that picks an action from what the robot observes


State, observation
The complete description of the world, and the partial view the sensors give


MDP
Markov decision process: states, actions, transitions and rewards


Return, discount
Total reward of a run, and the factor that makes later rewards count for less





After this week you can

Chain homogeneous transforms to move a point between frames, and count a robot’s degrees of freedom.
Explain why an obstacle in the workspace becomes a strangely shaped region in configuration space, and why inverse kinematics can have two answers.
Say what each term of a PID controller does, and why a quintic time scaling is kinder to motors than linear interpolation.
Write down an MDP, the probability of a trajectory, and the expected return, and compute them for a small example.
Explain why a sparse reward can stall learning.

title: Week 2 · Robot Control & MDPs
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Think of driving to a friend’s house. Somewhere in your head a decision is made: “turn left at the next corner”. That is the policy. Your arms translate “turn left” into a steering-wheel angle: inverse kinematics. You turn the wheel smoothly rather than yanking it: a trajectory. And while you turn, you keep correcting, because the road is bumpy and the car drifts: feedback control. This lecture covers the bottom three layers first, then gives the top layer, the decisions, a precise mathematical form.
