Figure 4: Robotics as multimodal sequence modeling. The camera image and the instruction become tokens; a transformer continues the sequence with action tokens; these are converted back to a continuous motion; the robot moves, and the next image starts the loop again.





How do you write a continuous action as a token? RT-2 cuts each action dimension into 256 equal bins and writes the bin’s number (Equation 4). That loses a little precision every step. The second toy replays a 0.6 m reaching motion through tokens. Replayed blind, the rounding errors add up; a robot that re-observes where it is and tokenizes the correction keeps the error to one rounding. With 256 bins the largest deviation from the demonstrated path is 0.37 mm replayed blind and 0.04 mm closed loop; with 16 bins, 2.4 mm and 0.6 mm.


Not quite: why robots aren’t chatbots
“So we train a large transformer on robot data and we’re done?” Not quite ▶ 52:36. Robot data is scarce, because a person usually has to teleoperate or supervise every minute of it. It is multimodal and heterogeneous, since every robot has different sensors and actuators. The model must run in real time on the robot, so a giant model behind a slow API won’t do ▶ 53:59. And evaluating a policy on real hardware is slow, expensive and hard to reproduce ▶ 54:27.


Two families of algorithms
Most of the course builds on two frameworks ▶ 54:45. Imitation learning is close to supervised learning: learn a function from observations to the expert’s actions. Reinforcement learning learns a policy by trial and error to maximize a reward. In both, the robot’s own actions change what it observes next, so its data are not independent samples (Equation 2), which breaks a basic assumption of supervised learning ▶ 56:28. Week 3 shows what that costs.


One shift, three fields
The lecture ends by showing the same change in three places ▶ 59:59. Housework: from the teleoperated PR1 of 2007 to recent videos of robots doing similar tidying tasks autonomously. Driving: from the 2005 DARPA challenge, where vehicles with stacks of sensors and probabilistic models struggled across the desert, to cars that now drive themselves to their buyers ▶ 1:01:00. Humanoids: from the 2015 DARPA Robotics Challenge, where the best machines struggled to open a door or walk straight, to the smooth, dexterous humanoid demonstrations of today ▶ 1:01:30. In each case the move is from hand-coded behaviour to learned behaviour, and the course is about the machinery behind that move. (These are the lecturer’s examples; the demos are companies’ own videos, with the caveats about demos that Week 11 spells out.)
Why study it? The lecturer gave three reasons ▶ 1:03:03: the field spans the whole stack, from reasoning in foundation models down to the PID controllers that move the motors; its algorithms carry over across robots, from cars to humanoids to planetary rovers; and it may be close to its own “ChatGPT moment”.

title: Week 1 · Introduction to Robot Learning
text:
Key concepts & formulae

Supervised learning assumes independent examples

\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta^\star &= \arg\min_\theta \; \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \ell\big(f_\theta(x_i),\, y_i\big) \\
(x_i, y_i) &\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} p(x, y)
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

In words. Fit a function so that its predictions match the labels on the training examples, where every example is drawn on its own from one fixed distribution.
Term by term.

\(f_\theta\): the model, with parameters \(\theta\); \(x_i\) an input, \(y_i\) its label.
\(\ell\): a loss that is small when the prediction matches the label, such as squared error.
i.i.d.: drawing \((x_1, y_1)\) tells you nothing about \((x_2, y_2)\), and test inputs come from the same \(p\) as training inputs. Classifying one cat photo does not change the next photo.



The robot loop breaks that assumption

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_t &\sim \pi(a_t \mid o_t) \\
s_{t+1} &\sim p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t) \\
o_{t+1} &\sim p(o_{t+1} \mid s_{t+1})
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]

In words. The robot picks an action from what it observes, the world moves to a new state that depends on that action, and the robot observes the new state.
Term by term.

\(\pi\): the policy, the thing robot learning produces.
\(s_t\): the true state of the world; \(o_t\): what the robot’s sensors report about it. They differ, which is exactly the state-estimation problem.
\(p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)\): the dynamics. Because \(a_t\) appears here, the next observation depends on the robot’s own choice: consecutive data points are not independent, and a different policy sees a different distribution of states. Week 2 builds this into Markov decision processes.



Open loop and closed loop

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{open loop:}\quad a_t &= \text{plan}_t(\hat{s}_0) \\
\text{closed loop:}\quad a_t &= \pi(\hat{s}_t)
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]

In words. An open-loop controller fixes every action in advance from one estimate of the start; a closed-loop controller computes each action from the latest estimate.
Term by term.

\(\hat{s}_0\), \(\hat{s}_t\): the robot’s estimates of its state at the start and at step \(t\), never exactly right.
\(\text{plan}_t\): the \(t\)-th action of a plan made once. An error in \(\hat{s}_0\) shifts the whole executed path, and motor errors add up step after step because nothing looks at the result.
\(\pi(\hat{s}_t)\): an action chosen from the current estimate. A motor error at step \(t\) shows up in \(\hat{s}_{t+1}\) and gets corrected.

Numeric check. In the doorway toy at σ = 0.2, sense-plan-act reaches the goal in 53% of episodes and closed loop in 100% (Figure 3).


Actions as tokens

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta &= \frac{a_{\max} - a_{\min}}{B} \\
k &= \min\!\Big(B - 1,\; \Big\lfloor \frac{a - a_{\min}}{\Delta} \Big\rfloor\Big) \\
\hat{a} &= a_{\min} + \big(k + \tfrac{1}{2}\big)\Delta \\
|a - \hat{a}| &\le \tfrac{\Delta}{2}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]

In words. Cut the range of one action dimension into \(B\) equal bins, write down which bin the action falls in, and later replace that bin number by the bin’s centre. The round trip is off by at most half a bin.
Term by term.

\(a\): one dimension of a continuous action, for example how far the gripper moves along \(x\) in one step.
\([a_{\min}, a_{\max}]\): the range covered by the bins; values outside are clipped to the end bins.
\(B\): the number of bins; RT-2 uses 256 per dimension.
\(\Delta\): the bin width, the precision of one token.
\(k\): the token, an integer from 0 to \(B - 1\), which a language model can emit like a word.
\(\hat{a}\): the bin centre, what the robot actually executes.

Numeric check. With 256 bins, this page’s worked example tokenizes one move with an error of at most half a bin (0.0349 mm in its wider dimension); replayed open loop over 100 steps, those errors grow to the 0.37 mm quoted above.


One sequence model for images, words and actions

\[
\begin{aligned}
&p\big(k_{1}, \dots, k_{D} \mid \text{image}, \text{text}\big) \\
&\quad = \prod_{j=1}^{D} p\big(k_{j} \mid \text{image}, \text{text}, k_{1}, \dots, k_{j-1}\big)
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]

In words. The model reads the image tokens and the instruction tokens, then writes the action one token at a time, each conditioned on everything before it, exactly as a language model writes a sentence.
Term by term.

\(k_1, \dots, k_D\): the action’s tokens, one per action dimension (RT-2 writes 8 integers per action).
The product: the chain rule of probability, which is how autoregressive transformers factor any sequence.
Image and text: inputs the model only reads; the same network, pretrained on web images and text, now also writes actions. Week 3 returns to this factorization as a way to represent several possible actions, and Week 7 covers the transformers that compute it.

title: Week 1 · Introduction to Robot Learning
Week 1 · Introduction to Robot Learning
text:
Algorithm & code

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def tokenize(a, lo, hi, bins) -> Array:
    """Index of the bin each value falls in: [lo, hi] cut into `bins` equal
    bins; values outside are clipped to the end bins. Same shape as a."""
    k = np.floor((np.asarray(a) - lo) / (hi - lo) * bins).astype(int)
    return np.clip(k, 0, bins - 1)

def detokenize(k, lo, hi, bins) -> Array:
    """The centre of bin k: the value a token stands for."""
    return lo + (np.asarray(k) + 0.5) * (hi - lo) / bins

def replay(path, bins, closed_loop=False):
    """Execute the path's moves after a round trip through tokens.
    Open loop: tokenize the demonstrated moves and add them up.
    Closed loop: at each step tokenize the move from where the robot
    actually is to the next point on the path.
    Returns the executed path (T+1, 2)."""
    moves = np.diff(path, axis=0)                   # (T, 2) actions
    lo, hi = action_range(moves)                    # per-dimension range
    p, out = path[0].copy(), [path[0].copy()]
    for t in range(len(moves)):
        want = path[t + 1] - p if closed_loop else moves[t]
        p = p + detokenize(tokenize(want, lo, hi, bins), lo, hi, bins)
        out.append(p.copy())
    return np.array(out)


import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

from rlc.toys import w01_intro as toy

torch.manual_seed(0)
BINS, CTX = 256, 16

# Tokenize the reaching motion: (100, 2) moves -> (100, 2) integers.
moves = np.diff(toy.reach_path(), axis=0)
lo, hi = toy.action_range(moves)
tokens = torch.tensor(toy.tokenize(moves, lo, hi, BINS))   # int64
seq = tokens.reshape(-1)        # (200,): x, y, x, y, ... like RT-2's ints

# Training windows: predict token j+1 from tokens up to j.
win = seq.unfold(0, CTX + 1, 1)                 # (185, CTX+1)
inputs, targets = win[:, :-1], win[:, 1:]       # (185, CTX) each


class TinyActionGPT(nn.Module):
    """A decoder-only transformer over action tokens. A real VLA puts
    image and instruction tokens in front of these in the same sequence."""

    def __init__(self, vocab=BINS, d=64, ctx=CTX):
        super().__init__()
        self.tok = nn.Embedding(vocab, d)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(ctx, d)
        layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, nhead=4, dim_feedforward=128,
                                           batch_first=True)
        self.body = nn.TransformerEncoder(layer, num_layers=2)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d, vocab)

    def forward(self, idx):                      # idx: (N, L) int64
        L = idx.shape[1]
        h = self.tok(idx) + self.pos(torch.arange(L))       # (N, L, d)
        # Causal mask: position j may only attend to positions <= j.
        mask = nn.Transformer.generate_square_subsequent_mask(L)
        return self.head(self.body(h, mask=mask, is_causal=True))


model = TinyActionGPT()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
losses = []
for _ in range(150):
    logits = model(inputs)                                  # (N, L, BINS)
    # cross_entropy wants (N*L, BINS) logits and (N*L,) class indices
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, BINS), targets.reshape(-1))
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    losses.append(loss.item())

assert logits.shape == (inputs.shape[0], CTX, BINS)
assert losses[-1] < losses[0] / 3



The NumPy code is everything the page’s tokenizer does: a floor and a clip to get the token, a bin centre to get back. The PyTorch sketch goes one step further, training a small transformer to continue the reaching motion’s token sequence, which is the core of how RT-2 and its successors produce actions.

title: Week 1 · Introduction to Robot Learning
text:
Papers
There are no discussion papers in Week 1. These are papers the lecture relies on.

Key papers from the lecture






Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models Open X-Embodiment Collaboration · ICRA 2024
Pools robot-learning data sets from many labs into one standardized collection and trains a single policy on all of it. The question is whether robot learning can follow the recipe of vision and language: one large model trained on diverse data from many robots, rather than one model per robot and task.

A data set of more than a million robot trajectories from 22 robot embodiments, contributed by 21 institutions (Sec. I, Fig. 1).
RT-1-X and RT-2-X, versions of RT-1 and RT-2 trained on the mixture (Sec. IV).
Positive transfer: RT-1-X’s mean success rate is 50% higher than that of either the original method for each data set or RT-1 (Fig. 4).

On this page: Week 1: the lecture’s case for generalist robot policies and for data as the bottleneck, and the worked example on data-set sizes. Week 9: the data behind Octo and CrossFormer, and the positive transfer this page’s first toy reproduces.









RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control Brohan et al. · CoRL 2023
Takes a vision-language model trained on web data and fine-tunes it to output robot actions written as text tokens, alongside its usual web tasks. The resulting vision-language-action model (VLA) follows commands that never appear in the robot data and can do simple reasoning about which object to pick.

Actions as tokens: each continuous action dimension is cut into 256 uniform bins, so an action becomes 8 integers that the language model writes like words (Sec. 3.2).
Co-fine-tuning on robot trajectories and web vision-language tasks, so the robot policy keeps the web knowledge (Abstract).
Over 6,000 evaluation trials showing better generalization to new objects and emergent abilities such as picking the smallest object or an improvised hammer (Abstract).

On this page: The second toy on this page, which tokenizes a motion the same way, and the lecture’s view of robotics as multimodal sequence modeling.

title: Week 1 · Introduction to Robot Learning
text:
Solved problems
1. Token precision. A robot’s end effector moves at most 2 cm per control step along each axis, and each axis is tokenized into 256 uniform bins over [−2 cm, 2 cm]. What is the largest rounding error per step, and how many tokens does one action with 3 position axes, 3 rotation axes and a gripper need?






TipSolution





Bin width \(\Delta = 4\,\text{cm} / 256 \approx 0.156\) mm; the largest error per axis is half of that, about 0.078 mm (Equation 4). One action needs one token per dimension: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 tokens. RT-2 adds an eighth for “episode finished” (Sec. 3.2 of the paper).



2. Blind replay. Suppose every move of a 100-step motion rounds the same way, by \(+0.05\) mm along \(x\). How far off is the end of a blind replay? And with closed-loop correction?






TipSolution





Blind: the errors add up to \(100 \times 0.05 = 5\) mm. Closed loop: each step aims at the next point of the path from where the robot actually is, so the previous error is part of the correction; what remains after any step is one rounding, at most half a bin. Systematic rounding is the worst case for open loop and harmless for closed loop. In this page’s toy, rounding is partly systematic, which is why the open-loop error grows (Figure 8).



3. A plan made from a wrong start. A sense-plan-act robot believes it starts 0.3 to the left of where it really is. Ignoring motor noise, where does its executed path end, and does it get through a door 0.8 wide?






TipSolution





Executing the plan moves the robot by exactly the planned displacements, so the whole executed path is the planned path shifted 0.3 to the right: it ends 0.3 from the goal. At the door it passes 0.3 off the door’s centre line, inside the 0.4 half-width, so it gets through, but with only 0.1 to spare; add a little motor drift and it hits the frame. A closed-loop robot’s next estimate would show it is off course, and it would correct.



4. Is it a robot? Classify a dishwasher, a teleoperated surgical robot and a chatbot on a phone by the two tests from the lecture’s class discussion: does it change the physical world, and does it act on its own?






TipSolution





Dishwasher: changes the world (cleans dishes) and runs on its own, but only one fixed program in a fixed environment. Surgical robot: changes the world with great dexterity, but a surgeon makes every decision; it is teleoperated, like the 2007 PR1. Chatbot: reasons generally and acts autonomously in conversation, but has no body and changes nothing physical. Robot learning aims for all three at once: physical effect, autonomy, and generality.



5. Why the data are not i.i.d. A cleaning robot records (camera image, action) pairs while it works. Give two reasons these pairs are not independent and identically distributed samples.






TipSolution





Not independent: consecutive images are nearly identical, and each action determines the next image (Equation 2). Not identically distributed: change the policy and the robot visits different places, so the distribution of images changes; a policy trained on one robot’s data then meets different states when it acts itself. Week 3 shows how this makes small imitation errors snowball.

title: Week 1 · Introduction to Robot Learning
text:
Recap

Sense-plan-act needs an exact picture of the world. Why it matters: it explains both the success of factory robots and the falls of humanoids, and motivates closed-loop, learned policies.
Feedback beats precision. In the doorway toy, re-estimating at every step kept success at 100% up to σ = 0.25, while planning once fell below half by σ ≈ 0.21. Why it matters: every policy in this course is a closed-loop controller.
Moravec’s paradox: physical skill is the hard part, and its data is scarce. Why it matters: data collection is a theme of nearly every week, from demonstrations (Week 3) to human video (Week 3’s guest) to pooled data sets (Week 9).
Write actions as tokens and robotics becomes sequence modeling. Why it matters: this is how vision-language-action models reuse web-scale pretraining (Weeks 7 and 9), at the cost of a small, controllable loss of precision.
Robot data are not i.i.d. Why it matters: it is the root of compounding error in imitation (Week 3) and of the exploration problem in reinforcement learning (Weeks 4–5).

title: Week 1 · Introduction to Robot Learning
text:
Cheat sheet & connections








Name
Formula
Where




Supervised learning
\(\min_\theta \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)\), i.i.d. data
Equation 1


Robot loop
\(a_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid o_t)\), \(s_{t+1} \sim p(\cdot \mid s_t, a_t)\)
Equation 2


Open vs closed loop
\(\text{plan}_t(\hat{s}_0)\) vs \(\pi(\hat{s}_t)\)
Equation 3


Tokenization
\(k = \lfloor (a - a_{\min})/\Delta \rfloor\), \(\lvert a - \hat{a} \rvert \le \Delta/2\)
Equation 4


Sequence model
\(\prod_j p(k_j \mid \text{image}, \text{text}, k_{<j})\)
Equation 5



Common pitfalls.

Treating robot data like a supervised data set. Consecutive samples are correlated, and the policy changes the distribution it is evaluated on.
Assuming tokenized actions are exact. They are rounded to the bin centre; count the bins against the precision the task needs.
Judging a robot demo without asking whether it was teleoperated.

Connections. Next week formalizes the robot loop as a Markov decision process. Week 3 is the first family of algorithms, imitation learning, and shows what the non-i.i.d. data cost; Weeks 4 and 5 are the second, reinforcement learning. The action tokens on this page return in Week 7, with RT-2’s bins and their compressed successor FAST, and the vision-language-action models built on them in Week 9. Week 12 reviews the whole course in one table. In the ADM Companion, Chapter 1 introduces decision making under uncertainty, the broader setting of the robot loop.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
Week 2 set up the language: a robot observes \(o_t\), picks an action \(a_t\) from a policy \(\pi(a_t \mid o_t)\), and the world moves to a new state. It did not say where a good policy comes from. This week gives the first and most direct answer: copy a person who already knows how. Weeks 4 and 5 give the other answer, learning from reward by trial and error. Several ideas from this week return later: expressive action distributions in Week 6 (generative models), histories and transformers in Week 7, and imitation at scale in the generalist robot policies of Week 9.
The question this week answers: how do you turn a set of expert demonstrations into a policy, and why does straightforward copying break down?


The key ideas at a glance

Behavioral cloning (BC). Treat each demonstrated moment as a labelled example, “in this situation the expert did this”, and train a network to predict the expert’s action with ordinary supervised learning. It is simple and often works.
Distribution shift and compounding error. Training data come from the states the expert visited; at test time the policy sees the states it visits. A small mistake leads to a state no demonstration covers, where the next mistake is more likely. If each step has a small chance \(\varepsilon\) of an unrecoverable mistake, the expected number of bad steps over a task of length \(T\) grows like \(\varepsilon T^2\), not \(\varepsilon T\).
Show the policy how to recover. Either fake recovery data (side cameras labelled “steer back”), or run the policy, let an expert label the states it actually reaches, and retrain: DAgger. Letting a human take over only when the robot errs (human-gated DAgger) makes the labelling cheaper.
Non-Markovian behavior and causal confusion. People act on memory and on things the robot cannot see. Feeding the policy a history helps in principle, but a high-capacity network may then latch onto a signal that merely correlates with the expert’s action instead of its cause.
Multimodal behavior. When experts solve the same situation in different ways, a regression loss averages them, and the average of “left of the tree” and “right of the tree” is straight into it. Policies need distributions that can hold several peaks: mixtures of Gaussians, discretized actions, diffusion, or latent-variable models.
From one task to any goal. Conditioning the policy on a goal, and learning from unscripted “play” data, turns imitation into a way to learn many skills at once.



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Demonstration
A recorded run of an expert doing the task: the sequence of states (or observations) and actions


Expert policy \(\pi^*\)
The behavior being imitated, usually a person teleoperating the robot


Behavioral cloning (BC)
Supervised learning from (observation, expert action) pairs


Distribution shift
The states seen at test time differ from the states in the training data


Compounding error
Each mistake makes the next one more likely, so errors pile up over a trajectory


DAgger
Dataset Aggregation: label the learner’s own states with expert actions and retrain


Mode
One distinct way of doing the task, a peak of the action distribution


Causal confusion
The policy keys on a correlate of the expert’s action rather than its cause


Play data
Unscripted teleoperation with no fixed task, later relabelled with goals





After this week you can

Write down behavioral cloning as a loss and train it.
Explain, with the \(\varepsilon T^2\) argument, why small imitation errors snowball, and how DAgger changes the bound to \(\varepsilon T\).
Recognize when a policy needs a multimodal action distribution, and name four ways to build one.
Spot non-Markovian demonstrations and the risk of causal confusion when adding history.

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Imagine learning to drive only by watching dashcam videos of a careful driver. Every frame shows the car in the middle of its lane, so you learn exactly what to do there. Then, on your first drive, a gust nudges you towards the verge. Nothing you watched shows a car near the verge, so you have no idea that you should steer back. The fix is not more videos of perfect driving. It is videos of recoveries, or an instructor who tells you what to do in the situations you get yourself into.



Copy what the expert did
Behavioral cloning is the dashcam student. You collect pairs: “the car was a little left of the centre line, heading slightly right, the road curving left: the expert steered a little left.” A network learns to map the first half of each pair to the second. The lecture introduces it as the most straightforward version of imitation learning ▶ 03:58. Formally it is a regression loss, Equation 1.


One slip and you are somewhere new
The road toy on this page makes the analogy concrete. The expert keeps the car’s heading along the road and, like most drivers, ignores small offsets from the centre line; only past 0.3 (in road half-widths of 1.0) does it steer back. Its demonstrations were recorded on a calm day, so the car never left that band and the data never show a steer-back. At deployment, each step has a 0.2% chance of a gust that turns the car by 0.4 rad.




One gust, many clones, seen from above. The expert (black), the cloned policy of each of 10 training seeds (orange) and the DAgger policy of the same seeds (blue) drive the same stretch of road; at step 10 one gust turns them all towards the edge.

What to watch for. All the cars start together on the centre line and stay together until the gust: before it, the cloned policies drive as well as the expert. The gust pushes every car towards the edge by about the same amount. From there the colours separate. The black expert and the blue DAgger cars turn back into the road. The orange clones fan out: some steer back by luck, some drift across the edge, and some turn sharply away, because nothing in their calm-day data said what to do there.








Figure 2: One gust, many clones. Each line is one car’s offset from the centre line; at step 10 the same gust turns every car towards the verge. The expert (dashed) steers back. Orange: the BC policy of each training seed that is stable on a calm day; blue: the DAgger policy of the same seeds. Dashed grey lines are the road edges. Offsets beyond ±4 are drawn at ±4.





The gust pushes every car out by about the same amount at first. The expert’s offset peaks at 0.60, past its deadband, and it steers back. The cloned policies split. They were trained only on near-centre states, so what each does further out is an accident of its training run: of the 10 BC policies, 6 happen to steer back, 4 end off the road, and 3 of those end more than five units from the centre line. This is the lecture’s tightrope walker: once you fall off, no demonstration shows how to get back on ▶ 15:16. The general version is distribution shift: the states the policy visits stop matching the states the expert visited ▶ 06:18. The formal cost of it is Equation 2.


Ask the expert about your own mistakes
If the problem is missing recovery data, supply it. NVIDIA’s self-driving car added two side cameras and labelled their images “steer right” and “steer left”, which creates recovery examples without ever crashing ▶ 12:01. DAgger does the same thing systematically: drive with the current policy, ask the expert what it would have done at each state the policy reached, add those pairs to the data, and retrain ▶ 18:44. In the road toy, DAgger’s policies (blue above) have seen post-gust states labelled with the expert’s steer-back, and every one of them recovers. Asking an expert to relabel thousands of states afterwards is tedious, so in practice a human often watches and takes over only when the robot is about to fail (human-gated DAgger) ▶ 20:48. The formal version is Equation 3.


What the expert knew that the robot didn’t
Experts are not Markovian: a driver brakes because of how a cyclist moved over the last few seconds, and a teleoperator sees the scene from angles the robot’s camera does not ▶ 25:38. Giving the policy a history of observations is the obvious fix. It can backfire. In the lecture’s drawer example, the demos always show a 10 N force spike when the gripper grasps the handle, so the network learns “pull when the force reads 10 N” instead of “pull when the handle is grasped”; if the gripper slips and reads 2 N, it never pulls ▶ 29:56. This is causal confusion, the subject of one of this week’s papers.


Two good answers can average to a bad one








Figure 3: Half the demonstrations (grey) pass the obstacle on the left, half on the right. The MSE policy (blue) predicts the average sideways speed, which near the start is about zero, and runs into the obstacle. The binned policy (orange) keeps both options as separate peaks, takes the more likely one, and follows one side. One training seed; the hit rates over 20 seeds are in the text.





Real demonstrations rarely agree on one way to do a task: there are endless ways to close a drawer, and different operators pick different ones ▶ 32:11. A mean-squared-error loss is minimized by the average action, and the average of two good routes around a tree is straight into the tree ▶ 33:46. In this toy, with half the demos passing on each side, the MSE policy hit the obstacle in 50% of 20 training seeds and the binned policy in 0%. The fix is a policy that outputs a distribution able to hold several peaks ▶ 34:41: see Equation 4, Equation 5, and the latent-variable model in Equation 6.


From one task to any goal
Task labels are a blunt instrument: is a sliding door moved halfway “opened”? The lecture argues for goal-conditioned policies, \(\pi(a_t \mid s_t, s_g)\), that learn to reach any goal state from any start, and for play data: operators teleoperate the robot freely, with no task, and every window of that data is relabelled with its own final frame as the goal ▶ 43:37. Play data are cheap and diverse, but highly multimodal, which is why the lecture pairs them with a latent-variable policy (Equation 6).

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Key concepts & formulae
The lecture’s notation: \(s_t\) is the state, \(o_t\) the observation, \(a_t\) the action at time \(t\); \(\pi^*\) is the expert and \(\pi_\theta\) the learned policy with parameters \(\theta\); \(\mathcal{D}\) is the demonstration data set. ADM Chapter 18 writes the expert as \(\pi_E\).

Behavioral cloning

\[
\theta^\star = \arg\min_\theta \; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|} \sum_{(s, a^*) \in \mathcal{D}} \big\lVert \pi_\theta(s) - a^* \big\rVert^2
\tag{1}\]

In words. Pick the network weights that make the policy’s action as close as possible, on average, to what the expert did in the same state.
Term by term.

\(\mathcal{D}\): every (state, expert action) pair from every demonstration, pooled; the trajectory structure is thrown away.
\(\pi_\theta(s)\): the policy’s action in state \(s\), a deterministic network output here.
\(a^*\): the action the expert took in that state.
\(\lVert\cdot\rVert^2\): squared error, summed over action dimensions. Any regression or classification loss can stand here; the next sections replace it.

Why it holds: MSE predicts the average. For a fixed state, the number \(c\) that minimizes \(\mathbb{E}[(c - a^*)^2]\) over the expert’s possible actions satisfies \(\frac{d}{dc}\mathbb{E}[(c-a^*)^2] = 2(c - \mathbb{E}[a^*]) = 0\), so \(c = \mathbb{E}[a^* \mid s]\): the mean of the actions the expert took there. That is fine when the expert is consistent and disastrous when it is not.
Quick check. In the obstacle toy, the demonstrated sideways speeds near the fork \((x, y) = (2, 0)\) have mean +0.011 (from 48 demo steps, 28 steering left and 20 right). The MSE network outputs -0.001 there: close to that average, and close to neither group’s action.


Distribution shift and the \(\varepsilon T^2\) bound
BC minimizes its loss on states drawn from \(p_{\text{expert}}(s)\), the states the expert visits. What matters at test time is how it does on \(p_{\pi_\theta}(s)\), the states it visits. These differ as soon as the policy makes a mistake.

\[
\begin{aligned}
c(s, a) &= \begin{cases} 0 & a = \pi^*(s) \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
\Pr\big(\pi_\theta(s) \neq \pi^*(s)\big) &\le \varepsilon \quad (s \sim p_{\text{expert}}) \\[4pt]
\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^{T} c(s_t, a_t)\Big] &\le \varepsilon T \\
&\quad + (1-\varepsilon)\big(\varepsilon (T-1) + \dots\big) \\
&= O(\varepsilon T^2)
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]

In words. If the cloned policy errs with probability at most \(\varepsilon\) on the expert’s states, but an error takes it to states where it can no longer be trusted, its expected number of mistakes over \(T\) steps can grow with \(T^2\).
Term by term.

\(c(s, a)\): the cost of a step, 1 if the policy’s action differs from the expert’s.
\(\varepsilon\): the mistake rate on states the expert visits, which is what supervised training controls.
\(T\): the task length in steps.
\(\varepsilon T\): the cost of a first mistake at step 1, paid on all \(T\) steps (the tightrope: once off, always off).
\((1-\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon(T-1)\): no mistake at step 1, first mistake at step 2, paid on the remaining \(T-1\) steps; and so on.

Why it holds. A first mistake at step \(t\) costs at most \(T - t + 1\), and happens with probability at most \(\varepsilon\). Summing, \(\sum_{t=1}^{T} \varepsilon (T - t + 1) = \varepsilon \frac{T(T+1)}{2}\), which is \(O(\varepsilon T^2)\). Compare supervised learning on independent examples, where \(T\) predictions cost \(\varepsilon T\). The analysis is from Ross et al. (2011), cited in the lecture ▶ 15:16.
Numeric check. In the road toy, over 16 seeds × 200 cars, BC’s mean cumulative off-road steps are 1.5, 7.6, 27.1 and 82.5 at \(T =\) 50, 100, 200 and 400: a slope of 1.93 on a log-log scale, close to the quadratic’s 2. The measured rate at which an on-road BC car leaves is 0.0017 per step. If departures were permanent, that rate would predict 112 off-road steps by \(T = 400\); the toy measures 83, lower because 35% of the cars that left were back on the road at the end. DAgger’s policies, facing the same gusts, total 0.013.








Figure 4: Cumulative off-road steps per car against the horizon T, averaged over 16 training seeds and 200 cars each, all facing the same gusts. BC’s cost curves upward (shaded: ±1 standard error over seeds); the dashed line is the prediction from BC’s measured per-step departure rate if no car ever came back. DAgger’s cost stays near zero.

Figure 5: Behavioral cloning stops after the first training step. DAgger closes the loop: run the current policy, have the expert label the states it reached, add them to the data, and retrain.






\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{D} &\leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \big\{ (s, \pi^*(s)) : s \sim p_{\pi_\theta} \big\} \\
\theta &\leftarrow \arg\min_\theta \mathcal{L}(\pi_\theta, \mathcal{D})
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]

In words. Collect states by running the current learned policy, label each with the expert’s action, add them to everything collected so far, and refit.
Term by term.

\(s \sim p_{\pi_\theta}\): states drawn from the learner’s own trajectories, mistakes included. This is the distribution BC never trains on.
\(\pi^*(s)\): the expert’s label, “what I would do here”. The expert does not have to drive; it only has to answer.
\(\mathcal{D} \cup\): the old data are kept, so the policy does not forget earlier states (aggregation, the “Agg” in DAgger).
\(\mathcal{L}\): the same supervised loss as BC, for example Equation 1.

Why it helps. After enough rounds the training data cover the states the policy itself reaches, so the mistake rate \(\varepsilon\) holds where the policy actually is. A mistake no longer leads into unknown territory, and the bound drops from \(O(\varepsilon T^2)\) to \(O(\varepsilon T)\) (Ross et al., 2011). The cost is an expert who can be queried on states it did not choose, which the lecture flags as slow and costly in practice ▶ 19:55.


Expressive action distributions
When the expert’s action in a state has several modes, the policy must output a distribution \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) rather than a single action, and be trained by maximum likelihood instead of squared error.

\[
\pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k(s)\, \mathcal{N}\big(a;\, \mu_k(s), \Sigma_k(s)\big)
\tag{4}\]

In words. The network outputs \(K\) bell curves and a weight for each; the action is drawn from their weighted sum.
Term by term.

\(K\): the number of components, fixed in advance; the lecture notes this as the main limitation ▶ 34:41.
\(w_k(s)\): how likely mode \(k\) is in state \(s\); a softmax output, so the weights sum to 1.
\(\mu_k(s), \Sigma_k(s)\): the centre and spread of mode \(k\).

In the obstacle toy, two components would do: one centred on “steer left”, one on “steer right”, each with weight near one half at the fork.

\[
p(a_t \mid s_t) = \prod_{d=1}^{D} p\big(a_{t,d} \mid s_t, a_{t,1}, \dots, a_{t,d-1}\big)
\tag{5}\]

In words. Split the action into its \(D\) dimensions, chop each into bins, and predict the bins one dimension at a time, each conditioned on the ones already chosen.
Term by term.

\(a_{t,d}\): the bin chosen for dimension \(d\) (a class label), trained with cross-entropy.
The product: the chain rule of probability, exact for any joint distribution.
Why not one big grid: with \(D\) dimensions of \(B\) bins each, a joint grid has \(B^D\) classes; the product needs only \(D\) predictions of \(B\) classes each ▶ 35:27. This is how the first vision-language-action models emitted actions, as tokens from a transformer (Weeks 7 and 9).

The binned policy in the obstacle toy is the one-dimensional case, \(D = 1\) with 11 bins. At the fork its probabilities put 0.48 on the left-steering bins and 0.51 on the right-steering bins (Figure 6).
The lecture also previews diffusion policies, which turn noise into an action by repeated denoising and are the subject of Week 6 ▶ 37:32, and latent-variable policies, which receive an extra random input \(z\) that selects the mode ▶ 39:22. For the latter, the training objective is the evidence lower bound.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\log p_\theta(\tau \mid c) \;\ge\;\; & \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z \mid \tau, c)}\big[\log p_\theta(\tau \mid z, c)\big] \\
-\; & \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid \tau, c)\,\big\|\,p(z \mid c)\big)
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]

In words. We would like to maximize the likelihood of the demonstrated trajectory, but that requires averaging over every possible latent plan \(z\). Instead, maximize a lower bound: reconstruct the trajectory well from a plan inferred from it, while keeping that inferred plan close to what could be proposed from the start and goal alone.
Term by term.

\(\tau\): a short window of demonstration (states and actions); \(c = (s_c, s_g)\): its context, the current state \(s_c\) and the goal \(s_g\).
\(z\): a latent plan, a continuous vector that picks one way of getting from \(s_c\) to \(s_g\).
\(q_\phi(z \mid \tau, c)\): the posterior (“plan recognition”), which sees the whole window and infers which plan it followed.
\(p_\theta(\tau \mid z, c)\): the action decoder, the policy itself, rewarded for reproducing the window’s actions given the plan.
\(p(z \mid c)\): the prior (“plan proposal”), which sees only start and goal. The KL term pulls the recognized plans and the proposed plans together, so at test time the prior alone can propose plans.

Why it holds. For any distribution \(q\) over \(z\), \(\log p(\tau \mid c) = \log \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[p(\tau, z \mid c)/q(z)\big]\), which by Jensen’s inequality (\(\log\) is concave) is at least \(\mathbb{E}_q\big[\log p(\tau, z \mid c) - \log q(z)\big]\); splitting \(p(\tau, z \mid c) = p(\tau \mid z, c)\, p(z \mid c)\) gives the two terms. Because the plan absorbs the choice between modes, the decoder only has to model one mode at a time, as the lecture puts it ▶ 46:22.

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Algorithm & code

Behavioral cloning and DAgger

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def fit_policy(obs, actions, rng, epochs=300, hidden=32):
    """MLP from scaled observations to steering. Returns a batch policy
    (n, 3) -> (n,)."""
    X = obs / SCALE                         # (m, 3), each feature O(1)
    net = nn.init_mlp([3, hidden, hidden, 1], rng)
    params, _ = nn.fit(net, X, actions[:, None], "mse", "tanh",
                       alpha=0.01, epochs=epochs, rng=rng)
    return lambda o: nn.predict(params, o / SCALE)[:, 0]

def behavior_cloning(n_demos, T, rng):
    obs, act = expert_data(n_demos, T, rng)
    return fit_policy(obs, act, rng)

def dagger(n_demos, T, rng, eps=EPS, iters=4, stride=4, history=False):
    """Start from BC on the calm-day demos; then repeatedly drive the current
    policy at deployment (gusts included), ask the expert what it would have
    done at each visited state, add those (state, expert action) pairs, and
    refit on everything. Only every `stride`-th visited state is kept:
    neighbouring states are nearly identical, and fewer points fit faster.
    history=True returns the policy after every round, BC first."""
    obs, act = expert_data(n_demos, T, rng)
    policies = [fit_policy(obs, act, rng)]
    for _ in range(iters):
        starts = rng.uniform(0, WAVELEN, n_demos)
        _, new = rollout(policies[-1], T, eps, rng, starts)
        new = new[:, ::stride].reshape(-1, 3)    # (n_demos * T/stride, 3)
        obs = np.vstack([obs, new])
        act = np.concatenate([act, expert(new)])  # the expert relabels
        policies.append(fit_policy(obs, act, rng))
    return policies if history else policies[-1]


import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

from rlc.toys import w03_imitation as road   # the road toy on this page

torch.manual_seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
SCALE = torch.tensor(road.SCALE, dtype=torch.float32)

# Calm-day demos: obs (N, 3) = (offset, heading error, road turn),
# act (N,) = the expert's steering.
obs, act = road.expert_data(n_demos=10, T=200, rng=rng)
X = torch.tensor(obs, dtype=torch.float32) / SCALE     # (N, 3)
y = torch.tensor(act, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]    # (N, 1)

policy = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 32), nn.Tanh(),
                       nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 1))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=1e-2)


def train(X, y, steps):
    """Full-batch BC: regress the expert's action. Returns the losses."""
    losses = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss = F.mse_loss(policy(X), y)   # behavior cloning = regression
        opt.zero_grad()                   # .grad accumulates otherwise
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        losses.append(loss.item())
    return losses


losses = train(X, y, steps=300)
assert losses[-1] < losses[0] / 10
def as_numpy_policy(net):
    """Wrap the network for road.rollout: (n, 3) array -> (n,) array."""
    def act_fn(o):
        with torch.no_grad():               # acting needs no gradients
            x = torch.tensor(o, dtype=torch.float32) / SCALE
            return net(x)[:, 0].numpy()
    return act_fn


# DAgger: drive the current policy, let the expert label what it saw.
for _ in range(2):
    starts = rng.uniform(0, road.WAVELEN, 10)
    # Gust rate 1% (page: 0.2%) so two short rounds meet enough gusts.
    _, seen = road.rollout(as_numpy_policy(policy), 200, 0.01, rng, starts)
    seen = seen[:, ::4].reshape(-1, 3)              # (10 * 50, 3)
    labels = road.expert(seen)                      # "here I would do this"
    X = torch.cat([X, torch.tensor(seen, dtype=torch.float32) / SCALE])
    y = torch.cat([y, torch.tensor(labels, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]])
    train(X, y, steps=200)                          # refit on all data

assert X.shape == (2000 + 2 * 500, 3) and y.shape == (3000, 1)



The only difference between the two algorithms is the loop: BC trains once on the expert’s states; DAgger keeps adding the learner’s states, labelled by the expert (expert(new) in the NumPy version), and refits on everything.


A policy that can hold two modes

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def fit_mse(obs, acts, rng, epochs=400):
    """Regression: one sideways velocity per observation, MSE loss. Where
    demos disagree, MSE is minimized by their average."""
    net = nn.init_mlp([2, 32, 32, 1], rng)
    params, _ = nn.fit(net, obs / SCALE2, acts[:, None], "mse", "tanh",
                       alpha=0.01, epochs=epochs, rng=rng)
    return lambda o: nn.predict(params, o / SCALE2)[:, 0]

def to_bin(acts) -> Array:
    """Index of the nearest bin centre, (n,) ints."""
    return np.abs(acts[:, None] - BINS[None, :]).argmin(axis=1)

def fit_binned(obs, acts, rng, epochs=400):
    """Classification over BINS with cross-entropy. The network outputs a
    probability for every bin, so two modes stay two peaks. The policy takes
    the most likely bin."""
    net = nn.init_mlp([2, 32, 32, len(BINS)], rng)
    params, _ = nn.fit(net, obs / SCALE2, to_bin(acts), "cross_entropy",
                       "tanh", alpha=0.01, epochs=epochs, rng=rng)
    # (n, 2) -> (n, len(BINS)): one probability per bin, rows sum to 1
    probs = lambda o: nn.softmax(nn.predict(params, o / SCALE2))
    policy = lambda o: BINS[probs(o).argmax(axis=1)]
    return policy, probs


from rlc.toys.w03_imitation import (BINS, SCALE2, demos2, hits, rollout2,
                                     to_bin)

_, obs2, acts2 = demos2(20, 0.5, rng)                # half left, half right
X2 = torch.tensor(obs2 / SCALE2, dtype=torch.float32)   # (1000, 2)
target = torch.tensor(to_bin(acts2))                    # (1000,) int64 bins

binned = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.Tanh(),
                       nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.Tanh(),
                       nn.Linear(32, len(BINS)))        # one logit per bin
opt2 = torch.optim.Adam(binned.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
losses2 = []
for _ in range(400):
    # cross_entropy takes raw logits (N, K) and class indices (N,);
    # it applies log-softmax itself, so no softmax layer in the network.
    loss = F.cross_entropy(binned(X2), target)
    opt2.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt2.step()
    losses2.append(loss.item())


def most_likely_bin(o):
    """(n, 2) positions -> (n,) sideways speeds: the centre of the top bin."""
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = binned(torch.tensor(o / SCALE2, dtype=torch.float32))
    return BINS[logits.argmax(dim=-1).numpy()]     # argmax over bins


path, _ = rollout2(most_likely_bin)                 # (1, 51, 2)
assert losses2[-1] < losses2[0] / 2
assert not hits(path)[0]              # it commits to one side and clears it
assert abs(path[0, 25, 1]) > 1.0      # at x = 5 it is well off to one side



The binned network differs from the MSE one in two places: its last layer has one output per bin instead of one number, and its loss is cross-entropy over bin indices instead of squared error. Everything else, including the data, is identical.

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Papers

Papers discussed in class






Causal Confusion in Imitation Learning de Haan, Jayaraman & Levine · NeurIPS 2019
Giving a cloned policy more information can make it worse. With extra inputs, a network can reach low training error by relying on a signal that only correlates with the expert’s action, such as a dashboard brake light that comes on after the expert brakes, and then fails once its own actions change what it sees.

Names the failure, causal misidentification, and shows it in benchmark control tasks and a driving setting: the policy with more inputs does worse (Sec. 3).
Trains one network that masks its inputs according to a randomly sampled causal graph, so a single model holds a policy for every hypothesis about which inputs matter (Sec. 4.1).
Picks the right hypothesis with targeted interventions, using either environment reward or expert queries; in query mode it needs far fewer queries than DAgger (Sec. 2, Sec. 4.2).

On this page: The lecture’s drawer example, where a policy keys on a 10 N force spike instead of the grasped handle, and solved problem 5 on this page.









The Surprising Effectiveness of Representation Learning for Visual Imitation Pari, Shafiullah, Arunachalam & Pinto · RSS 2022
Splits visual behavior cloning into two separate jobs. First, an image encoder is trained with self-supervised learning on offline images; then, with no further training, the action for a new image is a distance-weighted average of the actions of its nearest demonstration frames in the encoder’s feature space (VINN).

A simple visual imitation method: a self-supervised (BYOL-style) encoder plus non-parametric locally weighted regression over the demonstrations (Sec. I).
Competitive with end-to-end behavior cloning on offline pushing, stacking and door-opening data (Sec. I).
On a real robot opening doors from 71 demonstrations: 80% success on doors seen in the data and 40% in new scenes, against 53.3% and 3.3% for the strongest baselines (Sec. I).

On this page: It keeps the behavioral-cloning recipe of copying demonstrated actions, but moves the hardest part, learning what to look at in an image, into a separate step that needs no action labels.









Transporter Networks: Rearranging the Visual World for Robotic Manipulation Zeng et al. · CoRL 2020
Treats pick-and-place as choosing pixels in a top-down view of the scene. One network scores every pixel as a place to pick; a second finds where to put the object by matching features cropped around the pick against the rest of the scene, at several rotations.

An action space that keeps the image’s spatial layout: actions are pixel locations and rotations, so what is learned at one position carries over to others (Sec. 1, Sec. 3).
Over 90% success on most of 10 simulated tabletop tasks from 100 demonstrations, where end-to-end baselines struggle with the same data (Sec. 1).
Its score maps can rank several good pick or place locations at once, so the policy can represent multimodal choices (Abstract).
Releases Ravens, a simulated benchmark for these tasks (Sec. 1).

On this page: A score map over pixels is a discretized action distribution, like the binned policy on this page: it can keep several good options as separate peaks instead of averaging them.





Key papers from the lecture






A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning Ross, Gordon & Bagnell · AISTATS 2011
Explains why copying an expert’s actions can go badly wrong (a learner’s mistakes take it to states the expert never showed, so errors compound) and introduces DAgger: repeatedly run the current policy, have the expert label the states it visits, add them to the data, and retrain. The result is a single deterministic policy with guarantees under the states it actually encounters.

Recalls that a classifier with mistake rate ε on the expert’s states can make on the order of εT² mistakes over T steps on its own states (Sec. 1).
DAgger (Dataset Aggregation), an iterative algorithm that trains one stationary, deterministic policy on the aggregated data from all rounds (Sec. 3).
Casts imitation as no-regret online learning and shows that any no-regret learner, under reduction assumptions, finds a policy that performs well on the states it induces (Abstract, Sec. 4).
Experiments on steering in the Super Tux Kart racing game, playing Super Mario Bros., and a sequence-labelling benchmark (Sec. 1, Sec. 5).

On this page: The εT² bound and the DAgger loop on this page; the road toy measures both.









End to End Learning for Self-Driving Cars Bojarski et al. · arXiv 2016
NVIDIA trained a convolutional network to map the image from a front-facing camera straight to a steering command, using only human driving as supervision. To teach recovery, the training images include views shifted off the lane centre and rotated, each labelled with a corrective steering command.

An end-to-end behavioral cloning system (DAVE-2), with no hand-designed lane detection or path planning, running at 30 frames per second (Abstract).
Recovery data without crashing: two off-centre views come from left and right cameras, and further shifts and rotations are synthesised by viewpoint transformation (Sec. 2, Sec. 5.2).
Reports driving autonomously about 98% of the time on a route in New Jersey, measured by counting interventions (Sec. 7.2).

On this page: The side-camera trick in the Intuition section and solved problem 3: synthetic recovery data instead of an expert in the loop.









Learning Latent Plans from Play Lynch et al. · CoRL 2019
Instead of recording demonstrations of specific tasks, operators teleoperate a robot freely (play). Play-LMP learns from windows of this data relabelled with their own final state as the goal, and organizes the different ways of reaching a goal in a latent plan space, which it samples from at test time.

Argues that play data are cheap (no task segmentation, labels or resets) and rich, covering about 4 times more interaction space than task demonstrations collected in the same time (Abstract).
Play-LMP: a goal-conditioned latent-variable policy trained with a plan-recognition posterior, a plan-proposal prior and an action decoder (Abstract, Sec. 1).
On 18 simulated visual manipulation tasks, a single play-trained policy substantially outperforms individual expert-trained policies, and it is more robust to perturbations (Abstract).

On this page: The goal-conditioned, latent-variable policy behind the ELBO equation on this page, and the lecture’s play-data case study.

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Guest spotlight
Danfei Xu (Georgia Tech) argues that robot learning should get its data the way language and vision models do: from people going about their lives, not only from people teleoperating robots ▶ 01:32. He frames robot learning as a triangle of data source, learning algorithm and physical system, and argues that changing one corner means redesigning the other two ▶ 02:07. Teleoperation ties all three together: data exist only where a person drives a particular robot, and the resulting policy works only on that robot.
His group’s EgoMimic records people doing tasks while wearing Meta’s Project Aria glasses, then treats human hands as one more embodiment alongside the robot’s arms and co-trains a single behavioral cloning policy on both ▶ 06:18. The robot even wears the same glasses as its camera, to shrink the viewpoint gap. In his scaling experiment, more teleoperation data improved the robot only gradually, while adding human data on top of a fixed amount of robot data gave a sharp jump; he also reports that people demonstrate some tasks up to ten times faster than teleoperators ▶ 11:27.
Co-training alone does not make human and robot data share a representation; inside the network they stayed in two separate clusters. EgoBridge adds a loss, based on optimal transport, that pulls the two distributions together while keeping their action structure, so that a task shown only in human data can transfer to the robot ▶ 15:11. The talk closes with EMMA, which extends the approach to mobile manipulation, and EgoVerse, a shared human-data set of about 1,300 hours at the time of the talk ▶ 29:11.
How it connects to this week. Every method in the talk builds on behavioral cloning; what changes is where \(\mathcal{D}\) comes from. Human data from wearable cameras is cheap and plentiful, but it is a different distribution from what the robot sees and does, which is this week’s distribution-shift problem at the level of the whole data set rather than a single trajectory.

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Solved problems
1. The bound, with numbers. A cloned policy makes an unrecoverable mistake with probability \(\varepsilon = 0.01\) per step on the expert’s states. For a task of \(T = 100\) steps, compare the BC bound with the \(\varepsilon T\) you would expect from independent predictions.






TipSolution





Independent predictions: \(\varepsilon T = 0.01 \times 100 = 1\) expected mistake. The BC bound from Equation 2: \(\varepsilon \frac{T(T+1)}{2} = 0.01 \times \frac{100 \times 101}{2} = 50.5\) expected bad steps, fifty times more. If departures are permanent and the rate is exactly \(\varepsilon\), the expected cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{100} \big(1 - 0.99^t\big) = 100 - 0.99 \cdot \frac{1 - 0.99^{100}}{0.01} \approx\) 37.2; the bound is looser because a car that has already left cannot leave again. Both are far above 1, and the gap grows with \(T\).



2. A lopsided fork. At the fork in the obstacle toy, suppose 70% of demonstrators steer left at \(+0.3\) and 30% steer right at \(-0.3\). What does a perfectly trained MSE policy output, and what does a binned policy that takes the most likely bin output?






TipSolution





MSE outputs the mean (Equation 1): \(0.7 \times 0.3 + 0.3 \times (-0.3) = 0.12\), a gentle left turn that no demonstrator made. Whether that clears the obstacle depends on whether the robot gets far enough to the side in time; set the explorer’s share to 0.7 and compare the seeds. The binned policy puts probability 0.7 on the \(+0.3\) bin and 0.3 on the \(-0.3\) bin and takes \(+0.3\): a real demonstrated action. Sampling from the bins instead would go right 30% of the time, also a valid way around.



3. Recovery labels without an expert in the loop. The NVIDIA car labels its left camera’s images “steer right”. Why does that produce the same kind of data DAgger collects, and what can it not provide?






TipSolution





The left camera sees the road as it would look if the car had drifted left: an off-centre state the expert never drove through. Labelling it “steer right” gives a (state, corrective action) pair, exactly what DAgger obtains by driving the learner and asking the expert. It is limited to the drifts the camera geometry simulates (a fixed sideways shift) and to a correction rule chosen by the engineer rather than an expert’s judgement; larger or different mistakes, such as the heading errors after a gust in the road toy, remain uncovered. DAgger covers whatever states the policy actually reaches.



4. Grids versus chains. A 7-dimensional arm action is discretized into 256 bins per dimension. How many classes does a joint grid need, and how many outputs does the autoregressive factorization (Equation 5) need?






TipSolution





Joint grid: \(256^7 = 2^{56} \approx 7.2 \times 10^{16}\) classes, impossible to train a softmax over. Autoregressive: 7 predictions of 256 classes each, 1,792 logits in total, produced one dimension at a time. The price is sequential decoding: 7 forward passes (or 7 steps of a transformer) per action.



5. Spot the causal confusion. A driving policy sees the camera image and the previous action. In the demos, the car brakes at red lights and keeps braking for several frames. The cloned policy brakes well when started at a red light but never starts braking on its own. What went wrong?






TipSolution





In the data, “previous action was brake” predicts “brake now” almost perfectly, far better than the small red light in the image does. The network learns to copy its previous action, a correlate, not the cause (the light). At test time nothing ever starts the braking chain. Remedies follow the papers: remove or randomly drop the previous-action input, or test which input the policy should rely on with a few targeted interventions (de Haan et al., 2019).

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Recap

Behavioral cloning is supervised learning on expert (state, action) pairs. Why it matters: it is the baseline every imitation method improves on, and at large scale it is the training recipe of the generalist policies in Week 9.
A cloned policy is tested on its own states, not the expert’s. Small mistakes lead to unseen states, and the expected cost can grow like \(\varepsilon T^2\); on the road toy it grew with slope 1.9 on a log-log scale. Why it matters: this is why “lower training loss” does not guarantee a better robot.
Recovery data fix it. Synthetic corrections (side cameras), DAgger’s relabelled states, or human interventions all show the policy how to get back. Why it matters: it reframes data collection: mistakes and recoveries are valuable data.
Experts are not consistent, and MSE averages their choices. Policies need multimodal action distributions: mixtures, discretization, diffusion, latent plans. Why it matters: Week 6’s diffusion policies and Week 7’s token-based policies are answers to exactly this.
More inputs can hurt. History and extra sensors invite causal confusion. Why it matters: it explains why later policies are careful about what context they condition on.

title: Week 3 · Imitation Learning
text:
Cheat sheet & connections








Name
Formula
Where




BC loss
\(\min_\theta \sum_{\mathcal{D}} \lVert \pi_\theta(s) - a^* \rVert^2\)
Equation 1


MSE minimizer
\(c^\star = \mathbb{E}[a^* \mid s]\)
Equation 1


BC compounding error ★
\(\mathbb{E}[\sum_t c] = O(\varepsilon T^2)\)
Equation 2


DAgger data rule, cost \(O(\varepsilon T)\)
\(\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \{(s, \pi^*(s))\}\), \(s \sim p_{\pi_\theta}\)
Equation 3


Mixture of Gaussians
\(\sum_k w_k \mathcal{N}(a; \mu_k, \Sigma_k)\)
Equation 4


Autoregressive actions
\(\prod_d p(a_{t,d} \mid s_t, a_{t,<d})\)
Equation 5


ELBO ★
\(\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(\tau \mid z, c)] - \mathrm{KL}(q \Vert p)\)
Equation 6



Common pitfalls.

Judging a cloned policy by its validation loss on held-out demos. Those are still expert states; only closed-loop rollouts measure distribution shift.
Collecting only clean, perfect demonstrations. They teach nothing about recovery.
Using MSE when demonstrators disagree. Check for multiple modes before choosing the loss.
Adding history “because it can only help”. It can hurt through causal confusion.

Connections. Week 2 gave the policy and MDP vocabulary used here. Weeks 4–5 learn from reward instead of demonstrations. Week 6 builds diffusion policies, the most common answer to multimodality today. Week 7 turns actions into token sequences, the autoregressive factorization above. Week 9’s generalist policies are trained largely by behavioral cloning, at scale. In the ADM Companion: behavioral cloning and DAgger in tabular settings, plus inverse reinforcement learning, which this lecture does not cover.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
Week 4 learned what every action is worth, a Q-function, and acted by taking the best one. That needs a maximum over actions, which is hard when actions are continuous and high-dimensional ▶ 01:30. This week skips the detour: give the policy parameters \(\theta\) and adjust them directly, so that actions which led to high reward become more likely ▶ 02:02. These are policy-gradient methods. The lecture builds them up one fix at a time, from the simplest (REINFORCE) to the two algorithms most used in robotics today, PPO and SAC, and ends by bringing value functions back as critics.
The question this week answers: how do you follow the gradient of expected reward when you cannot differentiate through the world, and how do you make that gradient precise and cheap enough in samples for a robot?


The key ideas at a glance

The log-derivative trick. The gradient of expected return can be written as an expectation, which samples can estimate, and the unknown dynamics drop out of it. The result is the policy gradient: imitation of your own actions, weighted by how well they turned out.
Variance is the enemy. The plain estimator (REINFORCE) is unbiased but noisy. Reward-to-go stops crediting actions for rewards that came before them; a baseline subtracts what was expected anyway. Neither changes the average gradient; both shrink its noise.
The advantage. The best baseline is the state’s value, which turns the weight into the advantage \(A = Q - V\): how much better this action was than usual.
Reusing data. Plain policy gradients must discard each batch after one step. Importance sampling reweights old samples so they can be reused, but only while the new policy stays close to the old one.
Staying close. An entropy bonus keeps the policy from becoming deterministic; TRPO limits each update with a KL divergence; PPO clips the importance ratio, which is simple and scales.
Actor-critic. PPO learns a value function alongside the policy. SAC learns a Q-function off-policy from a replay buffer and trains the actor through it with the reparameterization trick: the most sample-efficient of the lecture’s methods.



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Policy gradient
The gradient of expected return with respect to the policy’s parameters


Score function
\(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\): which way to move \(\theta\) to make \(a\) more likely


REINFORCE
The plain Monte Carlo policy-gradient algorithm (Williams, 1992)


Reward-to-go
The sum of rewards from step \(t\) to the end of the episode


Baseline
A number subtracted from the return to reduce variance without bias


Advantage \(A^\pi(s, a)\)
\(Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s)\): how much better \(a\) is than the policy’s average in \(s\)


On-policy
Each gradient step needs fresh data from the current policy


Importance ratio
\(\pi_{\theta'}(a \mid s) / \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\): reweights old samples for a new policy


Entropy \(\mathcal{H}\)
How spread out the policy’s action distribution is


Trust region
A limit on how far one update may move the policy


Actor, critic
The policy, and the learned value function that scores it


Reparameterization
Writing a sample as \(a = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon\), so gradients can flow through it





After this week you can

Derive the policy gradient with the log-derivative trick, and explain why the dynamics drop out.
Explain why reward-to-go and baselines reduce variance without biasing the gradient.
Define the advantage, and say how an actor-critic uses a learned value function.
Use importance sampling to reuse a batch, and explain why trajectory-level weights explode with the horizon.
Compare TRPO’s KL constraint and PPO’s clipped ratio, and say what each buys.
Explain what makes SAC off-policy and what the reparameterization trick is for.

title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Think of coaching a basketball player by watching games rather than drills. You cannot tell them the exact muscle commands for a better shot; you can only see which possessions ended in points. A sensible coach says “more of what you did on the possessions that went well, less of what you did on the ones that went badly”. A good coach adds three refinements. Judge each decision only by what happened after it. Compare a possession with how possessions usually go, not with zero, so that an ordinary basket is not celebrated. And change the playbook a little at a time, because the film from last week shows how the old playbook played, not the new one. Those three refinements are reward-to-go, the baseline (advantage) and the trust region.



Make good trajectories more likely
Parameterize the policy as \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\), for example a network that outputs the mean of a Gaussian over actions. Its quality is the expected return \(J(\theta)\) over the trajectories it produces. You can estimate \(J(\theta)\) by running the robot \(N\) times and averaging the returns; because the samples must come from the current policy, this is an on-policy estimate ▶ 04:37.
Improving \(\theta\) needs the gradient of \(J\), and the obvious route is blocked: the return depends on \(\theta\) through the robot’s sampled actions and the world’s response, and you cannot backpropagate through the physical world ▶ 05:38. The way round it is the log-derivative trick: \(\nabla_\theta p_\theta = p_\theta \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta\) turns the gradient of an expectation into an expectation of something you can compute for each sample ▶ 07:44. The sampling stays non-differentiable, but \(\theta\) now appears inside the expectation, where samples can estimate it ▶ 10:19. Better still, the log of a trajectory’s probability is a sum: start state, policy terms, dynamics terms. Only the policy terms depend on \(\theta\), so the unknown dynamics drop out of the gradient ▶ 11:51. The result (Equation 3) gives the algorithm REINFORCE (Williams, 1992): roll out, compute the gradient, step, roll out again ▶ 13:25.
The lecture’s intuition compares it with behavior cloning ▶ 14:58. The BC gradient raises the log-probability of every demonstrated action equally. The policy gradient does the same for the robot’s own actions, but weights each trajectory by its return: good trajectories are pushed up, bad ones down.


Credit only the future
An arm reaches towards a cup, moves well for most of the way, and overshoots at the end. REINFORCE multiplies every action’s score by the episode’s total return, so it penalizes the good early actions as much as the overshoot ▶ 16:00. Causality says an action at step \(t\) cannot have affected rewards before \(t\). Weighting each action by the reward-to-go, the rewards from \(t\) onwards, removes those irrelevant terms: the average gradient is unchanged, the noise is lower ▶ 17:03.


Better or worse than usual?
Now two reaches: one overshoots and scores 99, one is perfect and scores 101. REINFORCE pushes both up, by amounts proportional to 99 and 101; the useful signal is the difference of 2, buried under a common 100 ▶ 18:06. Subtracting a baseline \(b = 100\), the average return, gives weights \(-1\) and \(+1\): the overshoot is discouraged and the perfect reach encouraged ▶ 19:40. This is not cheating: a constant baseline leaves the expected gradient exactly unchanged and only removes noise ▶ 21:13.
This page’s reach toy makes the point with numbers. A point robot on a line starts at 0 and has 10 steps to reach a goal at 1; its policy moves by \(k\) times the remaining error, plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.3. The reward per step is minus the squared distance to the goal, plus a constant bonus \(c\) (think of a reward for every step the robot stays upright). The bonus changes nothing about which gain is best, \(k = 1\). It does change the noise. From batches of 16 episodes at \(k =\) 0.3, the true gradient is 8.78. With \(c = 0\) the four estimators of Figure 3 have standard deviations 8.53, 5.99, 4.14, 3.75: each fix helps. With \(c = 100\) the full-return estimator’s spread grows to 1,530, so the signal is 0.6% of the noise, while the estimators with a baseline stay at 4.20 and 3.81.


The advantage
Look at what the reward-to-go estimates: the expected sum of future rewards after taking \(a_t\) in \(s_t\) and following the policy, which is exactly \(Q^\pi(s_t, a_t)\). The reward-to-go is a one-sample, noisy estimate of Q ▶ 22:14. The natural baseline for a state is what the policy expects there on average, \(V^\pi(s_t)\). Their difference is the advantage: positive if the action did better than usual from this state, negative if worse ▶ 22:47. A state-dependent baseline accounts for how hard each state is; in the reach toy, a value function fitted on a separate batch beats the mean baseline (3.75 against 4.14).


Reusing data: importance sampling
Every estimate so far assumes the samples came from the current policy. After one gradient step the policy has changed, so the batch must be thrown away and a new one collected. For a real robot, where every episode costs time and wear, that is wasteful ▶ 24:53. Importance sampling estimates an expectation under one distribution using samples from another, by weighting each sample by the ratio of the two probabilities ▶ 25:54. Two caveats. The old policy must give nonzero probability wherever the new one does, or the ratio is undefined; and the estimate is only reliable while the two distributions are close ▶ 27:28.
For whole trajectories the dynamics cancel again, leaving a product of per-step ratios ▶ 28:30. Products of many factors explode or vanish: the variance grows exponentially with the horizon ▶ 30:03. If each step’s ratio compares two Gaussians whose means differ by 0.2 standard deviations, the trajectory weight’s effective sample size is 67% of the batch after 10 steps and 1.8% after 100 (Figure 4). So in practice each time step is reweighted by its own action ratio only, ignoring how the state distribution changed; TRPO and PPO justify that approximation by keeping updates small ▶ 31:36. With it, one batch can serve several gradient steps ▶ 32:37.


How far may one batch move the policy?
If the new policy puts probability on actions the old policy never took, the ratio is meaningless. An entropy bonus in the objective keeps the policy spread out, so that its support does not collapse ▶ 33:40. If the policy moves too far within one batch, ratios explode: an action the old policy took with probability 0.005 that the new policy takes with probability 0.10 gets weight 20 ▶ 35:45. TRPO maximizes the reweighted advantage subject to a bound on the KL divergence between old and new policies ▶ 36:46. It comes with a guarantee that each update does not make the policy worse, but the constraint needs second-order information about the KL divergence, which is expensive for large networks ▶ 37:50. PPO gets most of the stability with a first-order trick: clip the ratio to \([1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon]\) inside the objective, and take the minimum with the unclipped term ▶ 40:29. It works with ordinary optimizers such as Adam, which is why it also trains large language models (RLHF, GRPO); it gives up the guarantee and still needs many fresh samples ▶ 41:02.
The reuse toy measures what clipping buys. A one-step task with a continuous action: a Gaussian policy starting at \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), and a reward bump at \(a = 2\), observed with noise. Each run collects 30 batches of 32 samples and takes \(K\) gradient steps on each batch, over 50 seeds. One step per batch, the on-policy method, reaches an average expected reward of only 0.19 (the best possible is 1). Reuse helps a lot: with \(K = 10\) clipped steps per batch it reaches 0.96. Without the clip, more reuse becomes harmful. At \(K = 20\), 20% of the runs lose the bump entirely (expected reward below 0.05), and 44% at \(K = 100\); with the clip, none do at any \(K\) (Figure 5).




PPO-style learning on the one-step task: each batch of 32 actions is coloured by its advantage, and the policy moves a short way towards the better ones before the next batch is drawn.

What to watch for. In the first batch the samples spread from -2.3 to 1.4, none near the top of the bump. Far from the bump every reward is just noise, so blue and orange dots are mixed: off the bump, only 38% of the first ten batches’ samples are blue. The few samples that land on the bump’s slope are blue 89% of the time, and they do the pulling: the curve drifts right, and it even widens slightly, to a standard deviation of 1.27 at batch 3, since spreading out reaches more of the bump. From batch 12 the curve covers the bump and narrows. In the last ten batches every sample lands on the bump and blue sits above orange: which samples beat the average is now mostly noise (52% are blue), the pulls largely cancel, and the mean moves 0.026 per batch, against 0.123 in the first ten. After 30 batches the policy has standard deviation 0.15, is centred at 1.99, and the counter’s expected reward has risen from 0.09 to 0.96.


Actor and critic
PPO’s full objective has three terms: the clipped policy objective, a squared error that trains a value function, and the entropy bonus ▶ 43:05. The policy is the actor; the value function, which supplies the advantages, is the critic. Together they form an actor-critic: direct optimization of the behavior you care about, with a learned baseline to keep the variance low ▶ 44:37. The critic learns by temporal-difference updates, bootstrapping from its own next-state estimate instead of waiting for the episode to end: more sample-efficient, at the cost of a small bias ▶ 45:39. Since the critic is only needed during training, in simulation it can be given privileged information, such as exact object poses, that the deployed policy never sees ▶ 46:09.
The lecture’s robot examples: quadruped locomotion over rough terrain trained with TRPO in simulation and transferred to the real robot ▶ 39:25, and OpenAI’s Rubik’s-cube hand, 24 degrees of freedom, trained with PPO and heavy randomization of the simulator, with the cube’s pose estimated by a separate vision network ▶ 42:05.


Fully off-policy: SAC
Soft actor-critic closes the lecture’s arc from on-policy to off-policy. Its critic is a Q-function trained by TD updates on a replay buffer, as in DQN ▶ 47:13. Its actor maximizes the critic’s score plus an entropy bonus; the bonus also enters the critic’s target, which favours states with many good ways to proceed ▶ 48:16. The key move is that the actor takes old states from the buffer but asks the current policy what it would do there, and lets the critic estimate how good that new action is: the critic acts as a learned simulator ▶ 48:47. To pass the critic’s gradient back through the sampled action, SAC writes the sample as \(a = \mu_\theta(s) + \sigma_\theta(s)\,\varepsilon\) with fixed noise \(\varepsilon\): the reparameterization trick ▶ 49:17. In this page’s third toy, that pathwise gradient has 0.48 times the standard deviation of the score-function gradient for the same samples (Figure 6).
