title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Key concepts & formulae
The lecture’s notation: \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) for the policy, \(p_\theta(\tau)\) for the distribution over trajectories \(\tau = (s_0, a_0, s_1, \dots)\), \(R(\tau)\) for a trajectory’s return and \(J(\theta)\) for the expected return; \(\theta'\) is the new policy, \(\theta\) the one that collected the data. The ADM book writes \(U(\theta)\) for \(J(\theta)\) and calls PPO’s clipped objective the clamped surrogate.

The policy gradient

\[
\begin{aligned}
J(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim p_\theta(\tau)}\big[R(\tau)\big] \\
p_\theta(\tau) &= p(s_0) \textstyle\prod_{t} \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\, P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

In words. A policy is as good as the average return of the trajectories it produces. A trajectory’s probability is the start-state probability times, at every step, the policy’s probability of its action and the world’s probability of the next state.
Term by term.

\(R(\tau) = \sum_t \gamma^t r_t\): the (discounted) return of one trajectory, as in Week 2.
\(\pi_\theta\): the only factor we control. \(p(s_0)\) and \(P\) are the world’s, unknown to us.
The lecture estimates \(J\) by averaging the returns of \(N\) rollouts ▶ 04:37.


\[
\nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau) = p_\theta(\tau)\, \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)
\tag{2}\]

In words. The gradient of a probability equals the probability times the gradient of its logarithm.
Term by term.

It is the chain rule, \(\nabla \log p = \nabla p / p\), rearranged.
Its use: in \(\nabla J = \int \nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau) R(\tau)\, d\tau\) the integrand is not a probability times something, so samples cannot estimate it. After the trick it is \(p_\theta(\tau)\) times something, which is an expectation ▶ 09:15.


\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim p_\theta}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{t} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\; R(\tau)\Big]
\tag{3}\]

In words. To find which way to move \(\theta\), take each sampled trajectory, ask which direction makes its actions more likely, and weight that direction by the trajectory’s return. Average over trajectories.
Term by term.

\(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\): the score of one action. For a Gaussian policy with mean \(\mu_\theta(s)\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\) it is \(\frac{a_t - \mu_\theta(s_t)}{\sigma^2}\, \nabla_\theta \mu_\theta(s_t)\): the noise that was drawn, times how \(\theta\) moves the mean.
\(R(\tau)\): the weight. With \(R \equiv 1\) this would be behavior cloning on the robot’s own actions ▶ 14:58.
No \(P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)\) appears: the method is model-free.

Why it holds. Apply Equation 2 to \(\nabla J = \int \nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau) R(\tau)\, d\tau\) to get \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)\, R(\tau)]\). By Equation 1, \(\log p_\theta(\tau) = \log p(s_0) + \sum_t \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) + \sum_t \log P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)\); the first and last terms do not depend on \(\theta\), so their gradients vanish ▶ 12:55.
Numeric check. In the reach toy at \(k =\) 0.3, the average of Equation 3 over many batches of 16 is 8.91, against a true gradient of 8.78 (from 2 million episodes).


Less variance, same gradient

\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{t} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \big(\textstyle\sum_{t' \ge t} r_{t'} - b\big)\Big]
\tag{4}\]

In words. Weight each action by the rewards that came after it, minus a baseline. The expected gradient is the same as in Equation 3; the noise is lower.
Term by term.

\(\sum_{t' \ge t} r_{t'}\): the reward-to-go. Rewards before \(t\) are dropped: on average they contribute nothing, because the action at \(t\) cannot have caused them ▶ 17:03.
\(b\): the baseline, for example the batch’s average return ▶ 19:40. It may depend on the state, but not on the action.

Why it holds. For any \(b\) that does not depend on \(a_t\): \(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, b] = b \int \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, da = b\, \nabla_\theta \int \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, da = b\, \nabla_\theta 1 = 0\). The same argument removes past rewards, which are fixed by the time \(a_t\) is drawn.
Numeric check. A baseline must not use the episode it is subtracted from: the reach toy’s first version used the batch mean including the episode itself and a value function fitted on the same batch, and both estimates came out biased. The page’s version uses the mean of the other episodes and a value function fitted on a separate batch; all four averages agree with the true gradient within four standard errors, at every offset \(c\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
A^\pi(s, a) &= Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s) \\
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{t} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\; A^\pi(s_t, a_t)\Big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]

In words. How much better taking \(a\) in \(s\) is than what the policy does on average there. Using it as the weight pushes up better-than-usual actions and pushes down worse-than-usual ones.
Term by term.

\(Q^\pi(s_t, a_t)\): the expected reward-to-go; the observed reward-to-go is one noisy sample of it ▶ 22:14.
\(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}[Q^\pi(s, a)]\): the state-dependent baseline. In practice a learned critic estimates it.
\(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}[A^\pi(s, a)] = 0\): on average, the policy is exactly as good as itself.









Figure 3: Spread of four gradient estimators on the reach toy (standard deviation over 3,000 batches of 16 episodes, at gain k = 0.3), as a constant bonus c is added to every step’s reward. All four have the same mean, the true gradient (dashed). The full return and the reward-to-go carry the bonus into their weights, so their noise grows with c; the two baselines remove it.







Reusing data

\[
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\big[f(x)\big] = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q}\Big[\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\, f(x)\Big]
\tag{6}\]

In words. An average under \(p\) can be computed from samples of \(q\), if each sample is weighted by how much more (or less) likely it is under \(p\) than under \(q\).
Term by term.

\(p\): the new policy’s distribution, the one we want to evaluate; \(q\): the old policy’s, which produced the data.
\(p(x)/q(x)\): the importance weight. Its average under \(q\) is 1.
Requires \(q(x) > 0\) wherever \(p(x) > 0\); otherwise the weight is undefined ▶ 27:28.

Why it holds. Multiply and divide by \(q(x)\) inside the integral: \(\int p(x) f(x)\, dx = \int q(x) \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} f(x)\, dx\), the same “multiply by one” step as Equation 2.

\[
\nabla_{\theta'} J(\theta') \approx \mathbb{E}_{(s_t, a_t) \sim \pi_\theta}\Big[\frac{\pi_{\theta'}(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}\; \nabla_{\theta'} \log \pi_{\theta'}(a_t \mid s_t)\; A^{\pi_\theta}(s_t, a_t)\Big]
\tag{7}\]

In words. Reuse the old policy’s samples for the new policy’s gradient, weighting each step by its own action ratio.
Term by term.

The exact weight for a whole trajectory is \(\prod_t \pi_{\theta'}(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\), whose variance grows exponentially with the horizon (Figure 4).
The per-step version also needs the ratio of state distributions under the two policies, which would require the dynamics; it is approximated by 1 ▶ 31:36. That is accurate only while \(\theta'\) stays near \(\theta\).
At \(\theta' = \theta\) the ratio is 1 and this is Equation 5.

Numeric check. When each step’s two Gaussians have means \(\delta\) standard deviations apart, each ratio has \(\mathbb{E}[w^2] = e^{\delta^2}\), so the trajectory weight has \(\mathbb{E}[w^2] = e^{T\delta^2}\) and an effective sample size of \(e^{-T\delta^2}\) of the batch. For \(\delta = 0.2\) and \(T = 50\) that is 0.135; sampled weights give 0.130.








Figure 4: Why whole-trajectory importance weights fail. The effective sample size (as a share of the batch) of a product of T per-step ratios, when each step’s old and new Gaussian policies differ in mean by δ standard deviations. Lines: the closed form e^(−Tδ²); dots: 200,000 sampled trajectories for δ = 0.2.







Keeping the policy close

\[
\begin{aligned}
L(\theta') &= L_{\text{PG}}(\theta') + \beta\, \mathcal{H}\big(\pi_{\theta'}(\cdot \mid s)\big) \\
\mathcal{H}_{\text{Gauss}} &= \tfrac{d}{2}\big(1 + \log 2\pi\big) + \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{d} \log \sigma_i
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]

In words. Reward the policy for staying spread out, so it keeps giving some probability to actions it is not currently favouring.
Term by term.

\(\beta\): the temperature; larger means more spread, near 0 means greedy ▶ 34:11.
For discrete actions, \(\mathcal{H} = -\sum_a \pi(a) \log \pi(a)\) (Shannon entropy); for a Gaussian over \(d\) action dimensions, the second line, which depends only on the standard deviations ▶ 34:43.
With a Gaussian over an unbounded action space, the bonus grows without limit as \(\sigma\) grows, so a large \(\beta\) can make the policy ever wider. SAC squashes its actions into a bounded range with \(\tanh\), which keeps the entropy bounded.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\theta'}\; & \mathbb{E}_{s, a \sim \pi_\theta}\Big[\frac{\pi_{\theta'}(a \mid s)}{\pi_\theta(a \mid s)}\, A^{\pi_\theta}(s, a)\Big] \\
\text{subject to}\; & \mathbb{E}_{s}\big[D_{\text{KL}}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s) \,\big\|\, \pi_{\theta'}(\cdot \mid s)\big)\big] \le \delta
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\]

In words. Improve the reweighted advantage as much as possible, but never let the new policy’s action distribution move further than \(\delta\) from the old one, measured by KL divergence.
Term by term.

The objective is the off-policy surrogate whose gradient is Equation 7.
\(D_{\text{KL}}\): how different two distributions are; it is zero only when they are equal, and it becomes very large if the new policy gives almost no probability to actions the old one took.
\(\delta\): the trust-region size. Solving the constrained problem needs the Fisher information matrix (second derivatives of the KL), whose size is the number of parameters squared; TRPO approximates it with conjugate gradients ▶ 38:23.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\rho &= \pi_{\theta'}(a \mid s) / \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \\
L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta') &= \mathbb{E}\big[\min\big(\rho A,\; \operatorname{clip}(\rho, 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon)\, A\big)\big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}\]

In words. Use the reweighted advantage, but stop rewarding a sample once its ratio has moved more than \(\epsilon\) in the direction its advantage favours.
Term by term.

\(A\): the advantage \(A^{\pi_\theta}(s, a)\), from the critic.
\(A > 0\): the term grows with \(\rho\) only up to \(1 + \epsilon\); beyond that its gradient is zero. \(A < 0\): likewise below \(1 - \epsilon\).
The \(\min\) keeps the unclipped term when it is lower: a sample whose ratio moved the wrong way (an action with \(A > 0\) that became less likely) still pulls the policy back. The objective is a pessimistic bound.
\(\epsilon\): typically 0.1–0.3; the reuse toy uses 0.2.

Numeric check. On the explorer’s batch (seed 0, first batch of the reuse toy), the clipped objective is largest at \(\mu' =\) 0.10, \(\sigma' =\) 1.25, close to the old policy \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\). The unclipped objective has no maximum at all: it keeps growing as the new policy shrinks onto the batch’s single best sample, at \(a =\) 1.37. On a grid it peaks at the grid’s edge, \(\sigma' = 0.02\) (Figure 9).








Figure 5: Reusing each batch K times, on the one-step task (30 batches of 32 samples, 50 seeds, reward noise 0.3). Left: expected reward after the last batch, mean (line) and 10th percentile (dashed) over seeds, against the number of gradient steps per batch. Right: one unclipped run with K = 20 that loses the bump (the first seed for which that happens): its expected reward and its policy’s standard deviation per batch.





The right panel shows how an unclipped run fails. The policy first widens while it searches, then finds the bump and narrows. Without the clip it keeps narrowing: after 20 batches with \(K = 20\), the median standard deviation over the 50 seeds is 0.052 without the clip and 0.147 with it. In this run it is 0.046 at batch 28. The gradient with respect to the mean scales as \(1/\sigma^2\), so a few lucky samples in that batch move the mean by 43 standard deviations. Afterwards every sample in the batch has a ratio near zero (the largest is below \(10^{-3}\)): the new policy has left the data’s support, landed where the reward is flat, and never comes back.

\[
L^{\text{PPO}}(\theta') = \mathbb{E}\big[L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta') - c_1 \big(V_{\theta'}(s) - V^{\text{targ}}\big)^2 + c_2\, \mathcal{H}(\pi_{\theta'})(s)\big]
\tag{11}\]

In words. Maximize the clipped objective, train the value function towards its targets, and keep the policy spread out, all in one loss.
Term by term.

\(L^{\text{CLIP}}\): the actor’s term, Equation 10.
\((V_{\theta'}(s) - V^{\text{targ}})^2\): the critic’s regression loss, with a minus sign because the whole objective is maximized; the critic supplies the advantages ▶ 43:36.
\(c_1\), \(c_2\): weights of the critic loss and the entropy bonus (Equation 8).



Soft actor-critic

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{\text{actor}}(\theta) &= \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D},\, a \sim \pi_\theta}\big[\alpha \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s) - Q_\phi(s, a)\big] \\
y &= r + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{a' \sim \pi_\theta}\big[Q_{\bar\phi}(s', a') - \alpha \log \pi_\theta(a' \mid s')\big] \\
L_{\text{critic}}(\phi) &= \mathbb{E}_{(s, a, r, s') \sim \mathcal{D}}\big[(Q_\phi(s, a) - y)^2\big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}\]

In words. The actor picks actions the critic scores highly while staying random (high entropy). The critic regresses on a TD target that includes the entropy of the next action.
Term by term.

\(\mathcal{D}\): the replay buffer; states and transitions come from any past policy, so both losses are off-policy.
\(a \sim \pi_\theta\) in the actor loss: the current policy’s action in an old state, scored by the critic ▶ 48:47.
\(\alpha \log \pi_\theta\): minus the entropy, weighted by the temperature \(\alpha\) (the lecture’s \(\beta\) in Equation 8).
\(Q_{\bar\phi}\): a slowly updated target copy of the critic, as in DQN.


\[
\begin{aligned}
a &= \mu_\theta(s) + \sigma_\theta(s)\, \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \\
\nabla_\theta\, \mathbb{E}_a\big[Q(s, a)\big] &= \mathbb{E}_\varepsilon\big[\nabla_a Q(s, a)\; \nabla_\theta a\big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}\]

In words. Write the random action as a deterministic function of the parameters and of noise that does not depend on them. Then the gradient can pass through the action into the critic, by the chain rule.
Term by term.

\(\varepsilon\): drawn from a fixed distribution with no parameters, so nothing about the sampling needs a gradient ▶ 49:17.
\(\nabla_a Q\): the critic’s slope in the action, as in DDPG’s actor update (Week 4). The score-function estimator (Equation 3) does not need it; the pathwise estimator does.
Both are unbiased; the pathwise estimator is usually far less noisy.

Numeric check. For \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(0.5, 0.5^2)\) and the reward bump as \(Q\), the exact \(\partial_\mu \mathbb{E}[Q]\) is 0.2236. With 16 samples, the score-function estimate has standard deviation 0.168, 0.150 with a baseline, and the reparameterized one 0.080; all three average to the exact value.








Figure 6: Two unbiased estimators of the same gradient, the derivative of E[Q(a)] with respect to the policy mean, for a Gaussian policy and a smooth Q: the score function (as REINFORCE does), with and without a leave-one-out baseline, and the reparameterization (as SAC does). Standard deviation over 20,000 batches, against the batch size.

Moving the mean right raises the ratios of actions on the right and lowers those on the left. A sample is switched off when its ratio has already moved past \(1 \pm 0.2\) in the direction its advantage asked for: a right-hand action with \(A > 0\) and \(\rho > 1.2\), or a left-hand one with \(A < 0\) and \(\rho < 0.8\). Its gradient is then zero, so further steps on this batch are driven only by the remaining samples. A sample whose ratio moved the other way keeps its unclipped term, which is the smaller of the two, and pulls the policy back.


Example 3: the 99-and-101 reaches, with numbers
Two episodes with returns 99 (overshoot) and 101 (perfect), and suppose the summed scores of their actions are \(g_1 = +0.5\) and \(g_2 = -0.3\) (random numbers, as they would be). REINFORCE’s estimate is \(\frac{1}{2}(99 \times 0.5 + 101 \times (-0.3)) = 9.6\): dominated by the large common return, with the first, worse episode’s direction winning. With baseline \(b = 100\): \(\frac{1}{2}((-1) \times 0.5 + 1 \times (-0.3)) = -0.4\). The weights now reflect that episode 2 was better: its direction is followed, episode 1’s is reversed. On average over many episodes both estimates agree; in any one batch the first is mostly noise.

title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Algorithm & code
The course’s homework asks students to implement PPO (its clipped objective, value loss, entropy term and KL check) and SAC (its critic target, actor and temperature losses, and target-network update), so this page shows equations and results for those, not code. The code below covers the rest of the lecture: the REINFORCE estimators, with reward-to-go and baselines, and the reparameterization trick.

REINFORCE: four weightings of the same score

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def reach_rollouts(k, n, rng, c=0.0) -> tuple[Array, Array, Array]:
    """n episodes from x_0 = 0 with gain k; reward c - (x_{t+1} - g)^2 per step.

    Returns the errors e_t = g - x_t, the score d/dk log pi(a_t | x_t),
    and the rewards, each of shape (n, T).
    """
    x = np.zeros(n)
    e, a, r = (np.empty((n, T)) for _ in range(3))
    for t in range(T):
        e[:, t] = GOAL - x
        a[:, t] = k * e[:, t] + SIGMA * rng.standard_normal(n)
        x = x + a[:, t]
        r[:, t] = c - (x - GOAL) ** 2
    # log N(a; k e, sigma^2) = -(a - k e)^2 / (2 sigma^2) + const, so its
    # derivative in k is (a - k e) e / sigma^2: noise times state, scaled.
    score = (a - k * e) * e / SIGMA**2
    return e, score, r

def reward_to_go(r) -> Array:
    """sum_{t' >= t} r_t' for every t: a reversed cumulative sum, (n, T)."""
    return np.cumsum(r[:, ::-1], axis=1)[:, ::-1]

def fit_value(e, rtg) -> Array:
    """Per-step least squares V_t(e) = w0 + w1 e^2; returns weights (T, 2)."""
    w = []
    for t in range(T):
        X = np.stack([np.ones(len(e)), e[:, t] ** 2], axis=1)   # (n, 2)
        w.append(np.linalg.lstsq(X, rtg[:, t], rcond=None)[0])
    return np.array(w)

def gradient_estimates(k, n, rng, c=0.0) -> dict[str, float]:
    """One batch of n episodes, four estimates of dJ/dk (same samples)."""
    e, score, r = reach_rollouts(k, n, rng, c)
    rtg = reward_to_go(r)
    # A baseline must not depend on the episode it is subtracted from, or it
    # biases the estimate: use the mean of the *other* n - 1 episodes, and
    # fit V on a separate batch, as a critic trained on earlier data would be.
    loo_mean = (rtg.sum(0) - rtg) / (n - 1)
    e_fit, _, r_fit = reach_rollouts(k, n, rng, c)
    w = fit_value(e_fit, reward_to_go(r_fit))     # (T, 2)
    V = w[:, 0] + w[:, 1] * e**2                  # (n, T), broadcast over n
    weights = (r.sum(1, keepdims=True), rtg, rtg - loo_mean, rtg - V)
    return {name: float((score * wt).sum(1).mean())
            for name, wt in zip(ESTIMATORS, weights)}


import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from rlc.toys import w05_pg as reach   # the reach task on this page

torch.manual_seed(0)
T, G = reach.T, reach.GOAL

# Policy: mean = k * error, with a learned log std (starts at sigma = 0.3).
policy = nn.Linear(1, 1, bias=False)
nn.init.zeros_(policy.weight)                    # k = 0: does not move
log_std = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(-1.2))
# Critic: V(t / T, error), a small MLP used only as a baseline.
value = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 1))
opt_pi = torch.optim.Adam([*policy.parameters(), log_std], lr=0.02)
opt_v = torch.optim.Adam(value.parameters(), lr=0.01)


def rollout(n):
    """n episodes in parallel. Returns log-probs (n, T),
    critic features (n, T, 2) and rewards (n, T)."""
    x = torch.zeros(n, 1)
    logps, feats, rewards = [], [], []
    for t in range(T):
        e = G - x                                    # (n, 1)
        dist = torch.distributions.Normal(policy(e), log_std.exp())
        # sample() cuts the graph: gradients reach theta via log_prob only
        a = dist.sample()
        logps.append(dist.log_prob(a).squeeze(-1))
        feats.append(torch.cat([torch.full_like(e, t / T), e], dim=-1))
        x = x + a
        rewards.append((-(x - G) ** 2).squeeze(-1))
    return (torch.stack(logps, 1), torch.stack(feats, 1),
            torch.stack(rewards, 1))


for it in range(500):
    logp, feat, r = rollout(64)
    rtg = r.flip(1).cumsum(1).flip(1)                # reward-to-go, (64, T)
    v = value(feat).squeeze(-1)                      # (64, T)
    # Advantage = reward-to-go minus the critic's baseline. detach(): the
    # policy loss must not push gradients into the critic.
    adv = (rtg - v).detach()
    loss_pi = -(logp * adv).sum(1).mean()            # minimize minus eq. rtg
    loss_v = ((v - rtg) ** 2).mean()                 # critic: fit the returns
    opt_pi.zero_grad(); loss_pi.backward(); opt_pi.step()
    opt_v.zero_grad(); loss_v.backward(); opt_v.step()

k = policy.weight.item()
assert 0.85 < k < 1.15, k                            # learned the best gain, 1



The four NumPy estimators differ only in the weight multiplied onto the same score; the PyTorch sketch uses the last one, with the baseline learned by a small critic network. Written as a loss, the policy gradient is “log-probability times a detached weight”, which automatic differentiation turns into Equation 4.


The reparameterization trick

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def mu_gradient_estimates(mu, sigma, n, rng) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Three unbiased estimates of d/dmu E[bump(a)] from one batch of n."""
    eps = rng.standard_normal(n)
    a = mu + sigma * eps
    q = bump(a)
    # d/dmu log N(a; mu, sigma^2) = (a - mu) / sigma^2 = eps / sigma
    score = eps / sigma
    loo = (q.sum() - q) / (n - 1) if n > 1 else 0.0     # leave-one-out baseline
    return {"score function": float((q * score).mean()),
            "score function, baseline": float(((q - loo) * score).mean()),
            # a = mu + sigma * eps, so da/dmu = 1 and the gradient is Q'(a)
            "reparameterization": float(bump_slope(a).mean())}


from torch.distributions import Normal

def q(a):
    """Stand-in critic: the page's reward bump, in torch."""
    return torch.exp(-0.5 * ((a - reach.BUMP_AT) / reach.BUMP_WIDTH) ** 2)


def per_batch_grads(reparam, B=4000, n=16):
    """B independent estimates of d/dmu E[q(a)], a ~ N(0.5, 0.5^2).

    Each batch gets its own copy of mu, shape (B, 1), so one backward pass
    of the summed loss leaves batch i's gradient in mu.grad[i]."""
    mu = torch.full((B, 1), 0.5, requires_grad=True)
    dist = Normal(mu.expand(B, n), 0.5)
    if reparam:
        a = dist.rsample()                       # mu + 0.5 * eps: graph kept
        loss = q(a).mean(1).sum()
    else:
        a = dist.sample()                        # no graph: use log_prob
        loss = (q(a) * dist.log_prob(a)).mean(1).sum()
    loss.backward()
    return mu.grad.squeeze(1)                    # (B,)


g_sf, g_rp = per_batch_grads(False), per_batch_grads(True)
exact = reach.mu_gradient_exact(0.5, 0.5)
assert abs(g_sf.mean() - exact) < 0.02 and abs(g_rp.mean() - exact) < 0.02
assert g_rp.std() < 0.6 * g_sf.std()            # same mean, much less noise



sample() returns a number with no history, so the score-function estimator must go through log_prob; rsample() builds the sample from \(\mu\), \(\sigma\) and fixed noise, so the critic’s slope flows back to \(\mu\). SAC’s actor loss (Equation 12) is computed on rsample() actions for exactly this reason.

title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Papers

Papers discussed in class






End-to-End Training of Deep Visuomotor Policies Levine, Finn, Darrell & Abbeel · JMLR 2016
Asks whether perception and control work better when trained together, and trains a convolutional network that maps camera images straight to motor torques on a PR2 robot. A trajectory optimizer that sees the full state during training acts as the teacher; the network, which sees only images and joint angles, learns from it by supervised learning.

Guided policy search turns policy search into supervised learning: simple trajectory-centric RL controllers, trained with the full state, supervise the image-based policy (Abstract, Sec. 1).
A 7-layer CNN with 92,000 parameters whose spatial softmax turns feature maps into image-space feature points (Sec. 1, Sec. 6.3).
End-to-end training beats vision trained separately for pose estimation: on the shape-sorting cube, 96.3% success at the training positions against 0% for the pose-prediction baseline (Fig. 9).
Each task took 156 to 288 five-second trials, about 15 minutes of robot time (Sec. 6.6, Table 4).

On this page: A policy-search alternative to this week’s model-free gradients, and an early case of the lecture’s ‘privileged information at training time’: the teacher sees the state, the deployed policy only pixels.









Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding Large Language Models Ma et al. · ICLR 2024
A coding language model (GPT-4) writes reward functions as Python code, given the environment’s source code and a task description. Candidates are scored by training a policy on each, and the best one, with a written summary of how training went, is fed back so the model can write improved versions.

Its rewards beat expert human-written rewards on 83% of 29 simulated tasks covering 10 robot morphologies, with an average normalized improvement of 52% (Abstract).
Evolutionary search in the model’s context: 16 reward samples per iteration, 5 iterations, 5 independent runs; ‘reward reflection’ reports per-component training statistics to guide the edits (Sec. 3.2, 3.3).
With a curriculum, a simulated Shadow Hand learns rapid pen spinning (Abstract).
Human feedback in words can steer the reward without updating any model weights (Abstract).

On this page: Every candidate reward is scored by a full PPO training run in GPU simulation (Sec. 4.2): this week’s algorithm is the inner loop, and the reward, which the lecture takes as given, becomes the thing optimized.









Latent Plans for Task-Agnostic Offline Reinforcement Learning Rosete-Beas, Mees, Kalweit, Boedecker & Burgard · CoRL 2022
TACO-RL learns long-horizon, goal-reaching manipulation from a fixed dataset of undirected teleoperated ‘play’. A low-level policy learns short latent skills by imitation; a high-level policy, trained by offline RL, picks which latent skill to run next so the skills chain towards a goal image.

Imitation for the short skills, offline RL (Conservative Q-Learning, initialized from the imitation prior) for chaining them, which shortens the horizon the RL part must handle (Abstract, Sec. 4.2).
Rewards come from hindsight relabeling: states reached later in the same play episode become goals, with deliberately chosen negative goals (Sec. 4.2).
Two tasks in a row from a single goal image: 27% success against 2.7% for imitation (LMP) and 2.4% for offline RL alone (CQL+HER) (Table 2).
On a real robot, one visuomotor policy for 25 tasks averages 61% success, against 40% and 11% for the same baselines (Table 4).

On this page: The far end of this week’s on-policy to off-policy arc: an actor-critic that learns from logged data only, never collecting new experience.





Key papers from the lecture






Simple statistical gradient-following algorithms for connectionist reinforcement learning Williams · Machine Learning 1992
Introduces REINFORCE: for networks of stochastic units, adjust each weight by the reward times the gradient of the log-probability of what the unit did. On average this follows the gradient of expected reward, without ever computing that gradient explicitly.

A broad family of update rules whose expected direction is the gradient of expected reinforcement, for immediate rewards and some delayed-reward settings (Abstract).
Shows how the rules combine with backpropagation (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s first policy-gradient algorithm, and the ‘full return’ estimator in this page’s variance toy.









Trust Region Policy Optimization Schulman, Levine, Moritz, Jordan & Abbeel · ICML 2015
Derives a policy update with a guarantee that it does not make the policy worse, then approximates it in practice: maximize the importance-weighted advantage subject to a limit on the average KL divergence between old and new policies.

A theoretically justified procedure with monotonic improvement, made practical for large neural-network policies (Abstract).
Results on simulated swimming, hopping and walking, and on Atari from pixels, with little hyperparameter tuning (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s KL-constrained answer to ‘how far may one batch move the policy?’









Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms Schulman, Wolski, Dhariwal, Radford & Klimov · arXiv 2017
Replaces TRPO’s constraint with a clipped importance ratio inside the objective, so one batch can be used for several epochs of ordinary minibatch gradient steps.

A surrogate objective that allows multiple epochs of minibatch updates per batch, where standard policy gradients take one step per sample (Abstract).
Keeps some of TRPO’s benefits while being simpler to implement and more general (Abstract).
Outperforms other online policy-gradient methods on simulated locomotion and Atari, balancing sample use, simplicity and wall-clock time (Abstract).

On this page: The clipped objective this page’s reuse toy compares with the unclipped one.









Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor Haarnoja, Zhou, Abbeel & Levine · ICML 2018
An off-policy actor-critic in which the actor maximizes expected reward plus the entropy of its own actions: succeed at the task while acting as randomly as possible.

Combines off-policy updates from a replay buffer with a stochastic actor in the maximum-entropy framework (Abstract).
State-of-the-art results on continuous-control benchmarks at the time, beating earlier on- and off-policy methods, with low variance across random seeds (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s endpoint: a replay buffer like DQN’s, an entropy bonus, and the reparameterization trick, which this page’s third toy measures.

title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Guest spotlight
Andrew Wagenmaker (UC Berkeley) argues that robots must learn from their own experience, as people do when they learn to iron a shirt: watch a video, then try, see what happens, and adjust ▶ 01:33. Each of today’s data sources falls short on its own: simulators struggle with cloth, internet video has no motor commands, and human demonstrations are expensive and still leave a gap between demonstration and deployment ▶ 03:35. The central difficulty of learning from experience, in his view, is exploration: collecting the experience that tells correct behavior apart from incorrect behavior ▶ 05:09. The textbook picture, an agent taking random actions until it stumbles on reward, does not scale to the physical world; a person exploring tries a handful of sensible options, such as picking up the iron, the shirt or the spray bottle ▶ 08:46.
His first idea gets that structured exploration from a behavior-cloning policy. A diffusion or flow policy maps Gaussian noise to an action that looks like a demonstration, so different noise inputs give different reasonable actions ▶ 11:21. Instead of exploring in action space, explore in the noise space: keep the trained policy fixed, and learn with RL a small noise policy, and a critic over noise, that choose which noise to feed it ▶ 13:57. This is DSRL (Diffusion Steering via RL, a Week 6 paper). On a real pick-and-place task its attempts looked purposeful from the start, while an action-space RL baseline flailed in free space; after 25 episodes it had locked onto the correct behavior ▶ 18:35. It also sidesteps the problem that diffusion policies have no tractable likelihood, which standard policy gradients need ▶ 19:06. He reports policies going from below 50% to 90–100% success in 30 to 90 minutes of online training ▶ 19:36.
His second idea asks whether behavior cloning is the right pre-training for RL at all ▶ 21:40. If the demonstrations never show a needed behavior, a cloned policy never tries it, and RL fine-tuning has nothing to reinforce ▶ 22:42. Adding random noise to the cloned policy trades performance against exploration ▶ 24:16. His answer is to model the uncertainty about what the demonstrator would do, and to explore more where demonstrations are scarce and less where they agree ▶ 25:18; the paper is Posterior Behavioral Cloning (arXiv 2512.16911). On a pick-and-place task both pre-trained policies started out similar, but online RL took the standard one to below 50% and his to 75% ▶ 26:20.
How it connects to this week. Both ideas are about the support problem that the lecture’s entropy bonus addresses: RL can only improve on actions the policy actually tries. Steering in noise space keeps every action inside what the demonstrations made plausible, while a posterior BC policy widens the support exactly where the data are uncertain. In the Q&A he contrasts his approach, refining a fixed policy with a second policy, with π*0.6’s advantage-conditioned training of one policy (a Week 9 paper), and says it is not yet understood when each is better ▶ 29:25.

title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Solved problems
1. Why a baseline is free. For a single-step task with a Gaussian policy \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), show directly that \(\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_\mu \log \pi(a)\, b\big] = 0\) for any constant \(b\).






TipSolution





\(\nabla_\mu \log \pi(a) = (a - \mu)/\sigma^2\). Its expectation under \(\pi\) is \((\mathbb{E}[a] - \mu)/\sigma^2 = 0\), so multiplying by a constant \(b\) still gives 0. More generally (Equation 4), \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla \log \pi] = \int \nabla \pi = \nabla \int \pi = \nabla 1 = 0\). The baseline changes each sample’s contribution, and hence the variance, but not the average.



2. Which baseline? In the reach toy with bonus \(c = 10\), why does the fitted value function \(V_t(e)\) help a little over the mean baseline, but the mean baseline already removes almost all of the problem?






TipSolution





The bonus adds the same amount, \(c\) times the number of remaining steps, to every episode’s reward-to-go at step \(t\). Any baseline that tracks the average reward-to-go per step removes it entirely; the mean of the other episodes does. What remains is the variation between episodes at the same step, which comes from how far each robot still is from the goal. The fitted value function predicts that from the current error \(e_t\), so it removes some of the remaining variation too: 3.96 against 4.36 here. The bonus was the big effect, and both baselines handle it.



3. A ratio, by hand. The old policy is \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) and the new one \(\mathcal{N}(0.5, 1)\). What is the importance ratio for the action \(a = 1\)? For \(a = -2\)? With \(\epsilon = 0.2\) and advantages \(A = +1\) at \(a = 1\) and \(A = -1\) at \(a = -2\), which of the two samples does PPO’s clip switch off?






TipSolution





\(\rho(a) = \exp\big(-\tfrac{1}{2}(a - 0.5)^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}a^2\big) = \exp(0.5a - 0.125)\). At \(a = 1\): \(e^{0.375} \approx 1.45\). At \(a = -2\): \(e^{-1.125} \approx 0.32\). The first has \(A > 0\) and \(\rho > 1.2\): the policy already favours it beyond the trust interval, so it is switched off. The second has \(A < 0\) and \(\rho < 0.8\): the policy has already moved away from it as far as the clip allows, so it is switched off too. Both samples got what they asked for; further steps on this batch would be driven by the other samples.



4. How long can a trajectory weight be trusted? Per-step ratios have \(\mathbb{E}[w_t^2] = 1.01\) each. After how many steps has the trajectory weight’s effective sample size halved? For a 500-step episode at 50 Hz (10 seconds), what is left?






TipSolution





For independent steps \(\mathbb{E}[w^2] = 1.01^T\), and the effective sample size is \(1/1.01^T\) of the batch. It halves when \(T = \ln 2 / \ln 1.01 \approx 70\) steps. After 500 steps, \(1.01^{-500} \approx 0.007\): about 0.7% of the batch, so a batch of 1,000 trajectories behaves like 7. This is why Equation 7 keeps only the per-step ratio.



5. Score function or reparameterization? For which of these can you use the reparameterization trick: (a) a learned critic \(Q_\phi(s, a)\), (b) the real robot’s reward, measured after the action, (c) a simulator written in a differentiable physics engine?






TipSolution





The pathwise gradient (Equation 13) needs \(\nabla_a\) of whatever is being maximized. (a) Yes: the critic is a network, and SAC does exactly this. (b) No: you cannot differentiate the real world with respect to the action, so you need the score function (Equation 3), which only needs the reward’s value. (c) Yes in principle, since the simulator provides gradients, though contact-rich simulators give gradients that are often uninformative. The critic in (a) is what makes SAC’s low-variance actor update possible without a differentiable world.

title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Recap

The policy gradient follows expected return without differentiating the world. The log-derivative trick turns it into an average of score-times-return, and the dynamics drop out. Why it matters: every method this week, and the RL fine-tuning of large robot policies in later weeks, starts from this estimator.
Variance, not bias, is the practical problem. Reward-to-go and baselines leave the average gradient unchanged and shrink its noise; a constant bonus in the reward can make the plain estimator useless. Why it matters: sample cost is the binding constraint on real robots.
The advantage is the right weight. \(A = Q - V\) asks whether an action beat the policy’s own average. Why it matters: it brings value functions back as critics, joining Week 4’s ideas with this week’s.
Importance sampling lets a batch be reused, within limits. Per-step ratios are usable; trajectory weights are not; any reweighting fails once the policy leaves the data’s support. Why it matters: the limit explains entropy bonuses, trust regions and the clip.
TRPO and PPO bound each update. TRPO with a KL constraint and a guarantee; PPO with a clipped ratio that is cheap and robust to how often a batch is reused. Why it matters: PPO is the default for simulated robot training and for language-model fine-tuning.
SAC is off-policy and pathwise. A Q-critic on a replay buffer, an entropy bonus, and gradients through reparameterized actions. Why it matters: it is the most sample-efficient of the lecture’s methods, and a common choice for RL on real robots.

title: Week 5 · Reinforcement Learning II
text:
Cheat sheet & connections








Name
Formula
Where




Objective
\(J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim p_\theta}[R(\tau)]\)
Equation 1


Log-derivative trick
\(\nabla p = p\, \nabla \log p\)
Equation 2

\(\mathbb{E}[\sum_t \nabla \log \pi\, R(\tau)]\)
Equation 3


Reward-to-go, baseline
\(\sum_{t' \ge t} r_{t'} - b\)
Equation 4

\(A = Q - V\)
Equation 5


Importance sampling
\(\mathbb{E}_p[f] = \mathbb{E}_q[\frac{p}{q} f]\)
Equation 6


Off-policy gradient
per-step ratio \(\times \nabla \log \pi \times A\)
Equation 7


Entropy bonus
\(L + \beta \mathcal{H}\)
Equation 8


TRPO ★
max \(\mathbb{E}[\rho A]\) s.t. KL \(\le \delta\)
Equation 9


PPO clip ★
\(\min(\rho A, \operatorname{clip}(\rho)A)\)
Equation 10


Full PPO
clip − value loss + entropy
Equation 11


SAC
\(\alpha \log \pi - Q\); soft TD target
Equation 12


Reparameterization
\(a = \mu + \sigma \varepsilon\)
Equation 13



Common pitfalls.

Letting the baseline depend on the action, or on the very episode it is subtracted from; both bias the gradient.
Forgetting .detach() on the advantage: the policy loss then pushes gradients into the critic.
Reusing a batch for many epochs without a clip or KL check; the policy can leave the data’s support.
Letting the policy’s standard deviation collapse; the ratios and the gradient scale (as \(1/\sigma^2\)) then explode.
Using sample() where the critic’s gradient must flow (SAC’s actor); it needs rsample().
Treating PPO as off-policy: it reuses a batch for a few epochs, then must collect fresh data.

Connections. Week 4’s smoothing toy showed why an expected reward has a gradient; this week computes it. Week 4’s DDPG actor update is the deterministic cousin of SAC’s reparameterized one. Week 3’s behavior cloning is the policy gradient with every weight set to 1, and the guest talk shows how cloned policies become starting points for RL. Week 6’s diffusion policies are what DSRL steers. In the ADM Companion: the likelihood ratio, reward-to-go and baselines; TRPO and PPO’s clamped surrogate; actor-critic methods.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
Every policy so far has been reactive: one observation in, one action out ▶ 00:21. Week 3 cloned such policies from demonstrations, and Week 6 made their action distributions richer. This week asks what a policy gains by looking at a sequence: the history behind the current observation, and a whole stretch of future actions instead of one. The tool is the transformer, the architecture behind large language models (LLMs), vision-language models (VLMs) and, from Week 9 on, the vision-language-action models (VLAs) that the rest of the course builds on.
The question this week answers: how do you turn a robot’s observations, instructions and actions into one token sequence that a transformer can learn from, and what goes wrong with actions that does not go wrong with words?


The key ideas at a glance

A snapshot is not enough. One camera frame shows neither how fast things move nor what the robot did a moment ago; a robot really acts in a partially observable world and needs history. Predicting one action at a time also tends to produce jerky motion.
Sequences factor into conditionals. By the chain rule, any distribution over a sequence is a product of “next element given everything before”. An autoregressive model learns that one conditional.
Attention instead of recurrence. A recurrent network squeezes the past into one state vector; attention lets every position look directly at every earlier one, in one step and in parallel. It has no sense of order, so positional encodings add it.
Tokens. Text is split into sub-words by byte-pair encoding, images into patches; once everything is a token, one transformer can read both. Vision and language are joined by contrastive alignment (CLIP), by feeding image tokens into a language model (LLaVA, early fusion), by cross-attention (Flamingo, late fusion), or by training on all modalities at once.
Scale. Transformers improve predictably with model size, data and compute; the Chinchilla rule says to grow model and data together, about 20 tokens per parameter.
Actions as tokens. Bin each action dimension at each step (RT-2, OpenVLA). At high control rates consecutive tokens nearly repeat, and next-token prediction learns little; FAST compresses each action chunk with a discrete cosine transform first.
Action chunks. Predict the next \(k\) actions at once (ACT) for smoother motion; a temporal ensemble averages overlapping chunks so the robot keeps reacting.



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Reactive policy
Chooses each action from the current observation only


POMDP
A decision problem where the robot observes only part of the state


Autoregressive model
Generates a sequence one element at a time, each conditioned on all earlier ones


Token
One unit of a sequence: a sub-word, an image patch, an action bin


Attention
Each position takes a weighted average of other positions’ values, with weights from query-key similarity


Causal mask
Stops a position from attending to later positions


Positional encoding
Information about order added to tokens or to attention scores


Teacher forcing
Training on the true previous tokens, not the model’s own predictions


BPE
Byte-pair encoding: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token


Scaling law
A fitted power law linking loss to model size, data and compute


Early, late fusion
Image tokens enter the language model’s input sequence, or reach it through cross-attention layers


Action chunk
The next \(k\) actions, predicted together


Temporal ensemble
Averaging the overlapping predictions that several chunks make for the same step


DCT
Discrete cosine transform: a signal written as a sum of cosines of rising frequency





After this week you can

Explain why robots need history and why single-step policies jitter.
Compute an attention head by hand, and say what the causal mask and positional encodings are for.
Describe teacher forcing, and why a transformer trains on a whole sequence in one pass.
Run byte-pair encoding, and explain how images and actions become tokens.
State the Chinchilla rule and use \(C \approx 6ND\) to size a model for a compute budget.
Explain why per-step action bins fail at high control rates, and how FAST’s compression fixes it.
Compare single-step control, action chunks and temporal ensembling.

title: Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Think of a pianist reading music. A beginner looks at one note, plays it, looks at the next: slow, and the phrasing is choppy. An experienced player reads a whole bar ahead and plays it as one gesture, while still glancing at what comes next and at the conductor. They also remember what they have just played: a repeat sign means something only if you know where you have been. Remembering the past is what attention gives a robot; playing a bar at a time is action chunking; still glancing at the page between bars is the temporal ensemble.



One snapshot is not enough
A reactive policy \(\pi(a_t \mid o_t)\) has two problems ▶ 00:21. The first is memory. A single frame does not show how fast a pedestrian is walking, or that the road was icy a few seconds ago. The second is smoothness: a policy that decides every step afresh can switch between slightly different decisions and produce jerky, oscillating motion ▶ 01:34. In the language of Week 2, the robot is not in an MDP but a partially observable one (a POMDP): the observation is not the state, and the state must be inferred from the history ▶ 02:22. The world produces a sequence, but the policy looks at one element of it ▶ 03:21.
This page’s first toy is that problem in its simplest form. A robot receives a stream of 16 tokens. Most are sensor readings with random values; twice, at random moments, a token announces a goal position, and the second announcement replaces the first (an operator corrects themselves). The last token asks: where should I go now? A reactive policy sees only that last token, which says nothing about the goal, so its best guess is 0, and its mean squared error is 1.00, the variance of the goal.


Sequences as products of conditionals
To model a whole sequence, use the chain rule of probability: any joint distribution, however complicated, is the probability of the first element, times that of the second given the first, and so on ▶ 03:53. A model that learns “next element given all earlier ones” can therefore represent any sequence distribution, and generate from it one element at a time. This is an autoregressive model (Equation 1). The hard part is the conditional itself: its input, the whole past, grows with the sequence and can be high-dimensional.
The first answer was the recurrent neural network (RNN): keep a hidden state that summarizes the past, and update it with each new input ▶ 04:56. It handles any length, but has three problems. Information from step 1 reaches step 100 only through 99 updates, so gradients over long ranges explode or vanish (LSTMs helped, but did not cure it) ▶ 05:19. Each step needs the previous one, so training cannot be parallelized over time ▶ 05:41. And however long the history, it must fit in a fixed-size vector ▶ 05:48.


Attention: look anywhere, in one step
A transformer replaces recurrence with attention: any position can draw information from any other position directly, so the path between two tokens has length one, whatever their distance ▶ 06:30. That removes all three RNN problems at once: long-range dependencies are one step away, there is no recurrence to serialize training, and nothing has to squeeze the history into a single vector.
How a position decides where to look ▶ 07:26: each token produces a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I offer?) and a value (what I hand over if chosen). The query is compared with every key by a dot product, the scores go through a softmax so they sum to one, and the output is the weighted average of the values ▶ 08:00. It is a soft dictionary lookup: instead of returning the one entry whose key matches, it returns a blend of all entries, weighted by how well each key matches. Because every step is differentiable, the network learns not only the representations but where to look ▶ 08:23.
In the goal toy, one attention head is enough: the last token’s query learns to match the keys of goal tokens, and the value carries the goal’s position. This head is small enough to write out in NumPy with its gradients (see Algorithm & code).


Order has to be added
Attention compares tokens by content only. Shuffle the inputs and every weight is the same: attention is a set operation, so “the robot picked up the spoon” and “the spoon picked up the robot” look identical ▶ 09:09. The fix is to inject order ▶ 09:27. The original transformer adds a fixed vector to each token according to its position, an absolute encoding; a position longer than any seen in training then has no meaningful encoding ▶ 09:52. A relative encoding instead adds a bias to each attention score that depends on the distance between the two tokens, so the same rule applies anywhere in the sequence ▶ 10:12.
The goal toy shows both halves of this. Trained without any positional information, the head finds both goals but cannot tell which came later. Its best option is to average them, and its error over 5 training seeds is 0.50: exactly the error of answering with the mean of two random goals, 0.5. With one learned parameter more, a bias \(-\lambda\) per step of distance on every score, the error falls to 0.0002: the head now prefers the more recent goal.
Does that relative bias let the head work on longer streams? The same trained head runs on streams of 256 tokens without change, which an absolute encoding could not do. It is still nearly perfect (error below 0.0001 in every seed) as long as the later goal is at most 14 steps back. Beyond 15 steps, the furthest training ever showed, it fails, with error above 1.0, worse than not looking at all (Figure 2). The learned weights say why. A goal token out-scores a sensor reading by about 55, the bias is \(\lambda \approx\) 3.6 per step, and their ratio is 15.1 steps, almost exactly the training range: training tuned the head to see goals as far back as it needed to, and no further. Relative encodings make longer sequences possible; they do not by themselves make longer-range dependencies work.








Figure 2: The goal toy, on streams of 256 tokens, with heads trained on streams of 16. Mean squared error against how far back the later goal is, for the head without positional information (orange) and with a relative-position bias (blue), one thin line per training seed. The shaded band is the range of distances seen in training; the dashed line is a reactive policy’s error.







Training on the whole sequence at once
The original transformer was built for translation, as an encoder-decoder ▶ 11:08. The encoder reads the source sentence with bidirectional attention, every word seeing every other. The decoder writes the translation with causal attention: each position may attend only to itself and earlier positions, enforced by setting the scores of later positions to \(-\infty\) before the softmax ▶ 11:48. Between them, cross-attention takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder: given what I have written so far, what in the source matters now? ▶ 12:23
Training uses teacher forcing: at every position the model is given the true previous tokens, not its own guesses, and is asked to raise the probability of the correct next token ▶ 12:56. With the causal mask, one forward pass computes the loss at every position of the sequence at once; an RNN needs one step per token ▶ 13:25. (Teacher forcing has a cost that Week 3 already met: at test time the model conditions on its own outputs, which it never saw in training.)


What is a token?
Before any of this applies, the input must be cut into tokens ▶ 13:48. Characters give a tiny vocabulary but very long sequences; whole words give short sequences but a huge vocabulary, and no way to write a word never seen before ▶ 14:03. Sub-words sit in between ▶ 14:51. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) builds them bottom-up: start from single characters, find the most frequent adjacent pair, merge it into a new token, and repeat \(k\) times ▶ 15:18. Frequent pieces such as “the” merge early; a rare word still splits into known pieces. Short sequences matter because attention’s cost grows with the square of the length. The more text BPE is trained on, the more it compresses ▶ 17:08. Example 2 runs it on a sentence.
Scaling to large language models changed a few details ▶ 18:07. The encoder is dropped: a decoder-only model trained on next-token prediction is simpler to scale. BPE runs on bytes instead of characters, so every input, emojis included, can be written ▶ 18:54. RoPE encodes position by rotating queries and keys, so their dot product depends only on the distance between tokens ▶ 19:13. FlashAttention computes attention in tiles in fast on-chip memory, never storing the full \(n \times n\) matrix, so memory grows linearly with length instead of quadratically ▶ 19:46.


What scale buys
The lecture’s history of the GPT models ▶ 20:24: GPT-1 (2018) needed fine-tuning for each task; GPT-2, ten times larger, began to do tasks zero-shot, without being trained on them ▶ 21:02; GPT-3 (175 billion parameters) showed in-context learning, picking up a task from a few examples in the prompt with no gradient update ▶ 21:31. Neither ability was designed in; both appeared with scale. Sutton’s bitter lesson (2019) generalizes this: over 70 years of AI, methods that scale with computation have eventually beaten methods built on hand-engineered knowledge ▶ 21:59. The open question for this course is what emerges when robot data is scaled the same way.
If scale is what matters, how should a fixed compute budget be spent? The Chinchilla study found that model size and training data should grow in equal proportion, and that many large models of the time, GPT-3 among them, were too big for the data they saw ▶ 23:45. The rule of thumb is about 20 training tokens per parameter ▶ 25:09. Because the curves are smooth, small, cheap runs can predict how a large run will turn out before the compute is spent. Some recent models are trained far past that point on purpose (the lecture’s example is Llama 3) ▶ 26:39: a smaller model that saw more data is cheaper to serve to millions of users ▶ 27:09.


Images become tokens too
A robot must see. The vision transformer (ViT) cuts an image into 16 by 16 pixel patches (a 224 by 224 image gives 196), flattens and linearly projects each patch, adds a position embedding, and feeds the patches to a transformer as if they were words ▶ 28:30. Patches play the role for images that sub-words play for text.
Putting image tokens and text tokens in one sequence is not enough: the model must also know that the word “apple” and the patches showing an apple refer to the same thing. The lecture describes four ways to get there (Figure 3):

CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder side by side, so that matching image-caption pairs end up close in a shared embedding space and mismatched pairs far apart ▶ 30:42.
LLaVA (early fusion) runs the image through a frozen CLIP encoder, maps the patch embeddings into the language model’s token space with a small trained MLP, and puts them in front of the text; the language model, fine-tuned on visual instructions, then attends over everything with no change to its architecture ▶ 32:16.
Flamingo (late fusion) leaves the language model’s own layers untouched and inserts new cross-attention layers in which text queries look at visual keys and values. Each new layer is gated by \(\tanh(\alpha)\) with \(\alpha\) starting at 0, so at the start of training the model is exactly the original language model, and vision is let in gradually ▶ 33:45.
Natively multimodal models are trained from scratch on interleaved text, images, audio and video, with no modality privileged ▶ 35:38.

The trade-off: early fusion lets images and words interact most freely but risks degrading the language model during fine-tuning; late fusion preserves it but restricts the interaction to the cross-attention paths; native training removes the constraints and costs the most. According to the lecture, open-source VLMs mostly use early fusion, while the large proprietary models are converging on native training ▶ 36:58.

Figure 3: Three ways to give a language model sight. Early fusion puts projected image tokens into the input sequence; late fusion injects them through gated cross-attention layers; a natively multimodal model is trained on interleaved tokens of every kind from the start.







Actions become tokens
Each step from the transformer to the LLM, the VLM and native multimodal models followed the same play: find a way to tokenize a new modality, feed it to the same architecture, scale. The robotics version adds one more modality, actions, and treats control as multimodal sequence prediction: language tokens, image tokens, then action tokens that drive the motors (Figure 4) ▶ 39:22. Attention over the whole history also answers the memory problem from the start of the lecture.
Actions are continuous, so the first VLAs (RT-2, OpenVLA) bin them, one dimension at a time and one time step at a time ▶ 40:22. Each dimension is normalized to \([-1, 1]\) using its 1st and 99th percentiles over the training data, clipped, and cut into 256 equal bins ▶ 40:46. RT-2 first used the minimum and maximum instead, but a single outlier then stretches the range: in this page’s action toy, one glitched reading among 30,000 makes min-max normalization use only 48 of the 256 bins for the real motions, against all 256 with the quantile bounds. The 256 bins become 256 tokens of the language model’s vocabulary, for example by overwriting its 256 least-used tokens ▶ 42:10, and the model is trained by next-token prediction with its usual loss. Chunks: plan a short trajectory, not a single step
Attention answers the memory problem; action chunking answers the smoothness problem ▶ 43:21. Instead of one action, the policy predicts the next \(k\), \(\pi(a_{t:t+k} \mid o_t)\), and the robot executes them before asking again. The motion within a chunk is planned at once, so it is coherent. But while a long chunk plays out, the robot is blind: a 100-action chunk at 50 Hz ignores the world for two seconds. The temporal ensemble fixes that: query the policy at every step anyway, keep every chunk’s prediction for the current step, and execute their weighted average ▶ 44:46. ACT, the policy of the ALOHA paper, used both, predicting chunks of 100 joint targets for two 7-joint arms at 50 Hz: 1,400 numbers per forward pass ▶ 45:16, and it learned precise two-arm tasks such as inserting a battery ▶ 45:51.
The third toy measures the trade-off. A robot at 50 Hz moves towards a goal it estimates from a noisy camera at every query; after 1.6 seconds the goal moves. Each planned chunk closes a fixed share of the remaining gap per step. Over 200 runs, with chunks of \(k =\) 25 (half a second):

Single-step control is the most jittery, since every step follows a fresh noisy estimate, but it is accurate at rest, because its small steps average many estimates, and it reacts fastest. Open-loop chunks are 2.4 times smoother, but each chunk trusts one estimate, so they are 2.7 times less accurate, and they notice the move only at the next chunk. The ensemble keeps most of the smoothness and is as accurate as single-step control, because it too averages many estimates. It reacts almost as slowly as open-loop chunks, though, because right after the move most of the predictions it averages were made before it.




One run of the chunk toy, three ways: single steps, open-loop chunks of 25 steps, and the same chunks with a temporal ensemble. The grey line is the goal; it moves partway through.

What to watch for. All three panels show the same run (seed 0), drawn together behind one cursor so the schemes can be compared step by step. In the top panel every step follows a new noisy estimate of the goal, so the orange line is slightly ragged all the way. In the middle panel a faint chunk appears every half second, and the line follows each one smoothly. Where one chunk hands over to the next and a new estimate takes over, it shows a small kink: the typical bend there is 18 times the typical one inside a chunk. When the goal moves, at 1.6 s, the orange line turns at once. The blue line stays level, carrying on with its old chunk until the next query at 2.0 s, and it ends a little off the new goal, since its last chunk trusted one estimate. In the bottom panel a chunk appears at every step, so a fan of overlapping predictions runs ahead of the line. The line is their average: as smooth as the blue one, and closer to the goal. After the move, the newest predictions bend down at once, and the green line starts down with them, but more gently than the orange one, because old predictions still hold it back. A last small kink near 2.1 s marks the step after which no chunk made before the move is left in the average.


Why bins break at high control rates
Chunks of 1,400 numbers were fine for ACT, which outputs them all at once. An autoregressive VLA must generate them one token at a time, and per-step binning breaks down as the control rate rises ▶ 47:06. At high rates consecutive actions barely differ ▶ 47:21. Next-token prediction learns from what each new token adds, and when tokens are this correlated, a model can get a low loss by copying the previous action token, without learning the skill ▶ 47:53.
The action toy measures this on smooth one-second motions in 2 dimensions, each a sum of 3 slow waves (up to 1 Hz). Binned at 5 Hz, “repeat the previous token” predicts 45% of a token’s variation; at 50 Hz it predicts 99.4% (Figure 5, right). Exact repeats remain rare, 11% at 50 Hz, since 256 bins resolve small changes: the token is not literally the same, it is just almost entirely predictable. Meanwhile the sequence gets long: 100 tokens for each second of motion.
The fix is to compress first ▶ 48:26: find units for motion larger than one time step and smaller than a whole trajectory, as sub-words are for text and patches for images. BPE alone suits discrete symbols, not continuous signals, and a learned vector quantizer adds another model to train. FAST borrows from JPEG instead ▶ 49:43. A smooth signal has nearly all its energy at low frequencies, so a discrete cosine transform of each action dimension leaves a few large coefficients and many near zero. Scale and round them, list them lowest frequency first, and run BPE on the resulting integers, which merges the runs of zeros and common patterns into a few dense tokens. In the toy at 50 Hz, a chunk becomes 10.7 FAST tokens on average instead of 100 bins, 9 times fewer, and reconstructs the motion with about the same error (0.049 against 0.044 for the bins, on motions with standard deviation 0.79). At 2 Hz there is little to compress: 2.7 tokens against 4, and a larger error than the bins.
In the paper’s experiments, with a VLA trained on FAST tokens, performance keeps improving at higher control rates where binning collapses ▶ 50:59. An autoregressive version of π0 trained on FAST tokens reached the performance of the flow-matching π0 (the Week 6 kind of action head) five times faster in training ▶ 51:56, followed language commands zero-shot in unseen kitchens after training on the DROID data set ▶ 52:13, and folded laundry at 50 Hz ▶ 52:36. (The lecturer is a co-author of FAST.)
The lecture’s summary ▶ 53:24: treat robotics as sequence modeling, build on transformers because they scale, find the right tokens for each modality, and let data and compute do the rest, which is the bitter lesson applied to robots ▶ 54:54.








Figure 5: The action toy at five control rates. Left: tokens per one-second, two-dimensional chunk, for per-step bins and for FAST (DCT, rounding, then BPE). Right: the share of a bin token’s variation that repeating the previous token already predicts.

title: Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
Key concepts & formulae
Notation follows the lecture: \(o_t\) and \(a_t\) for observation and action, \(x_i\) for a generic sequence element, \(Q, K, V\) for queries, keys and values, \(d\) for their width, \(k\) for a chunk length. The ADM book discusses partial observability in its belief-state chapters, where a policy acts on a belief computed from the history rather than on the raw history itself.

Sequence models

\[
p_\theta(x_1, \dots, x_T) = \prod_{i=1}^{T} p_\theta(x_i \mid x_{1:i-1})
\tag{1}\]

In words. The probability of a whole sequence is the probability of each element given everything before it, multiplied together. Learn the one conditional, and you can both score and generate sequences.
Term by term.

\(x_{1:i-1}\): the prefix, all elements before position \(i\); for \(i = 1\) it is empty.
\(p_\theta(x_i \mid x_{1:i-1})\): the model’s conditional, the only thing learned. A transformer computes all \(T\) of them in one pass.
Why it holds: it is the definition of conditional probability, \(p(a, b) = p(a)\,p(b \mid a)\), applied \(T - 1\) times. Nothing is assumed about the data.


\[
h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)
\tag{2}\]

In words. An RNN carries a state vector forward, updating it with each new input; its predictions are read from the state.
Term by term.

\(h_t\): a fixed-size summary of \(x_1, \dots, x_t\), the bottleneck.
\(f\): the same learned function at every step. Gradients from step \(t\) to step 1 pass through \(t - 1\) applications of \(f\), which is why they vanish or explode.



Attention

\[
\begin{aligned}
Q &= E W_Q, \quad K = E W_K, \quad V = E W_V \\
\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) &= \operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\Big) V
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]

In words. Every token makes a query, a key and a value from its embedding. A token’s output is an average of all the values, weighted by how well its query matches each key.
Term by term.

\(E\): the token embeddings, one row per token; \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\): learned matrices.
\(Q K^\top\): every query dotted with every key, a score matrix with one row per token.
\(\sqrt{d}\): divides the scores so that their spread does not grow with the vector width \(d\), which would push the softmax towards a hard choice and flatten its gradients.
Softmax, row by row: the attention weights \(\alpha_{ij} = e^{s_{ij}} / \sum_{j'} e^{s_{ij'}}\), which sum to 1 over \(j\).
Multiplying by \(V\): token \(i\)’s output is \(\sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_j\). In practice several such heads run side by side (multi-head attention).
Numeric check: Example 1 computes one head of the goal toy by hand.


\[
s_{ij} = \begin{cases} q_i \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d} & j \le i \\ -\infty & j > i \end{cases}
\tag{4}\]

In words. Before the softmax, every score for a later position is set to minus infinity, so its weight becomes exactly zero: a token can use only itself and its past.
Term by term.

With the mask, the output at position \(i\) depends only on \(x_{1:i}\), which is what Equation 1 requires of the conditional for \(x_{i+1}\).
That is also what makes teacher forcing one pass: every position’s prediction is computed at once without seeing its own answer.


\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{absolute:}\quad & e_i \;\to\; e_i + \mathrm{PE}(i) \\
\text{relative:}\quad & s_{ij} \;\to\; s_{ij} + b(i - j)
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]

In words. Absolute encodings tag each token with its position before attention; relative encodings bias each attention score by how far apart the two tokens are.
Term by term.

\(\mathrm{PE}(i)\): a fixed (sinusoidal) or learned vector for position \(i\). A position beyond the training length has no learned vector, or one the model has never seen.
\(b(i - j)\): a bias that depends only on the distance. The goal toy uses the simplest form, \(b(i - j) = -\lambda (i - j)\), one learned number \(\lambda\).
Numeric check: the toy’s trained \(\lambda\) is 3.61 (mean of 5 seeds), and a goal’s content score is 15.1 times larger: the distance at which the bias cancels it matches the 15-step range seen in training (Figure 2).


\[
(R_{i\omega}\, q)^\top (R_{j\omega}\, k) = q^\top R_{(j - i)\omega}\, k
\tag{6}\]

In words. Rotate the query and the key by angles proportional to their positions; their dot product then depends only on the difference of positions.
Term by term.

\(R_{i\omega}\): a rotation by angle \(i\omega\), applied to each pair of coordinates (with a different \(\omega\) per pair).
Why it holds: rotations satisfy \(R_a^\top = R_{-a}\) and \(R_{-a} R_b = R_{b-a}\).



Training and tokens

\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})
\tag{7}\]

In words. Average, over the positions of a training sequence, the negative log-probability the model gives to the true next token, with the true earlier tokens as input.
Term by term.

\(x_{<t}\): the ground-truth prefix, not the model’s own samples; that is teacher forcing.
The sum is computed in one forward pass of a causally masked transformer.
It is the cross-entropy of Week 1’s action tokens, applied at every position.

Byte-pair encoding has no equation, only a loop: start with all characters as the vocabulary; \(k\) times, find the most frequent adjacent pair \((t_L, t_R)\) in the corpus, add \(t_L t_R\) to the vocabulary, and replace every occurrence. To tokenize new text, apply the learned merges in the order they were learned (Example 2).


Scaling

\[
\begin{aligned}
C &\approx 6 N D \\
N^* &\propto C^{0.5}, \quad D^* \propto C^{0.5}, \quad D^* \approx 20\, N^*
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]

In words. Training compute is about six operations per parameter per token. For a given budget, the best model size and the best amount of data both grow as the square root of the budget, at about 20 tokens per parameter.
Term by term.

\(C\): training compute in floating-point operations; \(N\): parameters; \(D\): training tokens.
The 6 counts the forward pass (about 2 operations per parameter per token) and the backward pass (about 4).
\(N^*\), \(D^*\): the compute-optimal choices, fitted from hundreds of training runs.
Numeric check: with \(D = 20 N\), \(C = 120 N^2\), so a budget of \(10^{21}\) operations gives \(N^* \approx 2.9\) billion parameters and \(D^* \approx 58\) billion tokens (Problem 3).



Vision and language

\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CLIP}} = -\frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigg[ \log \frac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{s_{ij}/\tau}} + \log \frac{e^{s_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{s_{ji}/\tau}} \bigg]
\tag{9}\]

In words. In a batch of \(N\) image-caption pairs, each image should pick out its own caption among all \(N\), and each caption its own image.
Term by term.

\(s_{ij}\): cosine similarity between image \(i\)’s embedding and caption \(j\)’s; the diagonal \(s_{ii}\) holds the true pairs.
The first term is a softmax classification over captions for each image; the second over images for each caption.
\(\tau\): a learned temperature; small \(\tau\) sharpens the softmax (here \(\tau\) is not a trajectory).


\[
x \;\leftarrow\; x + \tanh(\alpha) \cdot \operatorname{CrossAttn}(Q{=}x,\; K, V{=}\text{visual tokens})
\tag{10}\]

In words. Each new layer adds what the text tokens find in the image, scaled by a learned gate that starts closed.
Term by term.

\(x\): the text tokens’ hidden states inside the frozen language model.
\(\alpha\): one learned scalar per layer, initialized to 0, so \(\tanh(0) = 0\) and the model starts as the original language model.



Actions

\[
\begin{aligned}
u &= \operatorname{clip}\!\Big(2\, \frac{a - q_{01}}{q_{99} - q_{01}} - 1,\; -1,\; 1\Big) \\
\text{token} &= \Big\lfloor \tfrac{u + 1}{2} \cdot 256 \Big\rfloor \quad (\text{capped at } 255)
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}\]

In words. Map each action dimension’s 1st-to-99th-percentile range onto \([-1, 1]\), clip the rest, and cut \([-1, 1]\) into 256 equal bins.
Term by term.

\(q_{01}\), \(q_{99}\): percentiles of that dimension over the training data, so a few outliers cannot stretch the range.
An action with \(D\) dimensions at \(f\) Hz costs \(D f\) tokens per second.
Bin width is \(2/256 \approx 0.008\) in normalized units; decoding returns the bin’s centre.


\[
\begin{aligned}
&\pi_\theta(a_{t:t+k} \mid o_t) \\
&a_t = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, A_t[i]}{\sum_i w_i}, \quad w_i = e^{-m i}
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}\]

In words. The policy predicts the next \(k\) actions from the current observation. With a temporal ensemble, the action executed at step \(t\) is a weighted average of every prediction that some earlier chunk made for step \(t\).
Term by term.

\(A_t[i]\): the predictions for step \(t\), from up to \(k\) chunks; \(i = 0\) is the oldest.
\(m \ge 0\): how fast weights fall with \(i\). With \(m = 0\) all predictions count equally. Larger \(m\) weights the oldest prediction most. In the ALOHA paper, a smaller \(m\) incorporates new observations faster.
Numeric check: in the chunk toy with \(k =\) 25, jitter grows with \(m\): 0.0036, 0.0062, 0.0097, 0.0177 for \(m =\) 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2. Here, the oldest prediction changes every step as it expires, so weighting it heavily passes on that change. Weighting the newest most (\(m < 0\), outside the paper’s definition) was smoother still, 0.0014 at \(m = -0.1\), because each new chunk starts from where the robot actually is. Whether that carries over to learned policies, this toy cannot say.


\[
c_j = \nu_j \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} u_n \cos\!\Big(\frac{\pi\, j\, (2n + 1)}{2N}\Big), \qquad q_j = \operatorname{round}(10\, c_j)
\tag{13}\]

In words. Write a normalized action dimension \(u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}\) as a weighted sum of cosines of rising frequency \(j\), and round the scaled weights to integers. FAST then flattens the integers, lowest frequency first, and compresses them with BPE.
Term by term.

\(c_j\): how much of frequency \(j\) the chunk contains; \(c_0\) is proportional to its mean.
\(\nu_j\): normalization, \(\sqrt{1/N}\) for \(j = 0\) and \(\sqrt{2/N}\) otherwise, which makes the transform orthonormal and exactly invertible.
10: the rounding scale, which trades token count against precision.
Numeric check: at 50 Hz, a toy chunk has on average 12.5 non-zero rounded coefficients out of 100 (Example 3).
