title: Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
Algorithm & code

One attention head and its gradient

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def attend(params, X, relative=True) -> tuple[Array, tuple]:
    """One attention head, read out at the last token: (n,) and a cache.

    score_i = q . k_i / sqrt(d) - lam * (how many steps back token i is).
    The last token is the query and every other token is in its past, so
    the causal mask removes nothing here. relative=False drops the bias,
    and the head then sees its inputs as an unordered set.
    """
    (W_q, W_k), (w_v, lam) = params
    L = X.shape[1]
    q = X[:, -1] @ W_q              # (n, d): what the query asks for
    K = X @ W_k                     # (n, L, d): what each token offers
    back = np.arange(L)[::-1]       # (L,): L-1, ..., 1, 0 steps back
    s = np.einsum("nld,nd->nl", K, q) / np.sqrt(D_K)
    if relative:
        s = s - lam[0] * back       # the same bias at every length
    a = softmax(s, axis=1)          # (n, L): weights, each row sums to 1
    v = X @ w_v                     # (n, L): what each token contributes
    return (a * v).sum(axis=1), (q, K, a, v, back)

def attention_grads(params, X, y, relative=True) -> tuple[float, list]:
    """Mean squared error and its gradient for every parameter, by hand."""
    yhat, (q, K, a, v, back) = attend(params, X, relative)
    dy = 2 * (yhat - y) / len(y)                  # (n,)
    da, dv = dy[:, None] * v, dy[:, None] * a     # yhat = sum_i a_i v_i
    # Softmax backward: ds_i = a_i (da_i - sum_j a_j da_j).
    ds = a * (da - (a * da).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    dw_v = np.einsum("nl,nlf->f", dv, X)
    dlam = np.array([-(ds * back).sum()]) if relative else np.zeros(1)
    dK = ds[:, :, None] * q[:, None, :] / np.sqrt(D_K)     # (n, L, d)
    dq = np.einsum("nl,nld->nd", ds, K) / np.sqrt(D_K)     # (n, d)
    dW_k = np.einsum("nlf,nld->fd", X, dK)
    dW_q = X[:, -1].T @ dq
    loss = float(np.mean((yhat - y) ** 2))
    return loss, [(dW_q, dW_k), (dw_v, dlam)]


import numpy as np
import torch

from rlc.toys import w07_sequence as w7

torch.manual_seed(0)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
params = w7.init_attention(rng)
X_np, y_np, _ = w7.cue_batch(64, 10, rng)


def head(X, W_q, W_k, w_v, lam):
    """The page's head in torch: X (n, L, 3) -> answer (n,)."""
    q = X[:, -1] @ W_q                               # (n, d)
    K = X @ W_k                                      # (n, L, d)
    back = torch.arange(X.shape[1] - 1, -1, -1)      # steps back, (L,)
    s = torch.einsum("nld,nd->nl", K, q) / K.shape[-1] ** 0.5
    a = torch.softmax(s - lam * back, dim=1)         # dim, not axis
    return (a * (X @ w_v)).sum(dim=1)


# Leaf tensors with requires_grad: autograd will fill .grad for each.
(W_q, W_k), (w_v, lam) = [(torch.tensor(a, requires_grad=True),
                           torch.tensor(b, requires_grad=True))
                          for a, b in params]
X, y = torch.tensor(X_np), torch.tensor(y_np)
loss = ((head(X, W_q, W_k, w_v, lam[0]) - y) ** 2).mean()
loss.backward()

# The hand-written NumPy gradients agree with autograd.
np_loss, np_grads = w7.attention_grads(params, X_np, y_np)
assert abs(loss.item() - np_loss) < 1e-9
torch_grads = [W_q.grad, W_k.grad, w_v.grad, lam.grad]
for g_t, g_np in zip(torch_grads, [g for pair in np_grads for g in pair]):
    assert np.allclose(g_t.numpy(), g_np, atol=1e-9)



The NumPy version spells out the softmax’s backward pass, \(\partial s_i = \alpha_i (\partial \alpha_i - \sum_j \alpha_j \partial \alpha_j)\); the PyTorch version gets the same numbers from autograd, which the snippet checks. In a real transformer this head is one of many, inside layers that also have a feed-forward network, residual connections and layer normalization.


Next-token prediction on action tokens

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def quantile_bounds(A, lo=1.0, hi=99.0) -> Array:
    """Per-dimension 1st and 99th percentiles over all samples: (2, dims)."""
    return np.percentile(A.reshape(-1, A.shape[-1]), [lo, hi], axis=0)

def normalize(A, bounds) -> Array:
    """Map [low, high] to [-1, 1] per dimension, clipping the rest."""
    low, high = bounds
    return np.clip(2 * (A - low) / (high - low) - 1, -1, 1)

def bin_tokens(A, bounds, bins=N_BINS) -> Array:
    """One integer in 0..bins-1 per dimension per step, same shape as A."""
    u = normalize(A, bounds)
    return np.minimum(((u + 1) / 2 * bins).astype(int), bins - 1)

def dct_coefficients(A, bounds, scale) -> Array:
    """Normalize, DCT along time, scale and round: integers (n, f, dims).

    A smooth signal puts nearly all its energy in the first few
    frequencies, so most rounded coefficients are zero.
    """
    c = dct(normalize(A, bounds), axis=1, norm="ortho")
    return np.round(scale * c).astype(int)

def bpe_merge(seq, pair, new) -> list:
    """Replace each non-overlapping occurrence of pair, left to right."""
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(seq):
        if i + 1 < len(seq) and seq[i] == pair[0] and seq[i + 1] == pair[1]:
            out.append(new)
            i += 2
        else:
            out.append(seq[i])
            i += 1
    return out

def bpe_train(corpus, k) -> tuple[list, list]:
    """Up to k merges of the most frequent adjacent pair.

    Returns the merges and the merged corpus. Ties go to the pair counted
    first (Counter keeps insertion order). Stops early when no pair occurs
    twice.
    """
    corpus, merges = [list(s) for s in corpus], []
    for _ in range(k):
        counts = Counter(p for s in corpus for p in zip(s, s[1:]))
        if not counts:
            break
        pair, c = counts.most_common(1)[0]
        if c < 2:
            break
        corpus = [bpe_merge(s, pair, pair) for s in corpus]
        merges.append(pair)
    return merges, corpus


import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

# Bin tokens of the action toy at 20 Hz: one dimension, 20 steps per chunk.
P = w7.signal_params(256, np.random.default_rng(1), dims=1)
A = w7.sample_actions(P, 20)                             # (256, 20, 1)
VOCAB = 64                                       # coarse bins keep it tiny
tokens = torch.tensor(w7.bin_tokens(A, w7.quantile_bounds(A), VOCAB)[..., 0])
L = tokens.shape[1]


class TinyGPT(nn.Module):
    """Token + position embeddings, one causal layer, a linear head."""

    def __init__(self, d=48):
        super().__init__()
        self.tok, self.pos = nn.Embedding(VOCAB, d), nn.Embedding(L, d)
        self.layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, nhead=4, dim_feedforward=96,
                                                batch_first=True, dropout=0.0)
        self.out = nn.Linear(d, VOCAB)

    def forward(self, x):                                # x: (B, T) token ids
        T = x.shape[1]
        h = self.tok(x) + self.pos(torch.arange(T))      # (B, T, d)
        # Causal mask: True above the diagonal = may not attend to the future.
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
        return self.out(self.layer(h, src_mask=mask))    # (B, T, VOCAB) logits


model = TinyGPT()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
inputs, targets = tokens[:, :-1], tokens[:, 1:]  # teacher forcing: shift
losses = []
for step in range(150):
    logits = model(inputs)                       # one pass: all positions
    # cross_entropy wants (N, classes): flatten batch and time together.
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, VOCAB), targets.reshape(-1))
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    losses.append(loss.item())

# A uniform guess costs log(64) = 4.16 nats; learning beats it by far.
assert losses[0] > 3.5 and losses[-1] < 0.5 * losses[0], losses[-1]



On the NumPy side are the two tokenizers this page compares: bins, and DCT coefficients that BPE then compresses. The PyTorch sketch trains a one-layer causal transformer on bin tokens by teacher forcing: inputs are the tokens shifted by one, and a single forward pass scores every position. This is the recipe of RT-2 and OpenVLA in miniature, without the images and the language model.


Executing chunks

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def plan_chunk(x, goal_seen, k) -> Array:
    """k planned positions closing RATE of the remaining gap per step."""
    return goal_seen + (x - goal_seen) * (1 - RATE) ** np.arange(1, k + 1)

def run_chunks(k, mode, rng, m=0.0, noise=OBS_NOISE, t_move=T_MOVE,
               keep=False):
    """Positions x_0..x_T under one execution scheme.

    The robot tracks each action exactly. mode "chunk": query every k
    steps and execute the whole chunk open loop (k = 1 is ordinary
    single-step control). mode "ensemble": query every step and execute
    the weighted average of every chunk that covers this step, weight
    exp(-m i) with i = 0 the oldest prediction, as in ACT. keep=True also
    returns every query's (time, planned chunk).
    """
    x = np.zeros(T_RUN + 1)
    preds = [[] for _ in range(T_RUN + k)]   # step t: predictions, oldest 1st
    plan, plans = None, []
    for t in range(T_RUN):
        goal = GOAL_A if t < t_move else GOAL_B
        if mode == "ensemble" or t % k == 0:
            # Each query sees the goal through a new noisy observation.
            seen = goal + noise * rng.standard_normal()
            plan = plan_chunk(x[t], seen, k)
            plans.append((t, plan))
            for j in range(k):
                preds[t + j].append(plan[j])
        if mode == "ensemble":
            p = np.array(preds[t])
            w = np.exp(-m * np.arange(len(p)))
            x[t + 1] = (w * p).sum() / w.sum()
        else:
            x[t + 1] = plan[t % k]
    return (x, plans) if keep else x


from collections import defaultdict

K_CHUNK, ACT_DIM, OBS_DIM = 10, 14, 32               # ACT: two 7-joint arms


class ChunkPolicy(nn.Module):
    """Observation features -> the next K_CHUNK actions, (B, K_CHUNK, ACT_DIM).

    ACT itself is a transformer trained as a conditional VAE; a plain MLP
    head shows the shape of the output and of the loss."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(OBS_DIM, 128), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(128, K_CHUNK * ACT_DIM))

    def forward(self, obs):
        return self.net(obs).view(-1, K_CHUNK, ACT_DIM)


policy = ChunkPolicy()
obs = torch.randn(256, OBS_DIM)
demo_chunks = torch.randn(256, K_CHUNK, ACT_DIM)     # stand-in demonstrations
opt = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
first = None
for step in range(100):
    loss = F.l1_loss(policy(obs), demo_chunks)   # ACT's reconstruction loss
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    first = first or loss.item()
assert loss.item() < first


def temporal_ensemble(policy, observations, m=0.0):
    """Query every step; average all stored predictions for this step."""
    buffer = defaultdict(list)                   # step -> preds, oldest first
    executed = []
    with torch.no_grad():                        # inference: no graph needed
        for t, o in enumerate(observations):
            chunk = policy(o[None])[0]               # (K_CHUNK, ACT_DIM)
            for j in range(K_CHUNK):
                buffer[t + j].append(chunk[j])
            preds = torch.stack(buffer.pop(t))       # (n_preds, ACT_DIM)
            w = torch.exp(-m * torch.arange(len(preds)))
            executed.append((w[:, None] * preds).sum(0) / w.sum())
    return torch.stack(executed)                     # (T, ACT_DIM)


acts = temporal_ensemble(policy, torch.randn(30, OBS_DIM))
assert acts.shape == (30, ACT_DIM)



The toy’s run_chunks does the same bookkeeping with plain lists. In ACT the policy is a transformer over camera features and joint positions, trained as a conditional VAE (the ALOHA paper’s card below has the details); the execution loop is the same.

title: Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
Papers

Papers discussed in class






Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Sequence Modeling Chen et al. · NeurIPS 2021
Treats offline reinforcement learning as sequence modeling. A GPT-style causal transformer reads the recent history of (return-to-go, state, action) tokens and is trained, like a language model, to predict the action. At test time you ask for a high return, and it generates actions meant to achieve it: no value function, no policy gradient.

Conditions on returns-to-go, the sum of future rewards, instead of past rewards, so the desired return is set at the start and decremented as rewards arrive (Sec. 3).
Matches or exceeds model-free offline RL baselines such as CQL on Atari, OpenAI Gym and Key-to-Door, with almost no change to a language-model architecture (Abstract, Sec. 4).
Context matters: with only the current step (K = 1) Atari scores drop sharply, e.g. Pong from 106.1 to 2.5 (Table 5).

On this page: This page’s view of a robot’s history as a token sequence, and its attention toy, which also needs past tokens to act. It also links back to Weeks 4 and 5: return is now an input rather than something to maximize.









Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware Zhao, Kumar, Levine & Finn · RSS 2023
ALOHA is a two-arm teleoperation system built for under $20k, with leader arms a person backdrives and follower arms that mirror them. ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers) learns from its demonstrations: a transformer predicts the next k joint targets at once from camera images, and overlapping predictions are averaged at execution.

Action chunking: predicting k = 100 actions per query at 50 Hz shortens the task’s effective horizon k-fold; success rose from 1% at k = 1 to 44% at k = 100, averaged over four simulated settings without the ensemble (Sec. IV-A, VI-A).
Temporal ensembling: query every step and average all predictions for the current step with weights exp(-m i), i = 0 the oldest (Sec. IV-A, Algorithm 2).
Trained as a conditional VAE to cope with noisy, multimodal human demonstrations, which the paper finds essential for precise tasks (Sec. IV-B).
80-90% success on tasks such as slotting a battery or opening a translucent condiment cup, from 10 minutes of demonstrations per task (Abstract).

On this page: The action-chunk toy and the hero clip on this page, which compare single-step control, open-loop chunks and ACT’s temporal ensemble.









Humanoid Locomotion as Next Token Prediction Radosavovic et al. · NeurIPS 2024
Casts humanoid walking as next-token prediction over sensorimotor trajectories. A causal transformer predicts both the next observation and the next action, so it can also learn from trajectories with missing parts, such as human videos without motor commands, by replacing the missing tokens with a learned mask token.

Training data from four sources: neural-network policies, model-based controllers, human motion capture and YouTube videos of people (Sec. 4).
A full-sized humanoid (Agility Robotics’ Digit) walks around San Francisco zero-shot, and the model transfers even when trained on only 27 hours of walking data (Abstract).
Follows commands never seen in training, such as walking backward (Abstract).
Predicting states as well as actions lowers tracking error compared with predicting actions only (Table 1d).

On this page: The lecture’s claim that robotics is a sequence-modeling problem, taken literally: the robot’s own trajectory is the sentence, and every token is predicted.





Key papers from the lecture






Attention Is All You Need Vaswani et al. · NeurIPS 2017
Introduces the Transformer, an encoder-decoder for sequence-to-sequence tasks built only from attention and feed-forward layers, with no recurrence or convolution. Every token can draw on every other token in one step, and training runs in parallel over the whole sequence.

Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention as the only way information moves between positions (Abstract).
Better translation quality than the best recurrent and convolutional models, while being more parallelizable and much cheaper to train (Abstract).
The template that GPT-style language models, ViT, VLMs and VLAs all reuse.

On this page: The attention equation boxed on this page and the attention toy, which implements one head and its gradient in NumPy.









An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale Dosovitskiy, Beyer et al. · ICLR 2021
Cuts an image into 16 by 16 pixel patches, projects each patch linearly into a token, adds a position embedding, and feeds the sequence to a standard Transformer. Without any convolutional backbone, the result competes with the best convolutional networks once pre-trained on enough data.

Image patches as tokens: the same interface as words, so images and text can share one sequence (Abstract).
When pre-trained on large data and transferred to benchmarks such as ImageNet and CIFAR-100, matches or beats strong convolutional networks with substantially less compute to train (Abstract).

On this page: This page’s section on tokenizing images, the step from language models to vision-language models.









Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models Hoffmann et al. · NeurIPS 2022
Asks how to split a fixed compute budget between model size and training tokens. From over 400 training runs, the answer is to grow both in equal proportion; most large language models of the time were too big for the data they saw.

Over 400 language models, from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, trained on 5 to 500 billion tokens (Abstract).
For every doubling of model size, double the training tokens too (Abstract).
Chinchilla, 70B parameters on 4 times Gopher’s data at the same compute, outperforms Gopher (280B) and GPT-3 (175B) on a wide range of tasks (Abstract).

On this page: The scaling-law equations on this page and the lecture’s question of what scale buys in robotics.









FAST: Efficient Action Tokenization for Vision-Language-Action Models Pertsch, Stachowicz et al. · RSS 2025
Per-dimension, per-step binning, the usual way to turn robot actions into tokens, fails for autoregressive VLAs trained on high-frequency, dexterous data. FAST compresses each action chunk first: a discrete cosine transform, rounding, then byte-pair encoding, which gives a few dense tokens per chunk.

Shows that simple binning performs poorly when learning dexterous skills from high-frequency robot data (Abstract).
A compression-based tokenizer built on the discrete cosine transform, which lets autoregressive VLAs train on tasks where binning fails completely (Abstract).
FAST+, a universal tokenizer trained on 1M real robot action trajectories (Abstract).
With the pi0 VLA, scales to 10k hours of robot data and matches diffusion VLAs while training up to 5 times faster (Abstract).

On this page: The action-token toy on this page, which runs a small version of the same pipeline next to plain binning. The lecturer is one of the paper’s authors.

title: Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
Guest spotlight
Ted Xiao (Project Prometheus, previously Google DeepMind) told the last decade of robot learning as three eras, mostly through the work of the Google teams he was part of, and said so ▶ 03:11. The starting thesis, around 2016, was that robot hardware was nearly ready (a teleoperated robot could already tidy a room decades ago) and that the missing piece was intelligence, which deep learning was then supplying in games such as Atari and Go ▶ 02:34.
The first era, existence proofs (about 2016 to 2021), asked whether end-to-end learning on real robots could work at all. Google built “arm farms” of many robots collecting grasps around the clock ▶ 05:38, and QT-Opt applied Q-learning to continuous actions and camera images, trained on over half a million grasps ▶ 06:25. Online RL at that scale proved hard to run, so the team bet more on imitation (BC-Z) ▶ 08:14 and on learning from unstructured play data ▶ 09:03, and then started over with a fleet of robots collecting demonstrations of hundreds of tasks for a year and a half ▶ 09:56.
The second era, foundation models, borrowed the recipe this lecture describes: treat everything as tokens, reuse pre-trained models, and learn offline from large demonstration sets ▶ 12:19. RT-1 was a 35-million-parameter transformer from images and instructions to discretized action tokens, running at 3 Hz across hundreds of tasks ▶ 13:34. Language models were also used off the shelf: as planners whose suggestions were grounded by a value function saying which skills the robot could actually do now ▶ 15:59, and for relabeling robot data with richer instructions ▶ 17:08. RT-2 then made a VLM itself the policy, answering “what should the robot do?” with action tokens, and co-trained on web and robot data so web knowledge transferred to new objects ▶ 18:11. The Open X-Embodiment project pooled data from many labs and robots (“over 30 research labs”, in his words) ▶ 19:35.
The third era, scale, is the present: large investments in turning those prototypes into products ▶ 22:01. His examples include Gemini Robotics, which combined a frontier multimodal model with dexterous data from the ALOHA platform (this week’s discussion paper) ▶ 22:52 and, in its 1.5 version, one policy trained across several robot bodies with a shared action space ▶ 23:45; new evaluation methods, since real-world comparisons need thousands of trials ▶ 25:52; and many competing bets on data: wearable gloves, egocentric video, deployment data ▶ 26:04. He closed with open questions: the role of world models, the value of robot-free data, reasoning models, and how to unite manipulation, learned mostly by imitation, with locomotion, learned by RL in simulation ▶ 27:29. In the Q&A he expects high-quality teleoperation data to stay essential until training on cheaper, broader data is better understood ▶ 29:31, and he sees video-pretrained models as promising but doubts they replace text-based reasoning ▶ 32:41.
How it connects to this week. The talk is the lecture’s thesis told as history: each era moved closer to “one transformer, tokens in and tokens out, trained on as much data as possible”. RT-1 and RT-2 are the per-step action tokens of this page, and the move from them to FAST and to diffusion and flow heads (Week 6) is the move this week’s last section explains. Week 9 takes up the generalist policies of the third era.

title: Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
Solved problems
1. Attention by hand. Three tokens have values \(v = (1, -1, 3)\), and the query’s scores against their keys (already divided by \(\sqrt{d}\)) are \((2, 0, 1)\). Compute the attention weights and the output. Then apply a causal mask that hides the third token, and recompute.






TipSolution





\(e^2 = 7.389\), \(e^0 = 1\), \(e^1 = 2.718\), summing to 11.107. Weights: 0.665, 0.090, 0.245. Output: \(0.665 - 0.090 + 3 \times 0.245 = 1.31\). With the third score set to \(-\infty\), its weight is 0 and the others renormalize: \(7.389 / 8.389 = 0.881\) and \(0.119\), so the output is \(0.881 - 0.119 = 0.76\). Masking changes the answer because the hidden token carried the largest value.



2. Why order needs encoding. Show that without positional information, permuting the input tokens permutes the attention outputs the same way, so a readout at the last position cannot depend on the order of the earlier tokens. What does this imply for the goal toy?






TipSolution





Each output \(\sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_j\) depends on the set of (key, value) pairs and on token \(i\)’s own query; the weights \(\alpha_{ij}\) depend only on the contents \(q_i \cdot k_j\). Reordering the other tokens reorders the terms of the sum without changing it. In the goal toy, the query is the last token, so its output is the same whichever goal came first: the head can only treat the two goals symmetrically. The symmetric answer with the least squared error is their average, and with independent standard normal goals its error is \(\mathbb{E}[(g_2 - g_1)^2] / 4 = 2/4 = 0.5\), which is what training reached (0.50).



3. Sizing a model. You have a training budget of \(10^{21}\) floating-point operations. Using \(C \approx 6ND\) and \(D \approx 20 N\), how many parameters and tokens are compute-optimal? If you instead train a model 4 times smaller with the same budget, how many tokens per parameter does it see?






TipSolution





Substituting, \(C = 6 N \cdot 20 N = 120 N^2\), so \(N = \sqrt{10^{21}/120} \approx 2.9 \times 10^9\) parameters and \(D = 20 N \approx 5.8 \times 10^{10}\) tokens. A model of \(N/4 \approx 7.2 \times 10^8\) parameters at the same compute sees \(D = C/(6 \cdot N/4) = 4 \times 5.8 \times 10^{10} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{11}\) tokens: 320 tokens per parameter, 16 times the Chinchilla ratio. It is worse to train for this budget, but cheaper to run, which is the Llama 3 trade-off.



4. The token bill of per-step bins. A VLA controls a 7-joint arm plus a gripper (8 action dimensions) at 50 Hz with one-second chunks, binned per dimension and per step. How many action tokens does one second of motion take? If the model decodes 200 tokens per second, can it keep up? What compression factor would let it plan each one-second chunk in a fifth of a second?






TipSolution





\(8 \times 50 = 400\) tokens per second of motion. At 200 tokens per second the model needs 2 seconds to plan 1 second of motion: it falls behind. To plan in 0.2 s it may use 40 tokens, a compression factor of 10. In this page’s toy, FAST compressed 50 Hz chunks by about 9 times; real motions with more dimensions and sharper features would compress differently, so this is only an indication.



5. Ensemble weights. With chunks of \(k = 4\) and a temporal ensemble queried every step, how many predictions are averaged at step 10? With \(m = 0.5\), what share of the weight does the oldest get, and what share the newest? After the goal moves, how many steps pass before every averaged prediction was made after the move?






TipSolution





Chunks from the queries at steps 7, 8, 9 and 10 cover step 10: four predictions. Weights \(e^{-0.5 i}\) for \(i = 0, \dots, 3\) are 1, 0.607, 0.368, 0.223, summing to 2.198; the oldest gets \(1/2.198 = 45\%\), the newest \(0.223/2.198 = 10\%\). After a move, the prediction made at the move’s step enters at once, but the oldest made before the move leaves only \(k - 1 = 3\) steps later, so from the fourth step on all four predictions know about the move. Weighting the oldest most, as larger \(m\) does, slows the reaction further.

title: Week 7 · Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
Recap

Robots need sequences, in and out. A single observation hides velocities and past events, and single-step decisions jitter. Why it matters: it is the reason the rest of the course uses history-conditioned, chunk-predicting policies.
Attention gives direct access to the whole history. Queries, keys and values implement a soft lookup; a causal mask makes it autoregressive; positional encodings supply order, and, as the goal toy shows, reach only as far as training required. Why it matters: this one mechanism underlies LLMs, VLMs and VLAs.
Everything becomes tokens. Sub-words by BPE, images by patches, vision and language aligned by contrastive training, early fusion, late fusion or native training. Why it matters: a robot policy built on a VLM inherits its tokenization and its knowledge.
Scale is predictable. Loss falls smoothly with model size, data and compute; Chinchilla’s rule splits a budget at about 20 tokens per parameter. Why it matters: it frames the course’s open question of what robot data at scale will buy.
Per-step action bins break at high control rates. Neighbouring tokens become almost entirely predictable from each other, and sequences become long; FAST compresses chunks with a DCT and BPE. Why it matters: high rates are what dexterous manipulation needs.
Chunks trade reactivity for smoothness. Open-loop chunks are smooth but blind and trust one estimate each; a temporal ensemble is smooth and as accurate as single-step control, but still reacts late. Why it matters: nearly every modern robot policy predicts action chunks.

Common pitfalls.

Forgetting the causal mask in training: the model sees each answer and learns to copy it, then fails at generation.
Assuming relative positional encodings give long-range memory for free: they let the model run on longer inputs, not use what lies beyond the distances it learned.
Min-max normalizing actions: one outlier wastes most of the bins.
Judging an action tokenizer by next-token loss alone: at high rates a low loss can mean “copy the last token”.
Executing long chunks open loop in a changing world: the robot is blind until the next query.
Comparing chunk sizes on smoothness only: accuracy and reaction time move the other way.

Connections. Week 1 introduced actions as tokens; this week explains the transformer that reads them and why the simplest tokenization fails at speed. Week 3’s behavior cloning is what ACT does with chunks, and chunking shortens the effective horizon over which Week 3’s errors compound. Weeks 4 and 5 maximize return, while the Decision Transformer conditions on it. Week 6’s diffusion and flow policies are the main alternative to autoregressive action tokens, and π0’s flow head is the comparison point for FAST. Week 9 builds generalist VLAs from all of these pieces. In the ADM Companion: beliefs and the belief update, the principled way to act on a history, and controllers that remember.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
The policies of Weeks 3, 6 and 7, such as ACT and Diffusion Policy, are specialists: superb at one task on one robot, and retrained for every new robot or task ▶ 00:30. The field’s goal is the opposite, a generalist robot policy: one model that controls many robots, in many places, on many tasks ▶ 01:32, so that you could download a “robot brain” and have it behave sensibly on your robot out of the box. Language and vision got there by training one large model on many tasks, which then beat the specialist models ▶ 03:06. This week asks what it takes to repeat that in robotics, where data are scarce, every robot is different, control must be fast, and every evaluation costs hours of robot time ▶ 04:40.
The question this week answers: where do the data for a generalist robot policy come from, how do you train one model on robots that see and act differently, and how do you tell whether it is any good?


The key ideas at a glance

Pool the data the field already has. Open X-Embodiment gathered over a million real-robot episodes from 22 robots and 34 labs into one format; one model trained on all of it beat the methods built for each data set.
Treat robotics as sequence modeling. Tokenize instructions, goal images and camera frames, run a transformer, read actions out (Octo). Different robots get different readout heads (CrossFormer), or one padded action space whose robot the model must infer (π0).
Pretraining pays most when the new task has little data. Pooled features need far fewer demos to learn a new robot; with plenty of data the advantage fades.
Start from a vision-language model. Fine-tune a VLM to output actions (a VLA), and protect its knowledge: co-train on web data, and stop the action expert’s gradients at the backbone.
Engineering decides a lot. Batching robots with different camera counts (padding or packing), how randomly the data loader mixes trajectories, and even data normalization can matter more than architecture.
Evaluate in simulation, for rankings. A simulator calibrated to the real robot cannot predict absolute success, but it can say which of two policies is better (SIMPLER).



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Generalist robot policy
One model that controls several robots on many tasks


Embodiment
A particular robot body: its sensors, its motors, its action space


Open X-Embodiment (OXE)
A pooled data set of over a million episodes from 22 robots


Positive transfer
Data from other robots making a policy better on yours


Goal-conditioned BC
Behavior cloning with the goal (an image or an instruction) as an input


Readout token
A placeholder token whose output embedding a head turns into actions


Action head
The part of the network that turns features into one robot’s actions


Action expert
A separate network (in π0, a flow-matching transformer) that produces continuous actions


VLA
Vision-language-action model: a vision-language model fine-tuned to output actions


Knowledge insulation
Training the action expert without letting its gradients change the VLM


Sequence packing
Laying samples of different lengths end to end in one sequence, instead of padding


Shuffle buffer
A pool of samples a streaming data loader draws batches from at random


Real-to-sim evaluation
Scoring real-world policies in a simulator built to resemble the real setup


MMRV
Mean maximum rank violation: how badly a simulator misorders policies





After this week you can

Explain why pooled multi-robot data can beat robot-specific data, and when it helps most.
Describe Octo’s tokens, block-wise causal attention and readout heads, and how it is fine-tuned to a new robot.
Compare per-robot heads with a padded action space, and say how each knows which robot it drives.
Describe how a VLM becomes a VLA, and why the current recipe uses co-training and a stop-gradient.
Compute the cost of padding a heterogeneous batch, and pack it correctly.
Explain advantage conditioning (π*0.6) and why it can use bad data that filtering throws away.
Judge a simulated evaluation by its ranking (MMRV), not its absolute numbers.

title: Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A driving instructor who has taught in cars, vans and tractors can learn a new vehicle in an afternoon. The hard part, reading traffic and planning a route, is the same in every vehicle; only the pedals and levers differ. A generalist robot policy is built the same way: one shared network learns the skill from every robot’s data, and a thin robot-specific part maps that skill to each robot’s motors.



Use the data that already exists
Robot data are expensive: every demonstration is a person teleoperating a robot ▶ 05:11, and nothing like the internet’s text or images exists for robot actions. But almost every robotics lab collects some data for its own papers ▶ 08:21. Open X-Embodiment asked labs worldwide for theirs and converted it to one common format, giving over a million real-robot episodes from 22 robots ▶ 09:23. The result was the first sign of a generalist: a single model trained on the whole mixture beat the best method designed for each individual setup ▶ 09:53.
The catch is that the data are heterogeneous: different cameras and camera counts, different action spaces, different control rates ▶ 05:43. This page’s first toy has the same problem in miniature. Four robots move a point round a post to a goal. The skill, how to get round the post, is the same for all four; but their motors differ: a plain point, one whose axes are turned and scaled, one with three wheels and one with four motors. Their data differ wildly in size: 40 episodes (point), 20 episodes (turned), 6 episodes (three wheels), 3 episodes (four motors).








Figure 2: First toy: success rate on 300 held-out tasks for each robot (mean ± standard error over 8 seeds). Specialist: one network per robot on its own demos. Heads: one network for all robots, a separate output head each. Padded + cue: one padded output, with a cue telling the robots apart; padded, no cue: the same without the cue.





Trained alone, the robots with plenty of data do well, and the one with 3 episodes reaches the goal in 60% of held-out tasks (Figure 2). Trained together, with a separate output head per robot, four motors rises to 80% and three wheels from 84% to 91%, while the two data-rich robots lose nothing. The shared layers learn how to get round the post from everyone’s demos; each head only has to learn its robot’s motor mapping, which is far less to learn from 3 episodes. That is positive transfer. It is not guaranteed: four motors gained in 7 of the 8 seeds, not all of them.




The first toy's data-poor robot, four motors, driven by its own specialist and then by one network trained on all four robots' demos (seed 0, 20 held-out tasks).

What to watch for. The table and the tasks stay the same throughout; only the network driving four motors changes. Trained on its own 3 demos, the specialist steers many runs from the upper starts into the post’s upper-left side: 8 of the 20 runs end at the post, and 11 reach their goals. After pooling, the network has learned how to get round the post from all four robots’ demos, and its four-motors head only converts that into this robot’s four motor commands: 15 runs reach their goals and 5 touch the post. Seed 0 is the seed whose gain from pooling is closest to the average over 8 seeds; the bar chart above shows the averages.


Robotics as sequence modeling
A VLM maps an image and a question to text: “what is in this picture?” → “the Statue of Liberty”. A robot policy maps an image and an instruction to actions. Squint, and the second is the first with a different kind of answer ▶ 13:02. So the generalist designs treat robotics as multimodal sequence modeling: turn everything into tokens and train a transformer ▶ 13:34. Gato, from Week 8’s guest, did this most literally: Atari frames, text, joint torques and button presses all became integers in one vocabulary.
Octo was the first open-source generalist policy, trained on 800,000 OXE trajectories ▶ 14:05. A language model encodes the instruction into task tokens; a shallow CNN turns image patches into observation tokens; a transformer much like a ViT processes them ▶ 15:08. Attention is block-wise causal: observation tokens see the task and earlier time steps, never later ones ▶ 16:10. Extra readout tokens collect what the actions need, and a diffusion head turns them into an action chunk ▶ 16:41 ▶ 17:44. It is trained by goal-conditioned behavior cloning, so the goal can be an image or an instruction.

Figure 3: Octo’s design, drawn from the lecture. Task and observation tokens enter one transformer with block-wise causal attention; readout tokens gather what the action head needs, and a diffusion head produces an action chunk. A new sensor or robot is added by new input tokens or a new head.





Two practical choices mattered. Octo did not align coordinate frames across data sets, which kept it scalable, but it did align the gripper command: early failures were mostly grasps at the wrong moment, because data sets encoded “open” and “closed” four different ways ▶ 18:45. And it was meant to be fine-tuned: a new sensor, such as a force-torque reading, enters as a few new tokens, a new action space gets a new head, and since most parameters sit in the transformer, most of the knowledge survives ▶ 22:58. Fine-tuning a generalist worked much better than starting from the best pretrained visual representations ▶ 24:01.


One network, many bodies
How does one network output actions for robots with 7, 14 or 2 action dimensions, at 5 or 50 Hz? There are two designs ▶ 45:49. CrossFormer gives each kind of embodiment its own action head on a shared transformer, so each head can predict a chunk of its own length and rate ▶ 28:11; one checkpoint drove arms, bimanual robots, quadrupeds, wheeled robots and drones, and matched the specialists ▶ 30:15. π0 has a single action expert writing into one padded action space as large as the biggest robot’s; smaller robots pad with zeros ▶ 46:51.
Then how does the network know which robot it is driving? With heads, it does not need to: the user picks the head ▶ 50:01. With one padded output, the model has to infer the robot from what it sees: the camera views, the joint readings it gets as input, even the instruction (“cut the sushi” is not a task for a vacuum robot) ▶ 50:33. The toy’s padded network gets a one-hot cue standing in for those signals. With the cue it matches the heads on three of the robots; without it, it fails on every robot (Figure 2), because positions and goals alone do not say whose motors are attached. On four motors it did no better than the specialist (61%), possibly because its fourth output is trained by four motors’ 3 episodes alone, while the heads network gives each robot its own output weights on shared features; we have not tested this further.

Pretraining pays most when data are scarce
Does pretraining on many tasks actually help a new one? Many believed so, but it was hard to show in robotics ▶ 30:46. TRI’s large-behavior-model study tested it with blind, randomized real-robot trials and found pretraining made fine-tuning about 3 to 5 times more sample efficient, with the largest gains when the new task had little data ▶ 32:50. It also found that how the data were normalized often mattered more than architecture or algorithm ▶ 33:20. (The 3 to 5 times is the lecturer’s summary; we checked only the paper’s abstract, which says new tasks are learned with less data but gives no single factor.)
The toy reproduces the pattern. A fifth robot arrives with a handful of demos. Either train a network on them from scratch, or keep the pooled network frozen and fit only a new linear head on its features.








Figure 5: First toy, a new robot: success rate against the number of its demos, for a network trained on them from scratch and for a new head on the frozen pooled network (mean over 8 seeds; shading: ± one standard error).





With 1 demo, the pooled features give 25% against 9%; with 4, 87% against 73% (Figure 5). Interpolating, the pooled network reaches 85% success with about 3.8 demos and the scratch network needs about 10.4, 2.8 times as many. By 32 demos the two are equal: with enough data of its own, the new robot no longer needs the others.


Start from a vision-language model
Even a million robot episodes are tiny next to what vision-language models are trained on, so the next question was whether internet-scale knowledge transfers to control ▶ 33:51. LLaVA showed the template: put image tokens in front of the text and let the language model attend over both ▶ 34:22. Treat actions the same way: turn them into tokens, add them to the vocabulary (overwriting the least used tokens), and fine-tune with the usual next-token loss ▶ 35:24. RT-2 and OpenVLA did this with the simple per-dimension binning of Week 7 ▶ 36:26.
The recipe many labs now follow comes from π0.5 and knowledge insulation ▶ 51:35. The VLM backbone is trained by next-token prediction on FAST-tokenized robot actions and web data; the web data keep it from forgetting what it knew ▶ 52:37. A separate action expert produces continuous actions by flow matching (Week 6); it reads the backbone, but a stop-gradient keeps its gradients out of it, which protects the VLM’s knowledge and speeds up training ▶ 53:08.

Feeding the model: batches and buffers
Pooled data break the simple assumption that every sample has the same shape. One data set has a single third-person camera, another adds two wrist cameras ▶ 39:03. Padding every sample to the longest one is easy, but in a mixed batch much of the compute goes on zeros ▶ 40:05. Sequence packing lays the samples end to end instead, so every token is real; the price is bookkeeping: the start of each sample, an attention mask that keeps samples from looking at each other, and positions that restart at each sample ▶ 40:35 ▶ 41:39. In the page’s example batch, two samples with 1 camera and two with 3, padding computes 232 tokens for 168 real ones, 28% wasted (worked example).
How randomly the loader mixes data mattered as much. Octo streamed trajectories from disk into a shuffle buffer and drew batches from it; with a buffer of 20,000 frames, batches held frames from too few trajectories and the policy generalized poorly, and enlarging it to 500,000 made a large difference with nothing else changed ▶ 42:41 ▶ 43:43. The toy streams 5,000 trajectories of 100 frames and draws batches of 256.








Figure 7: Third toy: the average number of different trajectories in a batch of 256 frames, against the shuffle buffer’s size (5,000 trajectories of 100 frames, streamed one trajectory at a time; 30 batches each). The dashed line is what drawing frames uniformly from the whole data set would give.





A batch from a 2,000-frame buffer holds frames from only 48 trajectories on average, so each gradient step sees a few situations many times over; a 20,000-frame buffer gives 156, and only a buffer near the size of the data set approaches the 250 of truly random draws (Figure 7). Loading by random reads from a flat index avoids the problem at the price of fast storage ▶ 44:14.


Learning from data of mixed quality
Pooling also mixes skill levels: careful demos, hesitant ones, the robot’s own failed attempts. Cloning all of it copies the average, mistakes included. This week’s guest showed that adding the lowest-quality data hurt π0.7 when the model was not told about quality, and helped when each episode came with metadata on its speed and quality ▶ 10:33. The discussion paper π*0.6 does this per action: a value function estimates each action’s advantage, the policy is trained on all data with one more input saying whether the advantage beat a threshold, and at test time it is asked for the good actions. Unlike filtering, nothing is thrown away: the bad steps still teach what the situations look like. The corridor example works this out exactly.


Evaluate in simulation, for rankings
A generalist must be tested on many tasks and robots, and real evaluation is slow and fragile: someone bumps a camera, a motor is replaced and the joint readings shift, and a single trial takes minutes ▶ 54:10 ▶ 55:13. Simulation is cheaper and reproducible ▶ 56:47. SIMPLER evaluates policies trained only on real data in simulated copies of the real setups ▶ 57:18, after narrowing two gaps: the control gap, by system identification so that the simulated arm responds to commands like the real one ▶ 58:52, and the visual gap, by green-screening real backgrounds behind simulated objects and projecting real textures onto them ▶ 59:23. What it promises is a ranking, not absolute numbers: 50% in simulation does not mean 50% on the robot, but if policy A beats B in SIMPLER, it should on the real robot too ▶ 60:55.
The second toy tests the control gap only. Nine policies, from 3 cloning budgets each run at 3 speed factors, are scored on the “real” point robot, whose motors are noisy, and in simulators whose motor gain is wrong (0.4 instead of 1) or estimated by system identification from 100 test commands.








Figure 8: Second toy (policy family 0): each dot is one of 9 policies, its real success rate (x) against its success rate in a simulator (y). Left: uncalibrated, motor gain 0.4 and no noise. Middle: gain identified from 100 real commands, no noise. Right: gain and motor noise identified. The diagonal marks equal success.





The uncalibrated simulator is badly wrong in absolute terms, 0.24 too low on average, because its weak motors leave the slowest policies far short of their goals: they score 0 in simulation and between 65% and 81% on the real robot (Figure 8). Identifying the gain brings the average much closer (now 0.05 too high) but not the ranking, because the simulator still lacks the motor noise, which hurts slow policies most: they now look 0.09 to 0.16 better in simulation than on the robot. With gain and noise identified, simulated and real success agree for every policy. Over 5 policy families the pattern holds: correlation 0.64–0.87 uncalibrated, 0.46–0.92 with the gain alone, and at least 0.967 fully calibrated. In this toy calibration closes the gap completely because the simulator’s model has the same form as the “real” robot; real setups always keep some gap, which is why SIMPLER reports rankings.

title: Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
text:
Key concepts & formulae
The lecture writes \(o_t\) for observations, \(a_t\) for actions and \(\ell\) for a language instruction; \(g\) is a goal, an image or an instruction. The ADM book writes the cloning objective as maximum likelihood over expert state-action pairs, the same thing without the goal.

Training on many robots

\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(o_{t-h:t},\, g,\, a_{t:t+H-1}) \sim \mathcal{D}}
\big[\log \pi_\theta(a_{t:t+H-1} \mid o_{t-h:t}, g)\big]
\tag{1}\]

In words. Make the demonstrated chunk of actions likely, given a short history of observations and the goal.
Term by term.

\(o_{t-h:t}\): the last \(h+1\) observations (Octo uses a short window).
\(g\): a goal image, or an instruction \(\ell\); one model learns to accept either.
\(a_{t:t+H-1}\): a chunk of \(H\) actions (Week 7); Octo’s diffusion head models its distribution, so the log-likelihood is replaced by the denoising loss of Week 6.
\(\mathcal{D}\): the pooled data of all robots and tasks.


\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta, f_1, \dots, f_K) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbb{E}_{(\tau, c) \sim \mathcal{D}_k}
\Big[ \textstyle\sum_{t} -\log \pi_\theta\big(a_t \mid s_t, f_k(c)\big) \Big]
\tag{2}\]

In words. Several data sets describe tasks in different ways; each gets its own encoder into one shared goal space, and one policy learns from all of them.
Term by term.

\(\mathcal{D}_k\): data set \(k\), demonstrations \(\tau\) paired with a task description \(c\) of kind \(k\): a goal image from hindsight relabelling, or a sentence.
\(f_k\): the encoder for kind \(k\); all map into the same latent goal \(z = f_k(c)\).
Why it pays: goal images come free (the last frame of any window), sentences cost an annotator; in Lynch and Sermanet’s paper under 1% of the data needed language.


\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{D} m_{ij}\,\big(\hat a_{ij} - a_{ij}\big)^2,
\qquad m_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}
\tag{3}\]

In words. The network outputs \(D\) numbers per sample; only the entries that belong to this sample’s robot count.
Term by term.

Padded action space (π0): \(D = \max_e d_e\); robot \(e\) fills the first \(d_e\) entries and \(m_{ij} = 0\) for the rest.
Separate heads (CrossFormer): \(D = \sum_e d_e\), each robot owns a block of columns, and \(m_{ij} = 1\) only on that block. Since the last layer is linear, a block of its columns is a separate head reading shared features.
Numeric check: the toy’s heads network has 11 outputs (2 + 2 + 3 + 4); a four-motors sample trains only the last four and leaves the other heads’ weights untouched.



Tokens for everything

\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{b=1}^{B} \sum_{l=1}^{L} m(b, l)\, \log p_\theta\big(s^{(b)}_l \mid s^{(b)}_1, \dots, s^{(b)}_{l-1}\big)
\tag{4}\]

In words. Next-token prediction over a flat token sequence of text, image patches, observations and actions, scoring only text and action tokens.
Term by term.

\(s^{(b)}_l\): token \(l\) of training sequence \(b\), from one shared vocabulary.
\(m(b, l)\): 1 if the token is text or an action, 0 for image and observation tokens, which are context only.
Tasks are told apart by prompting with a demonstration of the same task, not by a task id.


\[
F(x) = \operatorname{sgn}(x)\,\frac{\log(|x|\,\mu + 1)}{\log(M\mu + 1)}, \qquad \mu = 100,\; M = 256
\tag{5}\]

In words. Squeeze a real number into \([-1, 1]\) on a roughly logarithmic scale, so small values keep fine resolution and large ones share coarse bins.
Term by term.

Borrowed from audio coding (and WaveNet); Gato applies it to continuous observations, clips to \([-1, 1]\), cuts that range into 1,024 equal bins, and shifts the bin index past the 32,000 text tokens.
Numeric check: \(F(0.01) =\) 0.0683, so 1% of the input scale takes about 7% of the output range (worked example).



Batching heterogeneous samples

\[
\text{waste} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{B} L_i}{B \cdot \max_i L_i}
\tag{6}\]

In words. The share of computed tokens that are padding, when every sample is padded to the longest.
Term by term. \(L_i\): tokens in sample \(i\); \(B\): samples in the batch. Attention costs grow with the square of the padded length, so the wasted share of attention compute is larger still.

\[
\begin{aligned}
c_i &= \textstyle\sum_{j < i} L_j \quad (\texttt{cu\_seqlens}) \\
M_{pq} &= \mathbb{1}[\,\mathrm{seg}(p) = \mathrm{seg}(q)\,] \\
\mathrm{pos}(p) &= p - c_{\mathrm{seg}(p)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]

In words. Lay the samples end to end; remember where each starts; let a token attend only within its own sample; and number positions from 0 again in every sample.
Term by term.

\(\mathrm{seg}(p)\): which sample token \(p\) belongs to; \(M\) is block-diagonal (a causal model also needs \(q \le p\)).
Without the mask, a sample attends to its neighbours’ images; without the position reset, the fourth sample’s first token sits at a position no unpacked sample ever has.
Numeric check: in the toy batch, packed attention with the mask matches per-sample attention to 3e-16; without it the outputs differ by up to 0.73.



From VLM to VLA

\[
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{next token}}\big(\text{language, FAST tokens; robot + web data}\big)}_{\text{trains the VLM backbone}}
\;+\; \lambda\, \underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}\big(v_\phi(\cdot \mid \mathrm{sg}[h_\theta])\big)}_{\text{trains the action expert only}}
\tag{8}\]

In words. The backbone learns from discrete tokens, robot and web alike; the continuous action expert learns flow matching while reading the backbone’s features as constants.
Term by term.

\(h_\theta\): the backbone’s internal features; \(\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]\): stop-gradient, so \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}\) changes \(\phi\) but not \(\theta\).
\(v_\phi\): the action expert’s velocity field (Week 6’s flow matching).
FAST tokens (Week 7) give the backbone a robot-action target it can learn by next-token prediction.
\(\lambda\): a weight between the two losses. The equation is a schematic of the lecture’s summary; the paper gives the exact objective.
Why: the knowledge-insulation paper finds that letting the action expert’s gradients into the VLM slows training and loses the VLM’s semantic knowledge.

Training tips from the lecture. For a VLA with action tokens, wait until teacher-forced action-token accuracy reaches about 95% before trying the robot; below that, rollouts will not be good ▶ 37:29. Teacher-forced accuracy is not rollout performance, so also track the L1 and L2 error of the decoded continuous actions ▶ 38:32.


Learning from experience

\[
\begin{aligned}
A(o_t, a_t) &= \textstyle\sum_{t'=t}^{t+N-1} r_{t'} + V(o_{t+N}) - V(o_t), \qquad
I_t = \mathbb{1}\big[A(o_t, a_t, \ell) > \epsilon_\ell\big] \\
\min_\theta\; &\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\big[-\log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid o_t, \ell) - \alpha \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid I_t, o_t, \ell)\big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}\]

In words. Score each recorded action by how much better than usual it did, label it good or not, train one policy on all actions with that label as an extra input, and ask for “good” at test time.
Term by term.

\(V\): a value function of the data’s own behavior, fitted to observed returns (π*0.6 predicts steps to success).
\(A\): an \(N\)-step advantage estimate, as in Week 5; \(\epsilon_\ell\): a per-task threshold.
First term: plain cloning, which keeps the model able to represent all behavior; second term: cloning conditioned on the label, weighted by \(\alpha\).
Human corrections during deployment are always labelled good.
Why it holds: the paper shows that conditioning on “improvement” yields a policy that does at least as well as the data’s behavior, for a monotone notion of improvement; in the special case of their \(\beta = 1\), the improved policy is exactly \(\pi(a \mid I = 1, o, \ell)\).



Evaluating

\[
\mathrm{MMRV} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \max_{j}\; |R_i - R_j| \cdot \mathbb{1}\big[(R_{S,i} < R_{S,j}) \neq (R_i < R_j)\big]
\tag{10}\]

In words. For each policy, find the worst pair the simulator orders the wrong way round, measured by how far apart the two really are; average over policies.
Term by term.

\(R_i\), \(R_{S,i}\): real and simulated success of policy \(i\). MMRV = 0 means no pair is misordered.
A swap of two policies that are really 0.01 apart costs little; a swap of policies 0.3 apart costs a lot. Pearson’s \(r\) instead rewards a linear relation, and can penalize a simulator that ranks correctly but nonlinearly.
Numeric check: the toy’s uncalibrated simulator has MMRV 0.035 and \(r\) = 0.79; identifying the gain alone raises \(r\) to 0.85 but worsens MMRV to 0.050: the two metrics can disagree.


\[
\hat k = \frac{\sum_i a_i \cdot \Delta x_i}{\Delta t \sum_i a_i \cdot a_i}, \qquad
\hat\sigma = \operatorname{std}\Big(\frac{\Delta x_i}{\Delta t} - \hat k\, a_i\Big)
\tag{11}\]

In words. Send known commands to the real robot, measure how far it moves, and fit the simulator’s gain by least squares; what the fit cannot explain is the noise.
Term by term. \(a_i\): a test command; \(\Delta x_i\): the measured motion over one step \(\Delta t\). SIMPLER fits arm controller parameters the same way, matching simulated to real end-effector trajectories. Numeric check: from 100 commands the toy finds \(\hat k\) = 0.957 and \(\hat\sigma\) = 0.306 (true: 1 and 0.3).

\[
\mathrm{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p\,(1 - \hat p)}{n}}
\tag{12}\]

In words. A success rate measured from \(n\) independent trials is uncertain by about this much.
Term by term. With \(\hat p = 0.5\) and \(n = 20\) trials, SE \(= 0.11\): two policies 10 points apart cannot be told apart. This is why real-robot comparisons need many trials, blind scoring and randomized order, as in TRI’s study, and why cheap simulated trials are attractive.
