title: Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
text:
Algorithm & code

One network, many robots

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def fit_masked(params, X, Y, M, steps, rng, alpha=0.003, batch=256):
    """Adam on the squared error over the entries where the mask M is 1.

    X (n, d_in), Y and M (n, d_out). Entries with M = 0 are padding or
    another robot's head: they get no gradient, so whatever the network
    outputs there is never trained. Every method gets the same number of
    gradient steps, whatever the size of its data."""
    opt = nn.Adam(params, alpha)
    for _ in range(steps):
        idx = rng.integers(0, len(X), min(batch, len(X)))
        Yh, cache = nn.forward(params, X[idx])
        m = M[idx]
        dY = 2 * m * (Yh - Y[idx]) / len(idx)       # zero where masked
        params = opt.step(params, nn.backward(params, cache, dY))
    return params

def train_heads(data, seed) -> list:
    """One network, one output head per robot (CrossFormer style).

    The last layer is linear, so a block of its output columns is a
    separate linear head reading the same hidden features. Each sample
    is masked to its own robot's block: only that head, and the shared
    layers below it, learn from it. data: name -> (obs, act)."""
    cols = head_slices()
    n_out = sum(J.shape[1] for J in ROBOTS.values())
    obs, Y, M = [], [], []
    for name, (o, a) in data.items():
        y, m = np.zeros((len(o), n_out)), np.zeros((len(o), n_out))
        y[:, cols[name]], m[:, cols[name]] = a, 1.0
        obs.append(o), Y.append(y), M.append(m)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    params = nn.init_mlp([4, HIDDEN, HIDDEN, n_out], rng)
    return fit_masked(params, np.concatenate(obs), np.concatenate(Y),
                      np.concatenate(M), STEPS, rng)

def train_padded(data, seed, cue_on=True) -> list:
    """One network with one padded output of size D_MAX (pi0 style).

    A robot with d < D_MAX motors fills the first d outputs; the rest
    are padding, masked out of the loss. Nothing in the output says
    which robot is driven, so the network must infer it from its input:
    position, goal and, if cue_on, the embodiment cue."""
    obs, Y, M = [], [], []
    for name, (o, a) in data.items():
        y, m = np.zeros((len(o), D_MAX)), np.zeros((len(o), D_MAX))
        y[:, :a.shape[1]], m[:, :a.shape[1]] = a, 1.0
        obs.append(np.c_[o, cue(name, len(o), cue_on)])
        Y.append(y), M.append(m)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    params = nn.init_mlp([4 + len(ROBOTS), HIDDEN, HIDDEN, D_MAX], rng)
    return fit_masked(params, np.concatenate(obs), np.concatenate(Y),
                      np.concatenate(M), STEPS, rng)

def fit_new_head(params, obs, act, ridge=1e-3) -> tuple[Array, Array]:
    """A new linear head on frozen pooled features, by ridge regression:
    solves (H'H + ridge I) w = H'a, with a column of ones for the bias.
    Returns (W (H, d), b (d,))."""
    H = np.c_[features(params, obs), np.ones(len(obs))]
    w = np.linalg.solve(H.T @ H + ridge * np.eye(H.shape[1]), H.T @ act)
    return w[:-1], w[-1]


import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

from rlc.toys import w09_generalist as w9

torch.manual_seed(0)


class MultiHeadPolicy(nn.Module):
    """Shared trunk, one linear head per robot (CrossFormer style)."""

    def __init__(self, action_dims: dict, hidden=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.trunk = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, hidden), nn.Tanh(),
                                   nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.Tanh())
        self.heads = nn.ModuleDict({name: nn.Linear(hidden, d)
                                    for name, d in action_dims.items()})

    def forward(self, obs, robot):
        return self.heads[robot](self.trunk(obs))      # (B, d_robot)


names = {k: k.replace(" ", "_") for k in w9.ROBOTS}  # ModuleDict keys
data = {names[k]: tuple(torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32) for x in v)
        for k, v in w9.pooled_data(0).items()}       # obs (n, 4), act (n, d)
policy = MultiHeadPolicy({k: a.shape[1] for k, (_, a) in data.items()})
opt = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=3e-3)

# Each step takes a batch from every robot, so the trunk sees all of
# them; each loss term reaches only its own head (the masking of the
# NumPy version, done by indexing instead).
losses = []
for step in range(1500):
    loss = 0.0
    for robot, (obs, act) in data.items():
        idx = torch.randint(len(obs), (64,))
        loss = loss + ((policy(obs[idx], robot) - act[idx]) ** 2).sum(1).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    losses.append(loss.item())
assert np.mean(losses[-50:]) < 0.2 * np.mean(losses[:50])

# A new robot: freeze the trunk, fit only a fresh head on 4 demos.
obs, act = (torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32) for x in
            w9.demos(w9.NEW_ROBOT, 4, np.random.default_rng(1)))
policy.trunk.requires_grad_(False)
policy.heads["new"] = nn.Linear(64, act.shape[1])
opt = torch.optim.Adam(policy.heads["new"].parameters(), lr=1e-2)
for step in range(500):
    loss = ((policy(obs, "new") - act) ** 2).sum(1).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
assert loss.item() < 0.05, loss.item()



In the NumPy version, one output layer holds every robot’s columns and a mask picks the right block; the PyTorch version gives each robot its own nn.Linear and indexes by name. The two are the same model. requires_grad_(False) freezes the trunk in place (the trailing underscore marks an in-place method), so the new head trains on fixed features, as fit_new_head does by ridge regression.


Packing a batch

NumPy (runs on this page)PyTorch (sketch)


def pack(lengths) -> tuple[Array, Array, Array]:
    """Sequence packing: samples laid end to end in one sequence.

    Returns cu_seqlens, the prefix sums [0, L1, L1 + L2, ...] that mark
    where each sample starts; seg, the sample index of every token; and
    pos, every token's position within its own sample (it restarts at 0
    at each boundary)."""
    lengths = np.asarray(lengths)
    cu = np.r_[0, np.cumsum(lengths)]
    seg = np.repeat(np.arange(len(lengths)), lengths)
    pos = np.arange(cu[-1]) - cu[seg]
    return cu, seg, pos

def attend(q, k, v, allowed) -> Array:
    """Softmax attention, q k v (n, d), allowed (n, n) boolean: query i
    may look at key j only where allowed[i, j]."""
    s = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(q.shape[1])
    s = np.where(allowed, s, -np.inf)
    w = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True))
    return (w / w.sum(1, keepdims=True)) @ v

def packing_check(lengths, d=8, seed=0) -> dict:
    """Attention over a packed sequence, with and without the
    block-diagonal mask, against attention over each sample on its own.
    Returns the largest difference from the per-sample result for each."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    cu, seg, _ = pack(lengths)
    q, k, v = (rng.normal(size=(cu[-1], d)) for _ in range(3))
    alone = np.concatenate([attend(q[a:b], k[a:b], v[a:b],
                                   np.ones((b - a, b - a), bool))
                            for a, b in zip(cu[:-1], cu[1:])])
    block = seg[:, None] == seg[None, :]
    full = np.ones_like(block)
    return {"block-diagonal": float(np.abs(attend(q, k, v, block)
                                           - alone).max()),
            "no mask": float(np.abs(attend(q, k, v, full) - alone).max())}


import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
lengths = torch.tensor([26, 26, 58, 58])              # tokens per sample
cu_seqlens = torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.long),
                        lengths.cumsum(0)])           # [0, 26, 52, 110, 168]
seg = torch.repeat_interleave(torch.arange(len(lengths)), lengths)  # (T,)
pos = torch.arange(len(seg)) - cu_seqlens[seg]        # restarts at 0 per sample

T, H, D = len(seg), 2, 16                             # tokens, heads, head dim
q, k, v = torch.randn(3, 1, H, T, D).unbind(0)        # each (1, H, T, D)

# Boolean mask, True = may attend: same sample only (block-diagonal).
# Broadcasts over batch and heads: (T, T) -> (1, H, T, T).
allowed = seg[:, None] == seg[None, :]
packed = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=allowed)

# Reference: attend within each sample separately, then concatenate.
alone = torch.cat([F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q[..., a:b, :], k[..., a:b, :],
                                                  v[..., a:b, :])
                   for a, b in zip(cu_seqlens[:-1], cu_seqlens[1:])], dim=2)
leaky = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)        # no mask
assert torch.allclose(packed, alone, atol=1e-5)
assert (leaky - alone).abs().max() > 0.1
assert pos[cu_seqlens[2]] == 0 and pos.max() == lengths.max() - 1



Kernels such as FlashAttention’s variable-length mode take cu_seqlens directly and never build the \(T \times T\) mask; the dense mask here is for clarity. Positions must come from pos, not from torch.arange(T): with rotary or learned positional encodings, a token’s position is part of its input.

title: Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
text:
Papers

Papers discussed in class






Language Conditioned Imitation Learning over Unstructured Data Lynch & Sermanet · RSS 2021
Teaches one network to follow free-form typed instructions on a simulated tabletop, from pixels to continuous control, while asking people to label almost none of the data. Hours of unscripted teleoperated play are cut into windows and relabelled with the window’s last frame as its goal; a small fraction is also described in words after the fact, and one policy learns from both kinds of goal.

Multicontext imitation learning: one latent-goal policy trained on several data sets that describe tasks in different ways (goal images, language), each with its own encoder into a shared goal space (Sec. IV-B).
Language labels on less than 1% of the data, with goal-image relabelling of the rest supplying most of the perception and control (Abstract, Fig. 1).
68.6% success on single instructions over 18 tasks against 20.0% for language-conditioned cloning of conventional task demos, and 52.1% against 7.1% on four-instruction chains (Table I).
Feeding instructions through a pretrained multilingual sentence encoder raises success to 74.1% and lets the policy follow unseen synonyms, in 16 languages, without new demonstrations (Table I, Sec. IV-C).

On this page: The lecture’s ‘goal-conditioned behavior cloning’ with goal images or language, which Octo inherits; and an early answer to this week’s data question: label a little, relabel the rest.









A Generalist Agent Reed et al. · TMLR 2022
Trains a single 1.2-billion-parameter transformer, with one set of weights, to play Atari, caption images, chat, stack blocks with a real arm and much more. Every modality is turned into tokens from one shared vocabulary, and the model is trained like a language model on the flat token sequences; in context it decides whether to emit text, joystick buttons or joint torques.

One tokenization for everything: text as subwords, images as 16×16 patches, discrete actions as integers, and continuous values mu-law companded into [−1, 1] and cut into 1,024 bins placed after the 32,000 text tokens (Sec. 2.1, App. B).
A masked next-token loss: only text and action tokens are targets, observation tokens are context only (Sec. 2.3, Eq. 2).
Tasks are told apart by prompting with a demonstration of the same task rather than a task id (Sec. 2.3).
Over 450 of its 604 tasks above 50% of the expert’s score, from one checkpoint (Sec. 4.1).

On this page: The lecture’s ‘robotics as multimodal sequence modeling’, in its most literal form, and the ancestor of Octo’s tokenized observations; its author was Week 8’s guest.









π*0.6: a VLA That Learns From Experience Physical Intelligence · arXiv 2025
Makes a vision-language-action model improve from its own deployments by reinforcement learning. A value function, trained on demonstrations, autonomous attempts and human corrections, scores every action; the policy is trained on all of that data with one extra input saying whether an action’s advantage beat a threshold, and at test time it is asked for the good ones.

RECAP: collect rollouts with outcome labels and optional human interventions, fit a value function, then retrain the policy conditioned on a binarized advantage, and repeat (Sec. IV, Algorithm 1).
Advantage conditioning as policy extraction: unlike policy gradients it needs no tractable likelihood, so it works with flow-matching action experts, and unlike weighted regression it keeps every sample (Sec. IV-B, Eq. 3).
A multi-task distributional value function predicting steps to success, from a smaller VLM backbone (Sec. IV-A, Fig. 4).
More than doubled throughput and roughly halved failure rates on the hardest tasks; espresso drinks made for 13 hours straight (Abstract, Sec. I).

On this page: The worked example on advantage conditioning on this page; the guest’s talk on π0.7, which conditions on episode metadata in the same spirit; and the RL of Weeks 4–5 applied to a generalist policy.





Key papers from the lecture






Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models Open X-Embodiment Collaboration · ICRA 2024
Pools robot-learning data sets from many labs into one standardized collection and trains a single policy on all of it. The question is whether robot learning can follow the recipe of vision and language: one large model trained on diverse data from many robots, rather than one model per robot and task.

A data set of more than a million robot trajectories from 22 robot embodiments, contributed by 21 institutions (Sec. I, Fig. 1).
RT-1-X and RT-2-X, versions of RT-1 and RT-2 trained on the mixture (Sec. IV).
Positive transfer: RT-1-X’s mean success rate is 50% higher than that of either the original method for each data set or RT-1 (Fig. 4).

On this page: Week 1: the lecture’s case for generalist robot policies and for data as the bottleneck, and the worked example on data-set sizes. Week 9: the data behind Octo and CrossFormer, and the positive transfer this page’s first toy reproduces.









Octo: An Open-Source Generalist Robot Policy Octo Model Team (Ghosh, Walke, Pertsch, Black, Mees et al.) · RSS 2024
An open transformer policy trained on 800k trajectories from the Open X-Embodiment data. It takes language instructions or goal images, and is meant as a starting point: fine-tune it to a robot with new sensors or a new action space in a few hours on a consumer GPU.

Language or goal-image conditioning in one model, trained by goal-conditioned behavior cloning with a diffusion action head (Abstract; lecture).
Fine-tuning to new observation and action spaces by adding input tokens or a new head, evaluated on 9 robot platforms (Abstract).
Released weights and code, with ablations of architecture and data to guide later generalist models (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s main architecture; on this page, the pooled network with a new head added for a new robot.









Scaling Cross-Embodied Learning: One Policy for Manipulation, Navigation, Locomotion and Aviation Doshi, Walke, Mees, Dasari & Levine · CoRL 2024
CrossFormer, one transformer trained on about 900k trajectories from 20 embodiments, from arms to wheeled robots, quadcopters and quadrupeds. Observations of any kind become tokens, and each embodiment family has its own action head, so no observation or action spaces have to be aligned by hand.

A single set of weights controlling manipulators, wheeled robots, quadcopters and quadrupeds (Abstract).
Matches specialist policies trained for each embodiment, and beats earlier cross-embodiment methods (Abstract).
Embodiment-specific readout heads that predict action chunks of different lengths, for control rates from 5 to 50 Hz (lecture).

On this page: The multi-head network of this page’s first toy, and the ‘heads’ side of the heads-versus-padding diagram.









A Careful Examination of Large Behavior Models for Multitask Dexterous Manipulation TRI LBM Team · arXiv 2025
Toyota Research Institute’s study of whether multitask pretraining helps dexterous manipulation. Diffusion-transformer policies are pretrained on simulated and real robot data and compared with single-task policies in blind, randomized real-world trials analysed for statistical confidence.

An evaluation pipeline built for statistical confidence: blind, randomized comparisons in simulation and on real robots (Abstract).
Multitask pretraining makes policies more successful and robust, and lets them learn new complex tasks with less data (Abstract).
Performance improves predictably as pretraining scale and diversity grow (Abstract).

On this page: The new-robot curve on this page: pretraining helps most when the new task has little data. The lecture also quotes its finding that data normalization mattered more than architecture.









π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control Black et al. (Physical Intelligence) · RSS 2025
A VLA that grafts a flow-matching action expert onto a pretrained vision-language model, so it keeps the VLM’s web knowledge and outputs continuous action chunks. It is trained on a large mixture of data from several dexterous robots.

A flow-matching architecture on top of a pretrained VLM, producing continuous actions rather than tokens (Abstract).
Pretraining on many dexterous robot platforms, then evaluated zero-shot, on language following, and after fine-tuning (Abstract).
Long dexterous tasks such as folding laundry, clearing tables and assembling boxes (Abstract).

On this page: The ‘padded action space’ side of the heads-versus-padding diagram, and Week 6’s flow matching put to work.









π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization Physical Intelligence (Black et al.) · CoRL 2025
Builds on π0 with co-training on very mixed data: several robots, high-level subtask prediction, and web data. The claim is that this transfer is what makes the policy generalize to homes it has never seen.

Co-training on multi-robot data, semantic subtask prediction and web data in one model (Abstract).
An end-to-end learned system cleaning kitchens and bedrooms in entirely new homes, which the authors call a first (Abstract).

On this page: The lecture’s ‘current VLA recipe’ diagram, together with knowledge insulation; the base of the guest’s π0.6 and π0.7.









Knowledge Insulating Vision-Language-Action Models: Train Fast, Run Fast, Generalize Better Driess et al. · NeurIPS 2025
Asks what happens to a VLM’s knowledge when a continuous action expert is bolted onto it, and finds that naive training slows learning and loses semantic transfer. The fix trains the backbone on discrete action tokens and web data, while the action expert reads the backbone without sending gradients into it.

Shows that adding a diffusion or flow-matching action expert without precautions hurts both training speed and knowledge transfer (Abstract).
Knowledge insulation: next-token prediction for the backbone, a stop-gradient between backbone and action expert (Abstract; lecture).

On this page: The stop-gradient in the ‘current VLA recipe’ diagram and equation on this page; Week 7’s FAST tokens are the backbone’s action targets.









Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation Li, Hsu, Gu, Pertsch, Mees et al. · CoRL 2024
SIMPLER, simulated versions of common real robot setups, built to tell which of several real-world policies is better without running them on hardware. Instead of full digital twins it narrows two gaps: control (by system identification) and vision (by green-screening real backgrounds and matching textures).

Identifies the control gap and the visual gap as the main obstacles to trustworthy simulated evaluation, and ways to reduce them without a full digital twin (Abstract).
The mean maximum rank violation (MMRV), a ranking metric that weighs each misordered pair by its real-world gap (Sec. III, Eqs. 1–2).
Paired sim and real evaluations over about 1,500 episodes showing strong correlation, including under distribution shifts (Abstract).

On this page: This page’s second toy, which ranks policies in a miscalibrated and a calibrated simulator and scores them with MMRV.

title: Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
text:
Guest spotlight
Quan Vuong (co-founder of Physical Intelligence; earlier at Google DeepMind, where he started and co-led the RT-X and Open X-Embodiment projects) presented π0.7, whose main claim is a single model that performs many tasks at specialist level ▶ 01:01. That matters for scaling: until now, top performance on a task meant post-training a model for that task, and every extra checkpoint is one more thing to manage ▶ 01:32. It is hard because more data does not automatically mean a better model: train on everything you have and you usually get something worse than a carefully tuned specialist ▶ 02:34. He showed a symptom: a policy imitating teleoperation data was slower than the teleoperators themselves, while online RL made it faster than them ▶ 03:37.
The architecture is close to π0.5 and π0.6: a language model and a pretrained vision encoder with an action expert grafted on, prompted with the task, optionally a subtask, and metadata on the speed and quality of each training episode, plus a new ability to condition on goals ▶ 05:10. A separate high-level component, a person or a planner, proposes subtasks but never actions ▶ 06:45. One checkpoint matched or beat RL- and SFT-tuned specialists on laundry, tiny screws, box assembly and taking out the trash ▶ 08:23. His explanation for beating them: in real-robot evaluation every test is partly a generalization test, since something in the scene always changes, and a generalist is more robust to such changes ▶ 09:25. The metadata result is this page’s quality story: adding the lowest-quality data lowered performance without metadata and raised it sharply with metadata ▶ 10:33. Shirt folding learned on one robot pair transferred to a bimanual UR5 station that had no folding data at all ▶ 12:39, and a person coaching in language led it through tasks it had no data for ▶ 14:10.
He also described deployment with partner companies, such as folding customers’ laundry in a laundromat and packing orders through a full working day, where the question is whether remote interventions become rare enough to break even ▶ 16:47 ▶ 19:53, and said the open-sourced π0 and π0.5 weights are the same checkpoints the company’s researchers use ▶ 15:14. In the Q&A: multi-fingered hands are not yet cheap, reliable and easy to teleoperate all at once, so two-finger grippers serve research at scale better ▶ 21:57; what to scale (many tasks or many demos per task, human video, robots) is an open experimental question ▶ 25:34; whether VLAs or video action models scale better is undecided, with models heading from single-digit to tens of billions of parameters ▶ 30:15 ▶ 31:47; and home robots wait on model capability, since a robot that works in every home would mean physical intelligence is solved ▶ 24:34.
How it connects to this week. π0.7 is the lecture’s recipe pushed to the point where the generalist beats the specialists; its metadata conditioning and π*0.6’s advantage conditioning are the same move, telling the model about data quality instead of discarding the bad data; and the cross-embodiment folding result is positive transfer at full scale.

title: Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
text:
Solved problems
1. Padding a batch. A batch has 6 samples with one camera and 2 with three cameras; each image is 256 tokens and language plus actions add 20. How much of a padded batch is padding? What is cu_seqlens if you pack them in that order?






TipSolution





One camera: 276 tokens; three: 788. Real tokens: \(6 \cdot 276 + 2 \cdot 788 = 1656 + 1576 = 3232\). Padded: \(8 \cdot 788 = 6304\). Waste (Equation 6): \(1 - 3232/6304 \approx 49\%\): half the batch is zeros, the lecture’s warning. cu_seqlens = [0, 276, 552, 828, 1104, 1380, 1656, 2444, 3232].



2. Which robot am I? Two robots have the same cameras, the same 2-D action space and the same tasks, but one’s motor axes are mirrored. Your model has one padded action output. What happens, and what are two fixes?






TipSolution





Nothing in the input tells the robots apart, so the same observation is paired with two different correct actions; least-squares training averages them, and the average of an action and its mirror image moves the robot along only one axis or not at all, wrong for both robots (the toy’s “no cue” bars, Figure 2). Fixes: give the model a cue, such as an embodiment token, a camera view that shows the robot, or joint readings that differ; or use separate heads and let the user pick one, as CrossFormer does. Aligning the action spaces by hand also works, at the cost Octo and CrossFormer chose to avoid.



3. Is the new policy better? Policy A succeeded in 12 of 20 trials, policy B in 15 of 20. Is B better? How many trials per policy would make a 15-point gap at about these rates two standard errors of the difference?






TipSolution





\(\hat p_A = 0.6\), \(\hat p_B = 0.75\). Standard errors (Equation 12): \(\sqrt{0.6 \cdot 0.4/20} = 0.110\) and \(\sqrt{0.75 \cdot 0.25/20} = 0.097\); the difference has SE \(\sqrt{0.110^2 + 0.097^2} = 0.146\), so a 0.15 gap is about one SE: no evidence either way. For the gap to be two SEs, \(\sqrt{(0.24 + 0.1875)/n} \le 0.075\), so \(n \ge 0.4275 / 0.075^2 \approx 76\) trials per policy. That is hours of robot time for one comparison.



4. MMRV by hand. Three policies have real success 0.2, 0.5 and 0.6, and simulated success 0.3, 0.7 and 0.65. Compute the MMRV and the ranking error it describes.






TipSolution





Real order: 1 < 2 < 3. Simulated order: 1 < 3 < 2, so only the pair (2, 3) is misordered, and it costs \(|0.5 - 0.6| = 0.1\). Each policy’s worst violation: policy 1, none (0); policy 2, 0.1; policy 3, 0.1. MMRV \(= (0 + 0.1 + 0.1)/3 \approx 0.067\) (Equation 10). The simulator confuses two policies that are only 10 points apart in reality; it never confuses either with policy 1.



5. Advantage conditioning, quickly. Operators in a 20-cell corridor step forward with probability 0.9 and back with 0.1. Far from the start, how many steps per cell does a cloned policy take? What fraction of episodes would filtering keep if it kept only flawless ones, and how many steps does the advantage-conditioned policy take?






TipSolution





Each step moves forward on average \(0.9 - 0.1 = 0.8\) cells, so cloning takes about \(1/0.8 = 1.25\) steps per cell, about 25 steps for 20 cells (slightly fewer, since at cell 0 a back step cannot go further back). A flawless episode needs 20 forward steps in a row: \(0.9^{20} \approx 12\%\) of episodes. Forward steps have positive advantage and back steps negative, so conditioning on \(I = 1\) gives a policy that always steps forward: 20 steps, trained on all the data (Equation 9, Example 3).

title: Week 9 · Generalist Robot Policies
text:
Recap

Generalists are built from pooled data. OXE combined over a million episodes from 22 robots, and one model trained on it beat the per-data-set methods. Why it matters: robot data are scarce, so every lab’s data has to count.
One network can drive many bodies. Tokenize everything, share a transformer, and either give each robot a head (CrossFormer) or one padded action space whose robot the model infers (π0). Why it matters: it is how one checkpoint controls arms, quadrupeds and drones; in the toy it lifted the data-poor robot from 60% to 80%.
Pretraining helps most when the new task has little data. Why it matters: it is the case for robot foundation models, and it sets expectations: with plenty of task data, the advantage fades.
VLAs inherit web knowledge if you protect it. Actions as tokens, co-training with web data, and a stop-gradient between the VLM and the action expert. Why it matters: it is the recipe behind today’s strongest generalist policies and the guest’s π0.7.
Data quality must be represented, not ignored. Metadata (π0.7) and advantage labels (π*0.6) let bad data help instead of hurt. Why it matters: deployment produces exactly such mixed data, and it is how these policies keep improving after launch.
Evaluate by rankings. Real evaluation is slow and noisy; a calibrated simulator can rank policies reliably even when its absolute numbers are off. Why it matters: without cheap, trustworthy evaluation, no design choice in this list can be tested.

Common pitfalls.

Pooling data without aligning what must be aligned: Octo had to unify gripper conventions, while TRI found normalization mattered more than architecture.
Padding a batch where half the samples have three times the cameras, and paying for the zeros.
Packing without a block-diagonal mask, or without resetting positions.
A small shuffle buffer: batches full of frames from the same few trajectories.
A padded action space with nothing in the input that identifies the robot.
Fine-tuning a VLA’s action expert with gradients flowing into the VLM, and losing its knowledge.
Cloning mixed-quality data as if it were all good, or filtering away most of it.
Reading a simulator’s absolute success rates as predictions of real ones.
Declaring one policy better from 20 trials each.

Connections. Week 3’s behavior cloning is the training objective here, now goal-conditioned and multi-robot. Week 5’s advantages return in π*0.6, used to label data rather than weight gradients. Week 6’s diffusion and flow matching are Octo’s head and π0’s action expert. Week 7’s tokenization, transformers and action chunks are the building blocks of every model on this page. Week 8’s guest led Gato, and the choice between VLM and video backbones is still open, as this week’s guest said. Week 10 asks how such policies can reason before acting. In the ADM Companion: behavioral cloning and advantage estimation.

Figure 1: The course at a glance. Each box is a week (click to open it); this page’s week is orange. Arrows show how one week builds on another.







Where this week fits
This is the lecturer’s last lecture, and it looks ahead. Every week, someone announces that robotics is solved ▶ 01:02. Take one of those robots out of its lab, though, with new lighting, new objects or a new camera angle, and it breaks quickly ▶ 03:07. The lecturer’s not-so-secret recipe for an impressive demo: collect lots of data on your own robot, clone it until extrapolation becomes interpolation, and train and test on the same day ▶ 04:09. The real goal is generalization to the whole world, the way people cook in a kitchen they have never seen by composing what they already know ▶ 05:13. The lecture lays out what stands between the course’s tools and that goal, then gives advice on doing research, and the guest traces how vision itself got from “doesn’t work” to “solved”.
The question this week answers: what are the open problems of robot learning, why are they hard, and which ideas from the course point towards solving them?


The key ideas at a glance

Generalists versus specialists. Foundation models generalize but lack physical grounding; robot specialists are grounded and dexterous but narrow. The aim is both at once.
Open choices: backbone, data recipe, data collection. A vision-language model, a video model or training from scratch; web, simulated, human and robot data in some mix; collection interfaces that trade scale against fidelity to the robot.
Dexterity needs more than vision. Touch and force data are scarce, rarely paired with other senses, and different on every robot.
Knowing what you don’t know. Deciding when to act, when to think and when to ask for help requires a model that can tell when it is out of its depth: introspection.
Beyond imitation. Cloning is bounded by its demonstrations; RL can stitch pieces of different demonstrations and improve on them, and is the way to learn from a robot’s own mixed-quality experience (the data flywheel).
Lifelong learning, rapid adaptation, mobility and memory. Robots should improve with experience, adapt from a correction or a demonstration in context, move through buildings with one model, and remember across time scales.
From the guest: pre-train, mid-train, fine-tune; scale model, data and training time together; and look at your data.



Vocabulary







Term
Plain meaning




Physical grounding
Knowing what actually happens in the world, not only how to describe it


Backbone
The pretrained network a policy starts from: a VLM, a video model, or none


Data recipe
The mix and order of data a model is trained on


Embodiment gap
The difference between the body in the data (a human hand) and the robot’s


Introspection
A model’s ability to tell when it does not know


Ensemble disagreement
The spread of several independently trained models’ outputs, used as an uncertainty estimate


Stitching
Combining pieces of different trajectories into a new, better one (offline RL)


Data flywheel
Deploy, collect data, retrain, deploy a better robot, repeat


Co-training
Training on several data sources at once, such as expert demos and autonomous rollouts


Catastrophic forgetting
Losing old abilities when fine-tuned on new data


In-context adaptation
Adapting from a correction or demonstration given as input, without changing weights


Mid-training
Training after pre-training that teaches core skills (reading text, locating objects)





After this week you can

Name the main open problems in robot learning and say why each is hard.
Explain why a cloned policy cannot exceed its demonstrations, and how offline RL stitches.
Explain why mixing expert data with a robot’s own rollouts can make cloning worse.
Use ensemble disagreement to decide when to act and when to ask, and name a failure it cannot catch.
Describe CLIP and SigLIP training, and why contrastive pre-training misses relations.
Apply the lecturer’s checklist for choosing and running a research project.

title: Week 11 · Frontiers & Open Problems
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A new driver taught only on one commute can drive it perfectly, and nothing else. A good driver has seen enough roads to combine what they know on a road they have never driven, notices when the situation is beyond them, and keeps getting better from their own driving, including from their own mistakes. Robot learning today mostly produces the first driver; the open problems are what it would take to produce the second.



Generalists, specialists and the missing grounding
Vision-language models are trained on internet-scale data and generalize broadly, but they lack physical grounding: one can describe a glass on a table without knowing that pushing it off the edge breaks it ▶ 06:46. Video models render convincing liquids and falling objects that, on a close look, break basic physics ▶ 07:18. Robot specialists are the opposite: dexterous, using richer senses, and narrow ▶ 07:49. The path the lecture argues for is to feed foundation models embodied data, which is multimodal, spatial and temporal, so that they can act in the world and not only describe it ▶ 08:20. Brooks made a version of this argument in 1991 (see the discussion papers): intelligence built on representations disconnected from sensing and acting goes astray, and the world should be its own model.
Three questions follow, all still open. Which backbone? A VLM, for its semantic knowledge; a generative video model, because predicting how scenes evolve is closer to what a policy needs; or nothing at all, training from scratch on enough robot data ▶ 09:22 ▶ 10:22, the question Week 8’s guest addressed. Which data recipe? Web data, then simulation, then a little real data; or skip simulation; or video first, then human egocentric video, then robot actions; or real robot data only ▶ 11:25 ▶ 12:29. How to collect real data? Interfaces trade scale against how closely the data match the robot: egocentric human video offers tens of millions of hours but a human body; teleoperation matches the robot exactly but is slow and expensive; gloves and handheld grippers sit between ▶ 14:01 ▶ 15:04.


Dexterous generalists need more than vision
Dexterity and generalization have needed different ingredients: dexterity wants fast control and senses such as touch, generalization wants large, slow foundation models, plus mobility so that the robot sees many places ▶ 16:38 ▶ 17:41. The lecturer showed a robot from his PhD that predicted a mug’s shape from a single image, missed the handle, and crushed the mug, because it had no touch or force feedback; today’s VLAs are probably still crushing objects, mostly blind at the moment of contact ▶ 19:47. Simply adding touch and force to one big multimodal model runs into the long tail of robot sensing: such data are scarce, rarely recorded together with the other senses, and different on every robot ▶ 20:50 ▶ 21:20. One answer from the lecturer’s group, FuSe, uses language as the glue: tie touch and sound to descriptions, and a policy can “pick the object that feels squishy” or describe what it is touching inside a bag ▶ 22:23.


When should a robot think, and does it know when it doesn’t know?
Week 10 made robots reason. But a home robot should not deliberate before every familiar action: in distribution, act at full speed with no reasoning; near the edge of its experience, spend test-time compute; far outside it, stop and ask a person ▶ 24:29 ▶ 25:33. That whole scheme assumes the robot can tell which case it is in ▶ 26:35. This is the problem of introspection, and large models make it harder: they complete patterns well while being poorly calibrated about their own competence, and a new situation can look superficially familiar ▶ 27:05. In robotics a policy can fail along many axes at once: objects, environments, embodiment, tasks, sensor noise ▶ 27:37.

Figure 2: When to reason, after the lecture: an uncertainty estimate decides whether the policy acts directly, spends test-time compute, or hands over to a person. Everything depends on that estimate being right.





The third toy tests one popular answer, an ensemble: train 5 policies on the same demonstrations from different random starts and resamples of the data, and treat their disagreement as uncertainty. The task is Week 9’s: drive a point from the left of a table round a post in the middle to a goal on the right. Then test it four ways: on tasks like the training ones; mirrored, from right to left; turned, from bottom to top; and like the training ones but with the post moved 0.3 upwards, something the policy cannot see, because the post’s position is not one of its inputs.








Figure 3: Third toy: an ensemble of 5 cloned policies on 300 test tasks per condition (mean over 4 training seeds). Left: success rate of the ensemble’s mean action. Right: disagreement between the members, averaged over each run.





The ensemble does well on what it can see (Figure 3). On mirrored and turned tasks its members disagree 10 and 10 times more than on familiar ones, and those are exactly the tasks where it fails (success 0.07 and 0.33). With the post moved, success falls to 0.49, and the disagreement is exactly what it was on the familiar tasks: the inputs are the same, so every network computes the same outputs and drives into the post with full confidence. If the robot asks for help whenever disagreement exceeds what 99% of familiar tasks show, it asks on 100% of mirrored tasks and on 1.0% of the moved-post ones. Disagreement measures how unfamiliar the input is, not whether the world still works as the data said, which is the lecture’s warning about situations that look familiar.








Figure 4: Third toy: act on the share of tasks (x) with the lowest ensemble disagreement and hand the rest to a person; y is the success rate on the tasks the robot keeps. Blue: a mix of familiar, mirrored and turned tasks. Orange: the same mix plus the moved-post tasks.





Ranked by disagreement, the robot can keep the familiar third of the first mix and succeed on 99% of it (Figure 4). Add the moved-post tasks and no threshold separates them from the familiar ones: at half coverage success is only 74%. A useful introspection signal has to see the failure, which here would mean sensing the post or noticing contact.


Imitation is bounded by its demonstrations
Most robot policies in this course were trained by imitation, and a cloned policy is bounded by its data ▶ 28:38. The lecture’s example: demonstrations go from state 1 to 2 and from 2 to 3. However large the model, cloning cannot learn to go from 1 to 3, let alone that a better route exists ▶ 29:10. Offline RL can: it learns values for states from all the data and stitches sub-optimal trajectories into better ones ▶ 29:41. Getting RL to work at scale on real robots is, in the lecturer’s view, among the highest-impact problems to work on ▶ 30:45.
The first toy builds that example in a small building: two rooms joined by an opening, and a corridor below reached through two doors. Operators walk between landmarks A to F, mostly straight but straying a quarter of the time. Behavior cloning is goal-conditioned with hindsight relabelling: every step that some trajectory took on its way to a later visit of the goal becomes training data for that goal. Offline RL, in a deterministic world with one unit of cost per step, reduces to the shortest path through the transitions the data contain.




The lecture's example in the first toy's building: one demonstration from A to B and one from B to C. Asked to go from A to C, the cloned policy has no data and wanders; offline RL joins the two demonstrations.

What to watch for. The map stays still; only the paths change. The data are an operator’s walk from A to B (10 steps, with a stray step at the start) and another’s from B to C (12 steps). Asked to go from A to C, the cloned policy finds no step in the data that was on the way to C from A, so it acts at random and circles near A until its 40 steps run out. Offline RL treats the data as a set of moves: from A it follows the first demonstration down through the door, switches to the second where they meet, drops the stray step, and arrives in 16 steps, which is also the shortest path in the building (16 steps). Neither demonstration does that; together they contain it.








Figure 5: First toy: share of the 30 landmark-to-landmark tasks solved within 40 steps, against the number of operator trajectories (mean ± standard error over 8 seeds). Right: extra steps over the shortest path, on the tasks solved.





With 8 trajectories, cloning solves 44% of the 30 tasks and offline RL 72%; with 32, 83% against 100% (Figure 5). Cloning can only repeat a route some operator took from here to the goal, stray steps included: even on the tasks it solves it takes 4.5 extra steps at 32 trajectories, where offline RL takes 0.2. Offline RL joins pieces of different trajectories and drops their detours, so it can beat every operator. With only 2 trajectories there is little to join, and the two are close (0.19 and 0.23). Where a policy has no data for its goal, both move at random, so a few of these successes are luck.


The data flywheel, and why mixing data naively fails
The holy grail is a data flywheel: better models make more capable robots, which get deployed more widely, which produce more data, which make better models ▶ 31:16. The obvious way to start it is to co-train on the expert’s demonstrations and the robot’s own rollouts ▶ 31:47. It is harder than it looks: expert data are smooth, dense and near-optimal; autonomous rollouts are longer, jerkier and often sub-optimal, and naively cloning both confuses the model ▶ 32:18 ▶ 32:49. New algorithms are needed that learn from all of a robot’s experience, good or bad, and never throw data away ▶ 33:21.

Figure 6: The data flywheel, after the lecture. The step that decides whether it turns is the learning algorithm: it must extract signal from mixed-quality autonomous data without being dragged down by it.





The second toy runs the flywheel in the same building. A human operator gives 6 demonstrations of one task, always the long way round: down through the left door and along the corridor, 6–8 steps longer than the shortest route through the opening between the rooms. Then each round the robot is deployed 10 times from random places, exploring a little (a random move 20% of the time), its rollouts join the data, and it is retrained in one of three ways: clone everything; clone the expert plus only the rollouts that succeeded; or offline RL on everything.








Figure 7: Second toy: the policy after each round of deployment, evaluated from every cell of the building (mean over 8 seeds). Left: success within 30 steps. Right: mean steps over the shortest path, a failure counting as 30. Round 0 uses the expert’s demonstrations only.





All three start at the same policy (success 0.83; the expert’s demonstrations cover only the left room and the corridor). Cloning everything gets worse every round, ending at 0.64 with 10.0 extra steps: after 8 rounds the expert’s data are 7% of the total, and the policy is mostly copying its own exploration noise (Figure 7). Cloning only the successes avoids the decline but barely improves (0.86), since a successful rollout is still a wandering one. Offline RL uses every transition, including those of failed rollouts, and reaches 1.00 with 2.2 extra steps, shorter than the operator’s own habit: the robot’s exploration found the opening the operator never used.


Learning for a lifetime, adapting in a moment
The flywheel is one face of lifelong learning: a robot should keep improving from its experience, while today a model is trained, frozen and deployed ▶ 33:52. Fine-tuning on deployment data must also avoid forgetting what the model already knew ▶ 34:56. The immediate version is rapid adaptation: a new home robot struggles with the fridge handle; a word (“grasp a bit more to the left”) or a quick demonstration placed in the model’s context should be enough, without retraining, which is in-context learning for robots (Week 10’s ICRT) ▶ 35:27 ▶ 36:31.
Mobility raises its own questions. Mobile manipulators today navigate with a classical mapping-and-localization stack and switch hard to a learned policy only for manipulation ▶ 37:03. Open: one model for the whole body; how to represent a building (a 3-D map, a bird’s-eye view, a topological graph, or just a walk-through video in context) and cope with its changes ▶ 38:07; and memory at scale: what to store from streams of video, touch and language, at what time scale, and what to forget ▶ 39:40 ▶ 40:41. Example 1 shows why keeping everything is not an option. First steps from the lecturer’s group include VLMaps (vision-language features in a 3-D map) and LeLaN (navigation learned from YouTube videos, improving with more of them) ▶ 41:11. The lecture’s summary: embodied reasoning, dexterous mobile manipulation, lifelong learning and rapid adaptation are the pillars that must stand for robotics to work outside demo videos ▶ 42:45.


How to do research
The lecture’s second half is advice, and worth reading as such ▶ 43:45.

Uncomfortable facts. Most research is incremental (self-driving rests on 40 years of work); most ideas never become papers; most papers don’t stand the test of time; and in a world where scale matters, simple ideas have more impact because they scale ▶ 44:17 ▶ 45:51.
A good problem is important and comes with a plan of attack: “cure cancer” has no plan, and +1% on a saturated benchmark is not important. Ask what success would unlock ▶ 46:22.
Excitement carries you through failed experiments and rejections ▶ 47:56. Be your own reviewer two: before months of work, name the most likely reason the idea fails, to protect your time ▶ 48:59.
Problem-driven beats method-driven for a PhD: if a method fails you still have the problem ▶ 50:01.
Practice: start with something that must work, such as overfitting, then make it harder; visualize inputs and outputs; talk to people early; share results, code and data; polish figures; don’t over-hype ▶ 51:37 ▶ 52:40 ▶ 53:43.

He ended with his own PhD: frustrated by a pipeline of disjoint ROS modules and a robot that would not calibrate before a deadline, he set out to build one end-to-end, language-conditioned policy, spent a year building the robot setup, then a simulator to iterate faster, which, polished almost as an afterthought, became the CALVIN benchmark ▶ 54:45 ▶ 57:53.

title: Week 11 · Frontiers & Open Problems
text:
Key concepts & formulae

Imitation and its bound

\[
\hat\pi_{\text{BC}}(a \mid s) = \frac{N(s, a)}{\sum_{a'} N(s, a')}
\tag{1}\]

In words. With a table of states, the maximum-likelihood cloned policy takes each action as often as the data did in that state. A neural network smooths this between states, but where the data never act it has nothing to copy.
Term by term.

\(N(s, a)\): how many times the data take action \(a\) in state \(s\).
If \(\sum_{a'} N(s, a') = 0\), the state is unseen and the policy is undefined; the toys act at random there.
Why it holds. Maximizing \(\sum \log \pi(a \mid s)\) over the data, separately in each state, gives the empirical frequencies (the maximum-likelihood estimate of a categorical distribution).


\[
\mathcal{L}(\pi) = -\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{D}} \sum_{t < t'} \log \pi(a_t \mid s_t, g = s_{t'})
\tag{2}\]

In words. Any state a trajectory reached later counts as a goal that its earlier actions were heading for.
Term by term.

\(\tau = (s_0, a_0, s_1, \dots)\): a trajectory in the data set \(\mathcal{D}\).
\(g = s_{t'}\): a later state used as the goal. The toy uses landmarks as goals, so only \(t'\) where the trajectory is at a landmark count.
The bound: a pair (start, goal) is covered only if one trajectory goes from the start to the goal. Two trajectories that meet in the middle do not combine.


\[
V(s) = \min_{(s, a, s') \in \mathcal{D}} \big[\, 1 + V(s') \,\big], \qquad V(g) = 0
\tag{3}\]

In words. The cost-to-go from \(s\) is one step plus the cost-to-go of the best next state the data show you can reach from \(s\).
Term by term.

\((s, a, s') \in \mathcal{D}\): a transition seen in the data, from any trajectory.
\(1\): the cost of a step; \(g\): the goal.
Why it stitches. The minimum runs over transitions from all trajectories: a value computed along trajectory 2 flows back into trajectory 1 wherever they share a state. In a deterministic world with unit costs, the solution is the length of the shortest path through observed transitions, which the toy finds by breadth-first search. With randomness and function approximation, offline RL methods solve an approximate version, which is where most of the difficulty lies (Weeks 4 and 5).



Learning from your own experience

\[
\text{expert share after } k \text{ rounds} = \frac{N_e}{N_e + k\, M}
\tag{4}\]

In words. A fixed set of demonstrations is diluted by every round of autonomous data.
Term by term. \(N_e\): expert episodes; \(M\): autonomous episodes per round; \(k\): rounds. Numeric check. In the toy, \(N_e =\) 6 and \(M =\) 10, so after 8 rounds the expert’s share is 7%. A method that weights data equally ends up imitating mostly itself.


Knowing what you don’t know

\[
u(o) = \sum_{j} \operatorname{std}_{m = 1..E}\big[\pi_m(o)_j\big]
\tag{5}\]

In words. Ask several independently trained policies what to do; the more their answers spread, the less the data pinned the answer down.
Term by term.

\(\pi_m\): the \(m\)-th member, trained on its own bootstrap resample of the data from its own initialization; \(E\) is the ensemble size, 5 in the toy.
\(\pi_m(o)_j\): action dimension \(j\) for observation \(o\).
What it can and cannot see. Members agree where the data constrain them and diverge elsewhere, so \(u\) grows for inputs unlike the training data. If the input looks like training data but the world has changed, all members are wrong together and \(u\) stays small (the moved post).


\[
\text{act if } u(o) \le \tau, \qquad \text{coverage} = P\big(u \le \tau\big), \qquad \text{selective success} = P\big(\text{success} \mid u \le \tau\big)
\tag{6}\]

In words. Act on what you are sure of and hand over the rest; a good uncertainty signal keeps selective success high while coverage is large.
Term by term. \(\tau\): the threshold; coverage: the share of tasks the robot takes on; selective success: its success on those. Sweeping \(\tau\) traces the curve of Figure 4.


Vision pre-training (guest)

\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CLIP}} = -\frac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \log \frac{e^{t\, x_i \cdot y_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{t\, x_i \cdot y_j}} + \log \frac{e^{t\, x_i \cdot y_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{t\, x_j \cdot y_i}} \right]
\tag{7}\]

In words. In a batch of \(n\) image-caption pairs, each image must pick out its own caption among all \(n\) captions, and each caption its own image.
Term by term.

\(x_i\), \(y_i\): normalized embeddings of image \(i\) and caption \(i\); \(x_i \cdot y_j\) their cosine similarity.
\(t\): a learned temperature.
The two terms: a softmax over each row (image to captions) and over each column (caption to images) of the \(n \times n\) similarity matrix.


\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SigLIP}} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \log \sigma\big(z_{ij} (t\, x_i \cdot y_j + b)\big), \qquad z_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j \\ -1 & i \ne j \end{cases}
\tag{8}\]

In words. Every image-caption pair is a separate yes/no question: do these two belong together?
Term by term. \(\sigma\): the logistic sigmoid; \(b\): a learned bias, which starts very negative because almost all pairs are negatives; \(z_{ij}\): the label. No normalization over the batch, so batches can be split across devices freely.

\[
P(\text{another example with property } f) = 1 - (1 - f)^{n - 1}
\tag{9}\]

In words. To learn a distinction, the batch must contain an example that differs only in that distinction; if such examples are rare, the loss can be solved without learning it.
Term by term. \(f\): the fraction of the data with the property (say, another picture of a cat and a dog); \(n\): batch size. See Example 2.

\[
\text{tokens} = \text{seconds} \times \text{frames per second} \times \text{tokens per frame}
\tag{10}\]

In words. Keeping every frame in context grows linearly with time, so it cannot last a deployment. Term by term. All three factors are design choices; the last is set by the image encoder (a few hundred tokens per image is typical of the VLMs in this course).

Worked examples

Example 1: how long can a robot remember?
Suppose each camera frame costs 256 tokens (a ViT on a 16 × 16 grid of patches, as in Week 7).

A context of one million tokens, at 10 frames per second, holds 391 seconds, about 6.5 minutes, of video. A day at one frame per second needs 22 such contexts. Hence the lecture’s layers: dense recent frames for the next grasp, compressed semantic events (“opened the fridge, the milk is on the second shelf”) for task progress, and some form of long-term memory for a lifetime, with the questions of when to write and what to forget.


Example 2: why CLIP misses “left of”
The guest’s argument, in numbers. A CLIP batch of 32,768 pairs. Say one picture in 10,000 shows a cat and a dog together (\(f = 10^{-4}\)) and one in ten million shows a dog sitting to the left of a cat in a way a caption would describe (\(f = 10^{-7}\); both rates are illustrative).

With a cat-and-dog picture in the batch, the loss is usually solved by recognizing “cat” and “dog” alone: a second such picture is there 96% of the time, but the mirrored scene only 0.33% of the time. So the gradient almost never asks for “left of”. A captioner has to produce the word after “sitting”, which forces the distinction on every example. This is why the guest’s later encoders added a captioning loss.
